events.text: A prayer front reaches the Hall of No Shadow before dawn: ten thousand soldiers begging for a clear sky before a march. The Heralds argue over whose domain it falls in, since it has already rained on three.

effects.log: You answer it in person, which is unheard of, and by evening the marching road is quiet.

choices.text: Route it to the right god

effects.log: You send it on with a note. The god it lands on is irritated, then moved, and remembers who sent it.
It falls where it falls. Somebody far below wets their hair and calls it a blessing anyway.

events.text: The offerings of the month are weighed in the Hall of No Shadow. The greatest is a mirror the size of a lake, polished by a whole province. The smallest is a bronze button from a child's coat, left by someone who plainly had nothing else.

effects.log: The great offering is honoured with a hymn. It is a good hymn, and the province that gave it will hear of it for centuries.
You hold up the smallest offering before the whole of the Will of Heaven. Nobody says anything. Several look at their shoes.
You carry both to the fire and send them up in one smoke. It is the one thing that day nobody argues about.

events.text: At the Noon Unveiling the seating plan of the Will of Heaven is wrong: Mujin of the Thousand Banners has been placed below Cheonho Who Hangs the Stars, and all of the Hall of No Shadow pretends not to look. The Herald in charge has gone the colour of ash.

effects.log: You swap them with one sleeve. Nobody sees, which is the only way it works, and the Herald sobs into a ledger.
Watching is educational. By the soup course you have learned who owes whom across ten thousand years.
It is a scandal for a day. Then it is the custom, and nobody can remember it ever being otherwise.

events.text: A mortal far below prays to the Will of Heaven with real rudeness: "Come down and look at what the storm did to my roof." The prayer is not wrong, only unmannerly, and it has sat on the pile in the Hall of No Shadow for a week.

effects.log: You answer. The mortal faints, which counts as a conversion, and tells it at every wedding afterward.
You grant it, with a small teaching attached. It is received with more manners than it was sent.
You file it under Complaints, Justified. The Heralds have a whole shelf.

events.text: A tally-god from outside the Will of Heaven comes to count the faith owed to the Hall of No Shadow and finds two lamps lit that nobody can account for. The tally-god writes this down in a very small hand.

effects.log: You tell it straight. The tally-god looks up for the first time in a century and says only, "Ah."
The feast is long, and the tally-god leaves with a lighter ledger and a heavier stomach.
You find the error before the tally-god does, and are thanked in a tone that suggests it was nearly a crime.

events.text: Far below, mortals have built a temple to the Will of Heaven and got it wrong: the roof has a hole over the altar, so the light gets in, and the rain. The prayers it sends up arrive slightly bent, and the Heralds have grown fond of them.

You leave it as it is. Its prayers keep arriving bent, and are still the first read of the morning.
You bless it, flaw and all. The flaw becomes a feature of the faith by the next generation.

events.text: A guest from another pantheon admires the Standing Lamp aloud and asks, very politely, what it is for. The honest answer is: to be looked at, mostly.

events.text: A domain stands unattended: its god sleeps, and prayers pile in the Hall of No Shadow like snow against a door. A Herald with a tin trumpet keeps watch over the heap.

choices.text: Call on the ones still here

effects.log: You go door to door. Some are glad, some are only polite, and one of them weeps.

choices.text: Carry on as if no time passed

effects.log: You carry on, and it works, which is the best and the worst thing about being old.

events.text: A thousand years pass in the Root Hall between one council and the next, and you notice only because the sapling in the courtyard now needs a ladder to be seen.

effects.log: You take stock of all that has changed and all that has not. The second list is longer, and more frightening.

choices.text: Call on the ones still here

effects.log: You go door to door. Some are glad, some are only polite, and one of them weeps.

choices.text: Carry on as if no time passed

effects.log: You carry on, and it works, which is the best and the worst thing about being old.

events.text: A god of the Will of Heaven chooses to fade, and asks you to witness it in the Hall of No Shadow. Their last request is to be looked at until the last light goes.

effects.log: You grant it. They go slowly, and gladly, and a small light stays on in the hall for a year.
You ask them to stay. They smile and do not, but they tell you things before they go that you would not otherwise know.
You witness in silence. It is the longest hour of your life, and you carry every minute of it.

events.text: A god of the Silent Hall chooses to fade, and asks you to witness it in the Hall of Unspoken Names. Their last request is to be remembered wrongly, so someone has to ask.

effects.log: You grant it. They go slowly, and gladly, and a small light stays on in the hall for a year.
You ask them to stay. They smile and do not, but they tell you things before they go that you would not otherwise know.
You witness in silence. It is the longest hour of your life, and you carry every minute of it.

events.text: A god of the Green Assembly chooses to fade, and asks you to witness it in the Root Hall. Their last request is to be planted.

effects.log: You grant it. They go slowly, and gladly, and a small light stays on in the hall for a year.
You ask them to stay. They smile and do not, but they tell you things before they go that you would not otherwise know.
You witness in silence. It is the longest hour of your life, and you carry every minute of it.

events.text: The Hall of No Shadow has, by law, no shadows. Today a visiting votary of the Silent Hall stands in the doorway and leaves a long, clear, undeniable one across the floor. Forty gods stare at it as if it were a spill.

effects.log: You step over the shadow and stand in it. The hall exhales, and the votary leaves very quickly, apologising to the floor.
A cloud of lamps is brought and the shadow is, with a good deal of ceremony, lit out of existence. It will be told for ages.
You crouch beside it for an hour. It is the first shadow you have seen in a thousand years, and it is more interesting than anything else in the hall.

events.text: Once a century Mujin of the Thousand Banners counts the banners, and once a century the count is a thousand and one. Nobody has ever found the extra. It is wrapped, with some care, and put on a shelf, and the shelf is now quite full.

effects.log: The shelf holds nine banners from nine centuries, each a little different. You learn more about Mujin's temper from them than from any sermon.
You suggest counting backwards. It is tried, and the count is a thousand and one, but you are thanked for the idea.
You fly the extra banner from your own door for a day. It draws more attention than anything you have done in an age.

events.text: A star hangs a little crooked over the eastern mortals, and Cheonho Who Hangs the Stars has been seen looking at it for a century with hands folded. It turns out Cheonho is too proud to ask for a ladder.

effects.log: You bring a ladder, and say nothing, and Cheonho steps on it without a word. The star is straight by morning. A star-shaped candle is left at your door.
Cheonho talks for six hours about the star's temper. You come away knowing a great deal about the sky and rather less about ladders.
It stays crooked. Poets below take it for an omen, which is better than the truth, and some of them are right.

events.text: The First Hearth of Hwarin has never gone out, and the cook-gods who feed it say this is a burden, not an honour. You are asked to sit a night-watch on it. It turns out the work is mostly listening to it complain.

effects.log: You sit all night. The fire says a great deal about wood, and at dawn you realise you are warmer than you have been in an age.
You feed it a page of a forgotten hymn. It flares, and then it hums, and the cook-gods weep with relief.
You decline. A cook-god sighs in a way you will hear for decades, and then learns to like the next volunteer.

events.text: Mirrors arrive from below by the cartload, polished for the Will of Heaven by mortals who cannot imagine it has no use for them. In the pile you find one that shows you as you were, in your mortal life, thousands of years ago.

effects.log: You look until the mirror clouds. The face is a stranger's, and it is also yours, and you do not tell anyone in the hall about it.
You hang it where all can see. A dozen gods pass by and none can say what face they see, but each leaves quieter than they came.
You send it back. A year later a poet far below claims it fell from heaven to teach him humility. It is the best publicity the hall has had.

events.text: In the Will of Heaven, to rule is to be seen, so the gods keep a rota: whoever is on duty stands in the great window for an hour while the mortals look up. Your hour is the dull one, the middle of an ordinary afternoon.

effects.log: You stand perfectly still for the hour. Somewhere below, a mother tells her child you are the kind that listens. You will never know which one.
You do a small, graceful, unplanned thing with a sleeve. A whole valley will build a dance around it.

choices.text: Send in a Herald to stand for you

effects.log: A Herald stands in your place. The mortals look up and, to everyone's alarm, like the Herald better.

events.text: On the same night, the general of a river kingdom and the general of the kingdom across the river pray to Mujin of the Thousand Banners for victory, in almost the same words. The prayers arrive at the same hour, and the Heralds fan out to find you.

effects.log: You answer both with the same message: that Mujin is not a coin to be flipped. Both generals are baffled, and neither fights quite as hard.

choices.text: Answer the one with the lesser army

effects.log: You nudge the odds toward the weaker side. They win by an inch, and the other general demotes a staff officer.
You let the two prayers sit. The battle is fought. The Heralds say nothing, but the one on the left bows lower than usual.

events.text: Cheonho was a breath late with the dawn this morning, and a lot of people noticed. Mortals below are saying it is an omen. In the Hall of No Shadow, the omen is that Cheonho is mortified, and the petitions are piling up.

effects.log: You tell the Heralds the dawn was precisely on time. Cheonho never says thank you, but a very clear sunrise is delivered to your door.
You let the omen run. The mortals' piety shoots up, and Cheonho never forgives you, quite.
Cheonho admits, grudgingly, that a lark was singing a very good song. You write the lark's name down.

events.text: A rumour goes round the halls of the Will of Heaven that there is a shadow behind the sun, and in it a court of gods who meet in the dark. Nobody will say where they heard it. Everybody has an opinion.

effects.log: Nobody will tell you anything. But three of them stop talking when you come near, and that is a start.
You dismiss it loudly. The rumour grows quietly, as rumours do under a laughing contempt.
You start a small, quiet list of what you notice. By the end of the century it is longer than you like.

events.text: Herald Seon-ah is learning the trumpet, and the whole Hall of No Shadow knows it. The fanfare of the Noon Unveiling is due, and Seon-ah's tone has the quality of a goose being let out of a bag.

effects.log: You coach for a week. By the Unveiling the fanfare is nearly a fanfare, and Seon-ah looks at you as at a mountain.
A trumpeter is hired. Seon-ah says nothing about it for a century, then once, quietly, thanks you for the dignity.
It is bad. It is also the most-discussed Unveiling in an age, and a visiting god weeps with laughter.

events.text: The great windows of the Will of Heaven are polished so well that visiting gods have to be given tinted glass. One, a minor goddess of dusk, walks into a pillar. She is very gracious about it, and a little bruised.

choices.text: Offer your sleeve to steer her

effects.log: You guide her through the hall by the sleeve. She says it was the only time anyone has led her anywhere in an age.
The windows are dimmed for guests. The hall grumbles, and then begins to like the softer light.

choices.text: Say it is her own fault

effects.log: You say so. She laughs, and you realise it was a test of your temper, and you have been marked either way.

events.text: A great god of war is retiring, gently, to the quiet life of a minor garden god. The Will of Heaven gives them a parade, which they hate, and a gift, which is a plough. They look at the plough for a long moment, and then pick it up.

effects.log: You give the speech. It is short and true, and the retiring god nods once, which is the best review you have ever had.

choices.text: Tend their garden for a year

effects.log: You help with the first season of the garden. It is the most peaceful year of your long life, and the beans are excellent.
You stay out of it. The god never mentions it, but a bean arrives in your sleeve a century later.

events.text: Hwarin of the First Hearth preaches the Sermon of Small Fires: that a candle in a window is a bigger miracle than a burning city. The hall nods. Afterward a Herald asks, in private, what Hwarin does about the burning cities.

effects.log: Hwarin says, quietly, that the sermon is the part they can do. You are the first one to have asked in a very long time.

choices.text: Tell the Herald to ask elsewhere

effects.log: You tell the Herald it is not their place. The Herald goes pale, and the question keeps living in the hall regardless.
You light a candle in a mortal window far below, in the middle of a burning town. It is a small thing and it is remembered.

events.text: A prayer reaches the Will of Heaven scorched at the edges, still smoking. It reads, in a child's hand, 'please make it stop'. There is nothing else on it, and there is no one near to ask what it was.

effects.log: You follow it down, and the fire is a small one, in a stable, and a goat is saved. You do not explain how.
Hwarin reads it, folds it, and keeps it, and the hall's fire never smokes again in your presence.
You file it with the others. The shelf is thick, and you add a small note to your own conscience.

events.text: A crane flew too high this morning and has been seen, by mortals, to touch the edge of the sky. Cheonho wants it reprimanded. The crane, brought before the hall, says only that it was curious, and that the sky was softer than it looked.

effects.log: You plead for the crane, and it is let go. It never flies that high again, but it tells the other cranes, who do.
The crane is reprimanded, kindly, and sent home. It sulks for a decade and then writes a poem about it.
The crane describes the sky's edge for an hour. It is beautiful, and you wish you had gone yourself.

events.text: The Lamp-Warden, an old god called Ilbo, keeps the Standing Lamp lit through the long night, and has done for eleven thousand years. At three in the morning, Ilbo says, the lamp is the only company either of them has. You are invited to sit up.

effects.log: You sit up. Ilbo talks about the lamp as one speaks of an old friend, and at dawn you have a new respect for a job nobody sees.
You take a shift. It is harder than it looks, and Ilbo sleeps for the first time in a century.
You admire it very much and leave. Ilbo, polite, looks at the lamp, and the lamp does not look back.

events.text: The Votary's exam of the Will of Heaven is held in full glare, because to be tested is to be seen. A candidate freezes and stands, silent, for an hour. They have been told that in this pantheon, to be seen is to be, and they are clearly being seen to a fault.

effects.log: You step in front, taking the glare. The candidate recovers, and passes, and does not forget.
You let the examiners wait. The candidate, after an hour, says one very good thing, and passes by a hair.
You call it unjust. The hall grumbles, and next age the exam is held in dimmer light.

events.text: The Will of Heaven and the Throne of Storms are trading polite insults: the sun-gods have 'left some weather in the cupboard', and the storm-gods hope the sun is 'well, since it is so seldom heard'. You are asked to deliver the next insult.

effects.log: You deliver it perfectly, with the proper bow. The storm-gods are delighted and send a better one, and so it goes for a thousand years.
You soften it. The storm-gods notice and are insulted that it was softened, which is a victory of sorts.
You propose an armistice. It lasts three weeks and is considered a historic achievement.

events.text: The honour guard of the Will of Heaven drills in the high wind, and a banner takes a young recruit clean off the ground. They are hauled down by the ankles, bright red, and the whole guard salutes with studied calm.

effects.log: You steady the recruit and say it happened to Mujin once. It did not. The recruit is happier regardless.
You drill with the guard for a week. You are not good at it, and by the end you are somewhat better.
You watch. It is, honestly, one of the finest sights of the age, and you are the only one who says so.

events.text: A mortal king far below claims descent from the Will of Heaven, on the grounds that his grandmother was kind to a stranger once. The Heralds are amused. The stranger, if there was one, is not known to any god in the hall.

effects.log: You look into it. The stranger was a travelling lamp-seller, mortal, and a decent sort. The king's line turns out to be better than most.
You send a small sign. The king rules a little better for a generation, and puts up a statue of the lamp-seller.
You ignore it. The king, unrebuked, does decently, and his heirs less so.

events.text: A small clear shadow lies under one of the pillars in the Hall of No Shadow. It is the wrong shape for a pillar. Herald Seon-ah finds you at once, whispering, and asks, very much against protocol, that you not tell Mujin.

effects.log: You report it. Mujin, who has not seen a shadow in ten thousand years, looks at it with an expression you cannot read, and says only: leave it.

choices.text: Say nothing, and look into it

effects.log: You say nothing, and keep an eye on the pillar. The shadow, when you watch it, is sometimes a little smaller.
You walk on. A shadow is only a shadow, and the hall has other ills to be about.

events.text: You find the owner: Dusk-Wren, a minor god of the evening hour, who has lived in the shade of that pillar for three centuries to be near the light. They are terrified. They have been sweeping the hall at night so nobody would notice they are there.

choices.text: Give them a corner of the hall

effects.log: You give them a corner of a side-room, and a lamp with a green shade. Dusk-Wren weeps, and the hall is, you suspect, a little kinder for it.
You report Dusk-Wren. They are courteously escorted out, and the pillar's shadow fades by the next week, but not from your memory.

choices.text: Ask what they know of the dark

effects.log: Dusk-Wren whispers of a shadow beyond the sun, and of a place that gods go when they are done with being seen. You write nothing down.

events.text: Four hundred years on, the corner in the side-room has become the one place in the Hall of No Shadow where everyone, secretly, goes to rest their eyes. The Council demands to know why the hall's glare has a shaded alcove in it, and Dusk-Wren stands very still beside you.

effects.log: You defend it, saying that a hall which rules by being seen must have a place to be not seen. The Council grumbles, and then, in private, uses it.
Dusk-Wren speaks, haltingly, for the first time in four centuries. It is not eloquent. It is the most moving thing the Council hears that age.
You let the alcove go. Dusk-Wren leaves quietly the next morning, and the pillar casts a long, thin shadow in their honour.

events.text: Gobae, the Banner Quartermaster, finds that Mujin's Thousand Banners number nine hundred and ninety-nine, and for the first time in ten thousand years the count is short. Gobae, who has never lost a thing, comes to you grey in the face and asks you to find it before Mujin hears.

effects.log: You take it on. The banner's last inventory is two thousand years old, and its trail is by that mark cold, but not dead.
Gobae does, and Mujin takes it with a stillness that frightens the whole hall. Gobae is not dismissed, only watched.
A junior is sent. They return with the wrong banner, which is, curiously, also missing.

events.text: The banner is found far below, flying above a village that has never been at war. The villagers say it dropped from the sky a thousand years ago and has kept the wolves off since. They have made it the centre of a festival. They do not know the name of Mujin.

effects.log: You take it back at dawn, quietly. The village is bereft, and the wolves return, and you hear of it for centuries.

choices.text: Leave a sign and a copy

effects.log: You leave a sign of favour and a copy of the banner, and take the original. The village believes the copy is the original, which is a kind of miracle.
You report it as lost. Mujin knows, and says nothing, and nine hundred and ninety-nine banners are counted from then on.

events.text: Mujin sends for you. The Thousand Banners stand in a single great row, and Mujin asks, in a low voice, about the one that went to a village. You find you have to choose between a truth, and a kindness, and a long career.

effects.log: You tell the whole story. Mujin listens, and then does something you did not expect: smiles, very slightly, and asks the name of the village.
You say it is lost. Mujin knows you are lying, and thanks you for the courtesy, which is worse than anger.

choices.text: Offer to go and get it

effects.log: You offer to fetch it yourself. Mujin sends you, and you come back with the banner and a basket of village bread.

events.text: Cheonho has dropped a star. It was a little one, from the eastern edge, and it fell somewhere over the mortals. Cheonho, ashen, asks quietly whether anyone might go and retrieve it, as it would be a pity if it were noticed. You are the only god in the room who is not looking at the floor.

effects.log: You go down. The star lies in a lake, cooling, and the lake's whole village is on its knees along the shore.
A Herald goes and comes back a century later, ruffled, with no star and a good story.
You say it is Cheonho's star. Cheonho does not go, and the star lies in the lake an age.

events.text: The star is worshipped now: the lake villagers call it the Quiet Light, and a small temple stands beside it. A woman keeps the lamp there and says the Light has told her things. Everything she says is true, and nobody in heaven has told her any of it.

choices.text: Take the star back, as ordered

effects.log: You take it, and the temple's light goes out, and the keeper sits down on the step, not weeping, only still. You wish it were weeping.

choices.text: Leave it, and tell Cheonho it is lost

effects.log: You leave it, and make a report. Cheonho looks at the sky, where a star is missing, and does not ask.

choices.text: Ask the keeper what the light told them

effects.log: She tells you a thing that you had thought only you knew. You do not stay long.

events.text: A thousand years later the star is a pilgrimage, and the temple a small town. A new Herald of the Will of Heaven asks, with open eyes, why there is a star in the lake that is not on any chart. Cheonho is standing at your shoulder, and has just heard.

effects.log: You tell it. Cheonho says nothing for a time and then says, to the star, quite gently: I did not know you had been so well kept.

choices.text: Say it is a very old star

effects.log: You say it is old, and prized, and that is true enough. Cheonho gives you a look that is half thanks and half threat.
Cheonho, to the Herald's astonishment, goes down to the lake that night, in plain sight. The town does not stop talking for a thousand years.

events.text: High Votary Dalgwi has been a High Votary of the Will of Heaven for nine thousand years and wishes, quietly, to be Throne-Bearer. Dalgwi asks for your word at the next council. They say it with an air of having asked a great many gods, and been told the same thing.

choices.text: Give your word, and mean it

effects.log: You give it, and Dalgwi bows lower than a god of the hall should. You have made a friend, or a debtor, or a burden.
You say you will weigh it. Dalgwi nods, as if this was the answer expected, and leaves a small, perfect bronze mirror on your desk.

choices.text: Tell Dalgwi the truth about their chances

effects.log: You tell them gently that the Throne-Bearers do not rise by waiting. Dalgwi goes still, and then, slowly, thanks you.

events.text: The council is held. Dalgwi stands, and speaks for exactly the length of time allowed, and every word is perfect. It makes no difference whatever, because the seat has gone to someone who is simply louder. Dalgwi sits down, not smiling, and the whole hall pretends not to see.

choices.text: Speak up for Dalgwi after the vote

effects.log: You speak up, and make a small scene, and it is remembered. Dalgwi never says thanks, but you are seated beside them at every feast.
You keep your seat. The vote is the vote. Dalgwi does not look at you, then or later.
You invite them to dinner. They bring a mirror and two hundred years of grievances and, by dawn, a thaw.

events.text: Dalgwi, at last, is Throne-Bearer of the Will of Heaven: the loud god fell in a quarrel nobody explained, and the seat found the quiet one. At the ceremony, Dalgwi has one request: that you stand at their side, in plain sight, as the oldest of friends.

effects.log: You stand, and are seen, and Dalgwi's hand on your sleeve is as light as a lamp. It is the best moment of an age.

choices.text: Decline, to keep out of it

effects.log: You decline. Dalgwi hides the hurt and rules well, and you are one of the many in the crowd.

choices.text: Stand beside them, and give counsel

effects.log: You stand and give counsel, then and after. Dalgwi's reign is known as quiet, which in the Will of Heaven is the highest praise.

events.text: The Standing Lamp of the Will of Heaven gutters, once, in the night. The Lamp-Warden Ilbo goes the colour of old paper. The lamp has not flickered in eleven thousand years. Ilbo asks you, in a whisper, not to tell, until Ilbo can find out why.
events.arc: The Night of the Standing Lamp

effects.log: You keep it. The lamp is steady again by morning, but Ilbo's hands are not.
You tell. The Heralds fan out, and the whole hall learns of it by noon, and Ilbo, on the stairs, does not look at you.
You sit watch. The lamp stays bright, and Ilbo speaks of the first night, when the lamp was only an idea.

events.text: The lamp gutters again, longer. Ilbo has found that it is not the oil nor the wick: the lamp is tired. It has been seen by too many, for too long, and what is seen too much, thins. The whole premise of the Will of Heaven is in a single flame.
events.arc: The Night of the Standing Lamp

choices.text: Propose letting it be unseen for a year

effects.log: You propose a year of dark. It is a heresy, and Ilbo, after a long look, agrees.
A second lamp is lit. The first brightens, strangely, as though relieved. Ilbo is quietly furious.

choices.text: Say it is a trick of the light

effects.log: You say it is nothing. It is not nothing, and you both know it.

events.text: In the year of dark, the Hall of No Shadow has shadows. The gods find them unnerving, and a great many find them restful. A rumour goes about that in the shadow behind the sun, the Court of the Unlit Sun has noticed, and is amused. Ilbo, in a corner, sleeps.
events.arc: The Night of the Standing Lamp

effects.log: You hold the dark through the whole year, and answer every complaint. It is the hardest thing you have done, and it is right.
You light it early, to spare the hall's nerves. The lamp comes up pale, and Ilbo does not meet your eye.

choices.text: Visit the shadow behind the sun

effects.log: You go, quietly, to the edge of the light, and ask who is there. Something answers politely. You do not say what.

events.text: The lamp is relit at the Noon Unveiling, after a year of dark, and it burns clearer than anyone has seen. Ilbo is asked to speak, and stands for a long time, and then says: 'It is only a lamp. We looked after it. It looked after us.' The hall is very quiet.
events.arc: The Night of the Standing Lamp

effects.log: You rise first, and the hall rises after you, and the sound goes on a long time. It is remembered as the Night of the Lamp.
You stand at Ilbo's side. Ilbo's hand finds your sleeve, and is gone.

choices.text: Say nothing, and tend the lamp

effects.log: You tend the lamp that night yourself, and Ilbo sleeps, for the first time in eleven thousand years, all the way to morning.

events.text: Herald Seon-ah is the best-read Herald of the Will of Heaven, and also the shyest. In a pantheon that rules by being seen, Seon-ah has spent two thousand years standing a half-pace behind someone brighter. They ask, in a voice you have to lean in to hear, how one learns to stand in the light.
events.arc: The Herald Who Would Not Be Seen

effects.log: You offer. Seon-ah looks at you as if you had handed them the sun, and writes down every word you say.

choices.text: Tell them to stand where the light is

effects.log: You tell them it is all there is. Seon-ah nods and tries, and fails, and tries.

choices.text: Say that some gods are meant to stay behind

effects.log: You say it kindly. Seon-ah thanks you, and the corner they stood in is a shade darker afterward.

events.text: Seon-ah has been practising. At the Noon Unveiling, the Herald is to stand at the great window for a quarter-hour. They are shaking. They look at you across the hall, and you can see they are about to bolt, or to give the best quarter-hour of their life.
events.arc: The Herald Who Would Not Be Seen

choices.text: Stand in the window beside them

effects.log: You stand beside them. It is easier, and Seon-ah's quarter-hour passes in a kind of brightness, and when it is over they are weeping and radiant.
You nod. Seon-ah steadies, and stands alone, and when it is done there is applause, and Seon-ah looks at their own hands.
You look away. Seon-ah bolts, and is found in the lamp-room, and is not teased, because you intervene, too late.

events.text: Seon-ah is a High Votary now, very much seen, and says so wryly: 'It turns out being seen is mostly a matter of not minding it.' A minor god of the lower halls asks Seon-ah the same question Seon-ah once asked you. Seon-ah looks across the hall, straight at you.
events.arc: The Herald Who Would Not Be Seen

effects.log: You let them. Seon-ah's answer is better than yours was, and shorter, and the minor god bows.
You add a word, and the three of you stand there in the glare, none of you flinching.
You leave. It is theirs now, and has been for some time.

events.text: Seon-ah is made Throne-Bearer's Herald, which is not a throne, but nearly. At the ceremony, Seon-ah asks for you to be seated in the front row, and when the Will of Heaven rises to applaud, Seon-ah turns, bows to you, and is seen to do it by everyone.
events.arc: The Herald Who Would Not Be Seen

effects.log: You bow back, and the whole hall sees it. It is a small thing, and it is the thing the hall will talk about for an age.
You wave it away. Seon-ah smiles, and the Herald's bow, undeterred, is a lighter, happier thing the next time.
You sit back, in the shade of a pillar, and let Seon-ah have the whole of the room. It is enough.

events.text: Hwarin of the First Hearth has been asked to cook for the council of the three pantheons, and Hwarin, who has never cooked for more than a handful, is terrified in the way only fire-gods are: loudly and in all directions. You are asked to be the taster.

effects.log: You accept. The first course is a cinder, the second raw, and the third a marvel, and you note it all down as kindly as you can.

choices.text: Offer to help in the kitchen

effects.log: You help in the kitchen. Hwarin burns three pots and cannot be moved from the stove, but the soup is, in the end, the finest in a thousand years.
You refuse. Someone else tastes. The council is served a dish the Silent Hall describes as 'a lesson'.

events.text: The council feast goes well, which is to say nobody is hurt. Hwarin is offered the post of Hearth-Warden of the three pantheons, a high office, and Hwarin, in the middle of all the praise, looks at you, a flame guttering behind their eyes, and asks quietly whether they should.

effects.log: You say take it. Hwarin takes it, and the three pantheons eat better for ten thousand years, and fight less, though not by much.
You say refuse. Hwarin refuses, and goes back to the First Hearth, and is, for the first time in an age, very happy.
Hwarin asks the First Hearth. The fire says nothing, and then, gently, it crackles. Hwarin laughs and does as it likes.

events.text: Hwarin has come to a council with a small iron pot, and a quarrel between the pantheons that has gone on four hundred years. 'Sit,' says Hwarin, 'and eat. Nobody speaks until the pot is empty.' You find yourself, unexpectedly, at the head of the table.

effects.log: You keep it. The pot is emptied, and when it is, the quarrel has quietly died of embarrassment, as quarrels sometimes do.
You speak first. Hwarin looks at you, and the whole room does, and the pot goes cold.
You ladle for everyone, in order of age. It takes an hour and no one speaks, and that is its own peace.

events.text: Someone has written in the margin of the Long Ledger, in a small, crooked, living hand: 'Was this one kind?' It is beside the entry for a mortal tailor. In ten thousand years nobody has asked what a name was like, only that it was kept.

effects.log: You write 'Yes', in a hand as small as theirs. Nobody mentions it, but the next week there are four more questions in the margin and four answers.

choices.text: Find the one who wrote it

effects.log: You find an Incense Bearer, a young one, who is horrified and then relieved. You tell them to keep asking.
You rub it out. The Ledger is not for that. The mark will not quite come off, and stays faintly on the page, like a thumbprint.

events.text: The Reader of the Dead has read the Reading of the Dead for eleven thousand years, and this evening, at the forty-billionth name, the voice cracks. The whole Silent Hall hears it, and does not move, and nobody breathes, and the Reader, very quietly, goes on.

choices.text: Stand and take the next line

effects.log: You stand and read on, steady, for a quarter of an hour. The Reader sits, shaking, and at the end whispers a thanks you only half hear.
You hand them water, without a sound. It is the kindest thing anyone has done in the hall that age, and it is quietly remembered.
You keep still. It is the rule, and the Reader finishes, and later the rule feels a little thinner to you than it did.

events.text: Baekun the Pale Ferryman has crossed the river of the dead nine hundred billion times, and asks if you would take the oars for one crossing, for the experience. They say it with a perfectly straight face, and then, after a pause, add that it is a good job, mostly.

effects.log: You take the oars. The river is wide, and quiet, and the one passenger asks only that you not hurry. You do not.
Baekun, after a long silence, says it is like being at a very large wedding where everybody is going home. You do not forget that.
You decline. Baekun nods, and the oars are taken again, and you carry the offer around with you like a coin.

events.text: Your thread in the loom of Unmyeong the Weaver has tangled, as every god's does now and then: tied to a mortal's, in a place and an hour you do not remember. Unmyeong, shuttle in hand, says it is the tidiest knot they have seen, and asks if it should stay.

effects.log: You let it stay. Somewhere a mortal's whole life bends a little, and you feel it in an odd, warm way, for a century.

choices.text: Ask who it is tied to

effects.log: Unmyeong tells you. It is a surprise, and a small one, and not one you share.
Unmyeong cuts it, cleanly. You feel lighter, and then, a thousand years on, oddly lonely.

events.text: Mongsa the Sleeper has been sleeping for four thousand years, and the dreams leak. Tonight you are walking, quite clearly, through someone's dream of a bakery. The baker is very pleased to see you. It is not entirely clear that it is a dream.

effects.log: You buy a loaf, with dream coin, and it is the best bread you have eaten. You wake with crumbs on your sleeve and no explanation.

choices.text: Ask the baker who they are

effects.log: The baker says they are a dead woman, very old, and that this is how she is remembered, as a bakery. You are, for an hour, her most devoted customer.
You wake yourself, with effort. The bakery fades. In your hand is a small crust that does not melt.

events.text: In the Silent Hall, a cough is a scandal. A visiting Herald has coughed, and the whole Hall is looking at the floor with the fixed attention of those hearing a small bell struck. The Herald is mortified beyond speech.

effects.log: You cough, deliberately, in the silence. The Hall nearly dies. A very old god at the back starts to laugh, silently, shaking, and so does half the room.
You pass them a lozenge, noiselessly, from the sleeve. It is the oldest act of kindness the Hall knows.
You say nothing. The silence takes the cough in and carries on, as it always does, and the Herald does not come back for a century.

events.text: The Silent Hall keeps the names of the dead on river stones, one to a stone. Today a stone comes in with two names, scratched one over the other, so that neither can be read. Both families have sent a prayer. Neither can be told.

choices.text: Keep it as it is, two names

effects.log: You keep the stone as it is, and say that the Hall will remember both. It is not what the Ledger allows, and everyone is quietly relieved.
You choose by the older prayer, as is the rule. The other family's name is lost, and you remember it, privately, for the rest of your days.
You carve a second stone yourself. It takes a year and is slightly wrong, and it is perfect.

events.text: A ghost has arrived at the Hall of Unspoken Names, uninvited, from far below. It is a mortal, long dead, and insists, politely and without cease, that nobody has said their name for four hundred years and could the Hall please arrange for someone to.

effects.log: You say the name, once, clearly. The ghost thanks you and is gone, and the name is, for that one moment, the loudest thing in the Hall.
You enter it in the Ledger, in a good hand. The ghost watches, and nods, and leaves a smell of wet earth on the page.
You send the ghost to the Ferryman. It goes, uncomplaining, and a hundred years later you wonder whether you did right.

events.text: An erratum is found in the Book of Fates: a comma, in the fate of a sailor, three thousand years ago. It changes nothing, nobody died, and nobody can say whether the sailor would have turned left at a different comma. The Hall asks you to rule on whether to correct it.

effects.log: You correct it. The ink goes on, and a shiver goes through the page, and the sailor, wherever they are, turns left, or right, or never.
You leave it. A fate with a comma in it is still a fate, and the Hall nods, and a quiet note is made in the margin.
You send a dream to the sailor's descendants. The answer comes back in a lullaby: leave the comma.

events.text: The gods of the Silent Hall trade dreams, quietly, like pressed flowers. You are offered a swap: your dream of the home you had as a mortal, for one of the Sleeper's. Mongsa's is said to be a good one. It is also said to be very long.

effects.log: You swap. Mongsa's dream is a long walk across an empty field at dusk, and at the end of it you are, for a moment, entirely at peace.
You keep your own. It is smaller and warmer than you remembered, and you hold it a long time.
You offer a dream you have never had, a thing you made up. It is accepted, and for a thousand years someone dreams your invention.

events.text: The Silent Hall holds a Remembering contest, every age: whoever recalls the most of what the Hall has lost. You are in the final, against old Sori the Quiet, and you suddenly find that the thing you know best, you have forgotten, and the thing you have forgotten is a name.

effects.log: You admit it. The Hall, which has heard everything, has never heard a god admit a forgetting aloud, and the silence is respectful.
You guess. The guess is wrong in an interesting way, and the Hall remembers the mistake better than the name.
Sori, without a word, writes the name on a scrap and hands it over. The Hall is scandalised, and you win, and it feels like losing.

events.text: In a poor town far below, a widow lights a lamp every night for a man nobody else remembers. The prayer arrives each time, small as a moth. It has arrived for sixty years, and the Hall has never answered it. The widow is old now.

effects.log: You answer, the night before she dies, with a single warm word. She smiles in her sleep and does not wake, and the lamp goes out, unlit, at last.

choices.text: Enter the man in the Ledger

effects.log: You search, and find him: a drowned ferryman, entered wrongly. You correct the entry, and a quiet flame is lit in the Hall.
You leave it. The prayer is small, and the Hall is large, and you will think of the lamp, sometimes, in the long silences.

events.text: Herald Muk, who is the best whisperer in the Silent Hall, has been whispering lately in so quiet a voice that nobody can hear Muk at all. The Hall's business has slowed to a crawl. Muk, confronted, says, in a hush, that a loud word is a cruelty.

effects.log: You teach Muk, over a century, to be loud enough. It is lonely work, and Muk, when it is done, thanks you in a normal voice, which is a shock.
You learn to lip-read. The Hall's business flows again, and you become, quietly, the most informed god in it.
You appoint a reader. Muk gives a faint smile, and the two of them become the Hall's best-loved pair.

events.text: A visiting votary of the Will of Heaven finds the Hall of Unspoken Names too dark, and says so, repeatedly, with a lamp. The Silent Hall endures it with a politeness that is itself a sort of reproach. The votary's lamp, by the third hour, has gone mysteriously out.

effects.log: You relight it, quietly, and the votary leaves, bewildered, with no idea who was kind. You are, in the Hall, rather admired.
You let it stay out. The votary sits in the dark, and, to everyone's surprise, begins to listen, and the next age is a quieter one.

choices.text: Offer a tour of the dark

effects.log: You offer a tour of the dark rooms. The votary comes out three hours later, pale, thoughtful, and quite changed.

events.text: The Weaver has cut a thread in error, a thin one, of no fame, a shepherd on a hill. The mistake is noticed only after, and Unmyeong stands holding the end, very still. The Hall waits. To mend a cut thread is forbidden.

effects.log: You knot the thread, secretly, in the dark. The shepherd lives, and old, and never knows. Unmyeong never says a word, and sends a single grey thread to your door.

choices.text: Stand with Unmyeong at the rule

effects.log: You stand with Unmyeong while the Hall considers it. The shepherd's life ends with grace, and a quiet service is held in the weaving-room.

choices.text: Say the thread was thin anyway

effects.log: You say so. It is the truth, and a cold one, and Unmyeong looks at you a moment and then goes back to the loom.

events.text: The Silent Hall keeps a room of grey letters, written by the dead and never sent. Today the door is open, by a draught or a mistake, and a hundred letters are on the floor, each in its own hand. A young Incense Bearer is reading one, aloud, in tears.

effects.log: You gather every letter and put them back, without reading. The young one watches you, and later asks to learn how.
You read one. It is addressed to a daughter, and says only that the soup is on the stove. You close it, and say nothing for a long time.
You send one, down, into a dream. The recipient wakes weeping, and well, and nobody in the Hall scolds you.

events.text: The Silent Hall serves tea at the end of every council, cold, and in complete silence, and each guest must drink it down with no expression. A very old god has just been served theirs, tastes it, and, for the first time in four thousand years, wrinkles their nose.

effects.log: You wrinkle yours. The Hall bursts, silently, into a kind of fit, and the cold tea becomes, in spirit, a little less cold.
You say it is excellent, in a flat voice. The old god gives you a look of pure gratitude, and the Hall, bowing to form, resumes.
You ask for sugar. It is an outrage and a revelation, and sugar is found, in the end, in the third cupboard.

events.text: A god of the Silent Hall confides to you, over the cold tea, that they have been dreaming of being mortal: of a house, a window, a kettle. It is a very ordinary dream. They ask, in a whisper, whether this is allowed.

effects.log: You say it is allowed. They look at you, and then, slowly, at the wall, as if there were a window in it.
You say it is common. Their shoulders drop. It is the first thing in a thousand years that anyone has said to them that was simply true.
You say you will not tell. They nod, and a year later send you a kettle.

events.text: A death has come in for which the Book of Fates has no entry: a mortal, quite alive, quite unrecorded, died in a field, and nobody in the Hall can say where they were meant to be. The Hall looks, in unison, at the nearest god with free hands. You.

effects.log: You write the entry, in your best hand, and give them a fate that fits what happened. It is a strange feeling, to write a life backward.
Unmyeong, after a long silence, finds a loose thread in a far corner of the loom. It was theirs all along, and the entry is made.
You send them on, unwritten, to the Ferryman. It is irregular, and nobody can say it was wrong.

events.text: The Votary's exam of the Silent Hall is to recite the names of the dead without error, until the examiner raises a finger. A candidate has been reciting for seven days. The examiner, old Sori, has raised no finger, and appears to be asleep.

effects.log: You wake Sori with a touch. Sori raises a finger, quickly, and the candidate, who has memorised four million names, bursts into tears.
You let it run. On the ninth day the candidate stops of their own accord, and is, by Sori's finger, passed.
You recite beside them, softly, so they will not feel alone. You pass no exam by it, but the candidate does not forget.

events.text: A name has come up in the Ledger that nobody in the Silent Hall can place: Oh Duri, mortal, no dates, no trade, no kin. The Ledger Keeper, a thin god named Imsun, asks you to help find who kept it. Imsun has never been unable to place a name, and has gone a little bluish.

effects.log: You take it. The name is written, in the Ledger, in a hand that matches no god's, and that is a start.
You tell Imsun it is an error, and an old one. Imsun thanks you, and goes on worrying for three hundred years.
You pass it on. The junior finds nothing, and neither will they, and the name stays.

events.text: You find the trail: Oh Duri was a mortal bell-ringer in a small country town, dead nine thousand years, and kept in the Ledger by the town itself, who prayed her name aloud each year at a festival. The festival is still held. Nobody remembers what it is for.

choices.text: Go down and watch the festival

effects.log: You go down, in plain clothes, and stand at the back. A hundred people say 'Duri', and look at the sky, and eat dumplings.
You send a dream, in the shape of an old woman with a bell. The town wakes, and, struck, builds a bell-tower.
You leave it. A thing kept by a whole town does not need a god's help, and perhaps it does, and you will not know.

events.text: The town that remembered Oh Duri has, in its turn, been forgotten: a plague, a war, a long drift of centuries, and now only the festival's last echo lingers in one grey grandmother's songs. The Ledger Keeper brings you the dying entry, and asks, very low, whether the Hall can keep a name no mortal keeps.

effects.log: You decree the name kept, by the Hall itself, in perpetuity. It is the first name the Hall has ever adopted, and the Ledger shivers slightly.
You let it go, with a reading, and a lit lamp. It is the right end, and it hurts all the same.
You find, far down, a girl who rings a school bell. You do not tell her anything. The bell sounds, from then on, a little more like a name.

events.text: Baekun the Pale Ferryman asks you, as if it were nothing, to come down to the river of the dead on a certain night and 'hold a lantern'. That is all. Baekun will not say whose crossing it is. The Pale Ferryman, as a rule, does not ask for anything, and you cannot remember a time Baekun spoke first.

effects.log: You go, and hold it. The crossing is quiet, and long, and the one who crosses nods to you, in a way you will turn over for ages.
Baekun looks at you, the whole depth of that pale face, and says, 'A friend.' You go, and hold the lantern.
A Herald holds the lantern. Baekun does not ask again, and the river runs a little colder.

events.text: The passenger from that night, it turns out, was a god: an old one of the Silent Hall, gone to the river by choice. Baekun brings you their last gift, a small grey stone, and a message: 'They said you held the lantern steady.' The stone is warm, and has a name on it, which is not yours.

effects.log: You keep the stone. It is an odd weight in the sleeve, and sometimes it hums.
You enter the name, and place the stone in a niche. It is a small honour, and the Hall will not forget.
You give it back. Baekun takes it, nods, and puts it in the boat, among the oars, where it stays.

events.text: Ages later Baekun comes to the Hall, in plain daylight, and says the ferry has been rowed alone for too long. 'I will not ask you to take the oars,' says Baekun. 'I will ask you to sit in the boat.' It is the longest speech you have ever heard from the Pale Ferryman, and the quietest.

effects.log: You sit in the boat, and ride, and watch the river of the dead. It does not frighten you. It is, you find, mostly full of people going home.

choices.text: Offer to row a night a century

effects.log: You offer to row a night each century. Baekun takes it with a nod, and for the first time the oars are shared.
You say you are not ready. Baekun, without offence, says that is the right answer, and that they will ask again.

events.text: Unmyeong the Weaver comes to you at the loom, with a thread so long it is wound three times round a pillar. It belongs to a mortal, a nobody, who is, against every reckoning, still alive at four hundred. Unmyeong asks if you would be so kind as to look into it, because the Weaver does not like a thread that will not end.

effects.log: You trace the thread, down and down, to a small cottage and a very old man with a vegetable garden who does not know he is a mystery.
Unmyeong looks at you, appalled, and says that is not how it is done. You are not asked again.

choices.text: Suggest it is a clerical error

effects.log: You suggest the error is in the count. Unmyeong, a little relieved, adopts the theory and drops the matter.

events.text: The old man's name is Gu. He lives alone, and tends his beans, and says, when you visit in plain clothes, that he has outlived everyone, and that nobody has come to tell him it is time. He does not ask for more life. He asks, politely, whether there is a form to fill.

effects.log: You tell him the truth: that the Weaver lost his thread in a knot. He nods slowly, and says that explains the beans.

choices.text: Stay and help with the beans

effects.log: You stay a season and weed the rows. It is the most peaceful season of an age, and Gu says nothing of it.
You go. Gu looks up the road a long time after, as at a visitor who might have come back.

events.text: Gu is ready. He says so, in the garden, on a summer evening: the beans are in, and the garden is done, and he would like to go now. Unmyeong, at the loom, holds the shuttle still. The Weaver asks you to be the one to cut the thread, because Gu asked for you by name.

effects.log: You cut the thread. Gu goes in his chair, in the evening, with the sun on the beans. Unmyeong sits for a long time with the shuttle in their lap.

choices.text: Ask Gu to wait one more spring

effects.log: You ask. Gu gives you the look of an old man whose patience is a deep well, and says, 'One.' He sees it, and then he goes.
You hand the shears to Unmyeong. The Weaver's hands shake, and cut, and the loom is silent for a day.

events.text: Mongsa the Sleeper has begun dreaming aloud, and the dream has you in it. You walk into the Hall one morning, and everyone looks up, knowing you for a figure they have seen in the Sleeper's dream the night before. They are polite about it. A small crowd gathers.

choices.text: Ask what you did in it

effects.log: A Herald, blushing, says that you rescued a cat from a river. You have never rescued a cat.

choices.text: Say it was only a dream

effects.log: You say so, lightly. The crowd nods, and a few look disappointed, and the cat, they say, was very grateful.
You walk away. The whispers follow, politely, for about a century.

events.text: The dream has darkened. In it, you are walking through the Hall, and the Hall is empty, and the lamps are out, and a voice behind you is saying your name, over and over, in the voice of everyone you have ever lost. The Hall is anxious, and you are the only one who is not asleep.

choices.text: Go to the Sleeper and wake them

effects.log: You go to Mongsa's chamber, and put a hand on the sleeper's sleeve. The dream breaks, like ice, and Mongsa sits up, blinking, and apologises, again and again.

choices.text: Walk through the dream to its end

effects.log: You enter the dream, knowing, and walk it through. At the end is a small room with a table, and a cup, and your own name on it, and nothing worse.
You wait. The dream passes, as dreams do, and leaves a taste in the Hall for a year.

events.text: Mongsa asks you to sit with them, awake, beside the bed, and says the dream was theirs, and a dream of loneliness, and you were only the one who was near. 'A god who sleeps for four thousand years,' they say, 'wants to be told, on waking, that someone kept the lamp.'

effects.log: You say it, though it is not quite true, and Mongsa smiles, and sleeps, and the Hall is a kinder place.

choices.text: Tell the truth about the long sleep

effects.log: You tell the truth: the Hall has changed, and some of those who knew Mongsa are gone. The Sleeper cries, and is, afterward, lighter.
You stay the night. In the morning Mongsa wakes, and the first thing said is a thank you, and the first thing seen is a friend.

events.text: Mongsa the Sleeper wakes at last for good, and the Silent Hall holds a feast. At it, Mongsa presents you with a small, plain pillow, stitched, they say, from the best of their dreams, and warns you only that you will dream of cats. 'It was a kind dream,' they say, 'and you were in it.'

effects.log: You accept. That night you dream of a cat, a river, and a long lit road, and wake rested for the first time in an age.
You give Mongsa a lamp with a green shade. It stands by the bed, and the Sleeper, from then on, sleeps lightly.
You ask for the story of the first dream. Mongsa tells it for three nights, and it is the best you have heard.

events.text: High Votary Sori the Quiet took a vow of silence three thousand years ago, and kept it. The vow ends this winter. The Silent Hall, a place of silence, has, for the first time, a god who must now choose to speak. Sori asks, in writing, what they should say first.

effects.log: You write: 'Good morning.' Sori reads it for an hour and then folds it very small.
You write a name: the first name Sori ever kept. Sori reads it, and the hands that hold the paper tremble.
You write: 'Why break it?' Sori nods, and goes on, as ever, and the Hall hardly notices.

events.text: On the morning the vow ends, Sori opens their mouth, and nothing comes. The Hall waits in its best silence. Sori's eyes find you, in the crowd, and hold. They are frightened, and the whole Hall can see it, and are quite sure that not one of them will speak.

effects.log: You say it first. Sori's mouth, after a moment, forms the same words, and a sound comes out, thin and creaking, and the Hall, to a god, bows its head.

choices.text: Wait, and let them find it

effects.log: You wait. After a long time Sori speaks, quite alone, and the voice is smaller than anyone expected, and clear.

choices.text: Nod to the Herald to speak for Sori

effects.log: You nod. A Herald speaks, and Sori is spared, and never quite forgives you, or the Herald.

events.text: Sori speaks now, a little, and always to the point. At the council it is Sori who says what the Hall has been afraid of saying for an age: that the Silent Hall has been remembering the wrong dead, the grand ones, and forgetting the small. The Hall is not pleased. Sori looks at you, and waits.

effects.log: You rise, and say Sori is right. The Hall grumbles, and some of the oldest gods, quietly, agree, and a new Reading is begun for the small dead.
You back Sori in the corridor after. Sori nods, and says it is enough, and it is not, and both of you know.

choices.text: Say it is a matter for the Ledger

effects.log: You say it is a matter for the Ledger, and it is, and it is also a coward's answer. Sori says nothing.

events.text: The Reading of the Small Dead is held. It takes a thousand years, and Sori reads the first hour: a baker, a sweep, a girl who sold buttons. The Hall listens. When it is over, Sori turns to you and, in the plain voice that has become Sori's own, says 'Thank you for the morning.' The whole hall hears.

effects.log: You say you did nothing. Sori smiles, which is a thing the Hall had never seen, and says: 'Then it was a very good nothing.'

choices.text: Ask Sori to read the next hour

effects.log: Sori reads on, and you listen, and the Hall comes in, one by one, and sits.

choices.text: Add your own name to the Reading

effects.log: You write your own mortal name on the list, among the small dead. It is the right place for it.

events.text: The Long Ledger has, for the first time in its life, a second volume. The Hall is in an uproar of whispers. The Ledger Keeper, Imsun, is quite certain nobody has asked for it, and equally certain it has appeared, bound in grey, on the lectern. The first page is blank.

effects.log: You open it. The first page is blank, and then, as you watch, a name begins to appear, in a hand you know very well.
You close it. Imsun says nobody has the right to a second volume, and nobody has the right to refuse one, and the Hall, stalled, adjourns.
You leave it. By morning there is a line in it, and by evening three, and the Hall, helplessly, begins to read.

events.text: The second volume fills as the century goes on, and its entries are not names but small facts: a smell of bread, a joke, the colour of a mortal's door. It is the Ledger of what the dead were like. The Hall does not know who keeps it, and nobody, quite, dares to say.

choices.text: Read it aloud at the Reading

effects.log: You read a page at the next Reading. The Hall weeps, silently, in rows, and the Reader of the Dead stops, and says it is the first time the Reading has been alive.
You keep it, privately, in a drawer. It is the best thing you own, and you do not share it, and sometimes it is a little warmer.
You tell Imsun your suspicion: that it keeps itself. Imsun, quite grey, writes it down in the margin of the first volume.

events.text: The Second Volume, in the end, has an author, and it turns out to be an old and tired Incense Bearer, who had never dared say they kept a private ledger of small things. They come to you, in tears, and ask whether they are to be punished or praised, and Imsun, at your shoulder, says nothing.

effects.log: You praise them in the Hall, before all, and the Incense Bearer is made Keeper of the Second Volume. The Hall, to its own surprise, stands.

choices.text: Say it is allowed, and quietly

effects.log: You say it is allowed, and say no more. The Incense Bearer goes on writing, unnoticed, and the volume grows.

choices.text: Ask for a page of your own

effects.log: You ask for a page in it. The Incense Bearer writes it, and gives it to you, and it says one true thing about you that you did not know.

events.text: A deputation of mortals reaches the Root Hall with a petition about the old oak at the crossroads, which the village wants not to fall. They have carried it up on foot through nine dreams of the god of the road. It is, the Heralds agree, well written. The question is whether anyone must answer it.

effects.log: You answer it by appearing, briefly, in the dream of their leader. They wake knowing what to do about the roof, and do not know why.

choices.text: Pass it to Saengmo Mother of Seeds

effects.log: Saengmo Mother of Seeds reads it in one breath and answers with a sign nobody at the Root Hall expects. The deputation is delighted. You are quietly thanked.
It is filed. The deputation waits eleven years and then, being mortal, forgets. The petition remains, in the Root Hall, like a pressed flower.

events.text: A deputation of mortals reaches the Hall of Gales with a petition about a harbour wall that the sea keeps taking back. They have carried it up on foot through nine dreams of the god of the road. It is, the Heralds agree, well written. The question is whether anyone must answer it.

effects.log: You answer it by appearing, briefly, in the dream of their leader. They wake knowing what to do about the tide, and do not know why.

choices.text: Pass it to Haeryong King of the Tides

effects.log: Haeryong King of the Tides reads it in one breath and answers with a sign nobody at the Hall of Gales expects. The deputation is delighted. You are quietly thanked.
It is filed. The deputation waits eleven years and then, being mortal, forgets. The petition remains, in the Hall of Gales, like a pressed flower.

events.text: A week of offerings arrives at the Root Hall: a sheaf of the first grain, cut with a bread knife, a plain loaf, and a child's drawing of you with too many arms. The loaf is stale. The drawing is on the Seed Bell within the hour. A herald asks if it may be removed. It is a very enthusiastic drawing.

effects.log: You keep it. A child far below is, that night, mysteriously unafraid of the dark, and has no idea why.
You bless the child with a lifetime of small luck. It is a minor affair, but it makes a man of the herald, who weeps.
You eat a piece of the stale loaf. It tastes of home. Through the whole of the Root Hall the gods feel a small, inexplicable pang.

events.text: A week of offerings arrives at the Hall of Gales: a bowl of sea-water, carried inland in a bucket, a plain loaf, and a child's drawing of you with too many arms. The loaf is stale. The drawing is on the Weather Table within the hour. A herald asks if it may be removed. It is a very enthusiastic drawing.

effects.log: You keep it. A child far below is, that night, mysteriously unafraid of the dark, and has no idea why.
You bless the child with a lifetime of small luck. It is a minor affair, but it makes a man of the herald, who weeps.
You eat a piece of the stale loaf. It tastes of home. Through the whole of the Hall of Gales the gods feel a small, inexplicable pang.

events.text: A prayer arrives from a fishing family far below that is not a request but a complaint: you have been very quiet. They are not angry, only baffled. The Root Hall goes still. events.text: The Seed Bell of the Green Assembly rings once a year, at the thaw, and every seed in the cosmos is meant to hear it and wake. This year, one seed does not. Saengmo Mother of Seeds holds it in her palm in the Root Hall and asks the Assembly, softly, whether it should be woken or left.

events.text: The beasts of the Green Assembly hold a parliament once a century in the Root Hall, and every beast speaks in its own tongue. The speeches are interpreted by a very tired owl. This year the motion is whether the gods should be permitted to eat meat. The owl looks at you.

effects.log: You speak against it, quietly, to the rustle of a thousand ears. The motion fails by one hare. The Assembly is vegetarian for another century, and says it is your doing.

effects.log: The beasts consider this. A very old boar grunts approval. The compromise is chronicled in four hundred languages.

choices.text: Abstain, and fetch the owl a cup of tea

effects.log: The owl weeps with gratitude. The parliament goes on without you and, in the end, decides to adjourn for tea.

events.text: Pungnyeon of the Golden Field has refused to ripen the grain this autumn, in protest. He will not say why. The farmers far below are praying with a dull anger. The Assembly sits in the Root Hall in uncomfortable silence, and the oldest god among them turns, slowly, to you.

effects.log: You find him in the field at dusk, sitting on a rock. He says he is tired of being thanked only at harvest. You thank him, for the other eleven months, in full. He ripens the grain.
He ripens it, sullenly, and the grain tastes faintly of resentment. The Assembly commends you. Pungnyeon does not speak to you for a century.

choices.text: Hold a harvest festival in spring

effects.log: You declare a Festival of Thanks in the thaw. He is moved, and furious, and ripens the grain a week early out of embarrassment.

events.text: A hunter far below prays to Horang Lord of the Wild for a deer, and Horang agrees. The hunter prays again, the next year, and again. The deer are thinning. Horang has brought the matter to the Root Hall, as an aggrieved god of the wild who is also a god of hunts, and very much torn.

effects.log: Horang imposes a closed year. The hunter, puzzled, tracks nothing for a season and learns to fish. The deer return, in numbers. Horang thanks you with a whole forest of silence.

choices.text: Advise Horang to follow his heart

effects.log: He does, and the hunter has a good year and a bad one. Horang, brooding, has nobody to blame but himself, and thanks you for it a century later.

events.text: The ancient oak at the centre of the Root Hall has begun to speak. It says only two words: 'Not yet.' Nobody knows what it is not yet. The Assembly has convened five emergency sessions and the oak has repeated itself in each. Saengmo, tending its roots, has taken to saying it back.

effects.log: The oak is silent for a year, then says: 'Ask again.' You ask again, and it says 'Not yet.' A tradition begins in the Root Hall of asking the oak a question at dusk.

choices.text: Say it back to the oak

effects.log: You say 'not yet' to it. It is, you feel, quite satisfied. The words settle over the Hall like moss, and the Assembly sleeps better.

events.text: An ancient wolf-spirit comes to the Root Hall, thin as a rope, to ask for a boon: a single day without being hunted. The Assembly mutters. Horang is a predator among predators, and the wolf's kind have eaten his flock. The wolf asks the youngest god present to speak for it. That is you.

effects.log: You speak. The Assembly grants a day. The wolf spends it asleep in the sun on a hill, and the lambs, passing, give it a wide and respectful berth.
The wolf bows its head and goes. Two seasons later you hear it was brought down by a hunter, and you hold the silence in the Root Hall a little longer than the rest.

events.text: On the first warm day of the thaw, the Green Assembly holds the Planting of the Gods: each god plants a seed in the Root Hall's garden, to be tended by hand. Yours is a small green thing from a mortal windowsill. It will not tell you what it is. Saengmo winks.

effects.log: It grows into a very ordinary bean plant. Saengmo says this is the best thing you could have planted, and bakes you something.

choices.text: Plant it and sing to it

effects.log: It grows into a tree with your voice in its leaves. The Assembly sits in its shade for centuries and does not know why it is calming.

events.text: A river in the lowlands has been renamed by the mortals, three times, in a hundred years. The river-spirit, bewildered, has come to the Root Hall asking which name is its own. The Assembly is hushed. Nobody knows. The spirit looks at you with the sorrowful eyes of an enormous patient fish.

choices.text: Ask the spirit what it would like

effects.log: It would like, it says, to be called something that sounds like water. You give it a name that does. It sinks back into its river, rippling, and the mortals, after a while, take the name up.
The spirit thinks about this for a long time. 'Yes,' it says, finally. 'I do.' It goes home. The mortals keep renaming it, and it keeps answering to them all.

events.text: The Green Assembly is the oldest pantheon, and its Keeper of Ages has drawn up a ledger of every year it has endured. It comes to eleven million. The Keeper asks you, as a courtesy, to read the last page aloud. It is blank, except for a single line: 'And so on.'

effects.log: You read it. A hush falls, and then the Assembly, one by one, begins to laugh. It is the first laugh in the Root Hall in three hundred years.
You add a line: 'And so on, warmly.' The Keeper sighs and lets it stand. It is the only edit to the ledger in eleven million years.

events.text: A very small plague of beetles has fallen on a farm far below, and the farmer, a woman of enormous patience, has prayed to the Assembly each night for a month. The prayers are the same each night, in the same quiet words. Nobody has answered. She is not angry. She keeps asking.

effects.log: You send a flock of starlings. The beetles are gone by dawn. She prays one last time, only to say thank you, and sets out a dish of seed for the starlings, and keeps it filled for the rest of her life.

choices.text: Send a wise old toad in a dream

effects.log: She wakes with a plan, and the plan works, and she never knows it was a god. She thinks she is rather clever, and she is.

events.text: A god of the Green Assembly is found with a branch growing out of their shoulder. It is not theirs: it is a stranger's, grafted on during a nap. The branch has a name, and an opinion about the soil. The god is mortified. The branch is gently delighted. Saengmo asks you to decide what is to be done.

effects.log: You declare the branch a limb of the god, and so it is. The god accepts, with a tight smile, and starts to wear sleeveless robes. The branch is called Dal.

choices.text: Have the branch cut and replanted

effects.log: The branch is cut and replanted in the Root Hall's garden. It grows into a tree, and the god, relieved, visits it on feast days. The tree is called Dal, and is very forgiving.

events.text: Dal, the grafted branch, has grown to full size and acquired a following. Mortals far below pray to it, believing it a minor god of green things, and Dal, a little overwhelmed, is answering. The god it was grafted from watches with a face of conflicted pride. 'It is better at this than I am,' they confess.

effects.log: You raise Dal to godhood in a small, leafy ceremony. The Root Hall is full of rustling. Dal's first act as a god is to thank the god who grew it.
Dal is left a tree with a following. It prefers it. The mortals love it better for the lack of paperwork.

events.text: A thousand years on, Dal is the oldest living thing in the Root Hall's garden, and the god it was grafted from has passed into the long sleep. Their last wish was to be planted beside the tree. Dal asks you, in a rustle, to do it. It has already made room.

effects.log: You plant them. Dal's leaves bow. In spring the two are one canopy, and the mortals say, in a hundred languages, that the old god and the young tree are the same.

choices.text: Carry them to the sea first

effects.log: You carry them to the sea, as they wanted at the start, and then plant them beside Dal. The old god, you feel, is amused.

events.text: A season has gone missing. Nobody knows which: it simply is not on the calendar of the Green Assembly, though everyone remembers having lived through it. The farmers below are confused. The Keeper of Ages, rummaging in the ledger, finds the blank pages where it should be, and a pressed leaf.

effects.log: You search the Root Hall for a year. You find, finally, a small cold season folded in a drawer, shy and a little hurt. You unfold it and let it go. It rains, gratefully, for a week.
The season stays lost. Mortals adjust. A strange gap appears in the poetry of the age, a silence between autumn and winter, and it is beautiful and slightly sad.

events.text: The lost season has come back, and brought a friend: a smaller, odder season, with an interest in puddles. The Assembly is not sure either is on the calendar. The farmers below are overjoyed and have started holding festivals. Saengmo asks if you might, perhaps, give them official names.

effects.log: You name them with the light, lopsided words of the farmers below. The names stick. The Keeper of Ages writes them into the ledger with an indignant flourish.
A deputation of farmers is invited up. They argue for a night and name the seasons after a kind of soup. The Assembly is deeply moved.

events.text: The Green Assembly's tradition of the First Thaw demands that each god give back to the world something they once took. You have been dreading your turn, since the list of things you have taken is long and subtle. Saengmo, kindly, offers to help you choose.

choices.text: Give back a season of your own worship

effects.log: You give back a season. The world below blossoms in a way that does not quite make sense, and a thousand strangers wake up crying, and happy.
You give back a memory you stole from a dying mortal, long ago. They come, in a dream, and thank you, and you do not tell them it was a theft.

events.text: Horang Lord of the Wild invites you on a hunt through the Wild Dream, which is a hunt for the shape of a thing rather than the thing itself. You track it for nine days. It is a fox. It is also a river. It is also something that happened to Horang long ago, and he has never told anyone.

effects.log: At the end is a small clearing and a stone with a name on it. Horang kneels, and you stand behind him, and he thanks you for being the first to see it.
You let it run. Horang watches it go, and then, to your astonishment, he laughs. 'Good,' he says. 'You know when to stop.'

events.text: The Seed Bell has been stolen. Nobody can say when. The Root Hall finds only a dent in the moss and a faint smell of mint. Saengmo says, with admirable calm, that without it the seeds of the world will not wake this spring, and that this is, in all the circumstances, rather a lot.

effects.log: You track a faint smell of mint across eleven realms to a mortal child's pocket. The child has been ringing it, gently, at the bedtime of a sick friend. You let them keep it until morning.
You ring a spoon on a pot. The seeds wake, grumbling, a little late and a little off-key. Saengmo calls it the Spring of the Spoon, and the name sticks.

events.text: A ghost of a forest, a place that burned long ago, has come to the Root Hall asking to be replanted. It cannot be, the Assembly says, for the soil is gone. The ghost says it understands, politely, and stands in the corner for forty years, a green shimmer, waiting to be told.

effects.log: You plant a corner of the garden with its memory. In a century there is a forest in the Root Hall that does not remember burning, and the ghost goes quiet and complete.
You tell it the truth, kindly. The ghost nods and thins, and by dawn is only a faint stir in the moss. Saengmo sets a sprig on the spot.

events.text: The god of a single pond in the Green Assembly has been petitioning for a promotion for four thousand years. The pond is, by any measure, tiny. The god insists that it is the finest pond in the cosmos, and is, on the evidence, correct. Every year the Assembly nods and does nothing. This year it is your turn to nod.

effects.log: The pond is made a lake, by decree. It is unaffected, and the god weeps. A heron comes, and stays, and the pond's reputation flourishes.
You sit by the pond for an afternoon. It is, in fact, perfect. You tell the god so, and nothing more, and they say that is all they ever wanted.

events.text: At the First Thaw feast, the youngest god of the Green Assembly is made to eat the first spring shoot, which is always bitter. This year the shoot is not bitter. It is sweet. The youngest, dismayed, says it is a mistake. The oldest god, gravely, says it is a promise.

effects.log: It is sweet. You are silent for a long time. Later you find you have been humming. The Assembly takes it as a good omen, and so it is.

choices.text: Tell the youngest to enjoy it

effects.log: The youngest, red with embarrassment, eats it all. Spring that year is very kind, and the feast ends in a long, communal sigh.

events.text: A rumour among the beasts of the Green Assembly says that a dragon is sleeping beneath the Root Hall and that the oak's roots are all that hold it. The roots, of late, have been creaking. Saengmo's face is perfectly still. 'It is only a rumour,' she says. 'Probably.'

effects.log: You dig for a season. There is no dragon, only an enormous warm stone with a heartbeat. You cover it again, tenderly, and do not tell the beasts.

choices.text: Tell the beasts it is a rumour

effects.log: The beasts are reassured and a bit disappointed. A pinch of dust from the floor of the Hall blows up your sleeve and smells faintly of cinnamon and smoke.

events.text: At the Throne of Storms the gods argue in weather. A disagreement about fishing rights has been going on for sixty years, and the sea off the east coast has a permanent gale in the shape of an eyebrow. Haeryong King of the Tides asks, with tight politeness, for you to mediate.

effects.log: You propose a calm, a day at a time. The gale thins to a breeze, and then a shrug. Haeryong, grudgingly, says it is acceptable. The sea sighs.
You answer in thunder, for the room speaks that tongue. The argument ends in a draw, a shrug, and a very loud meal.

events.text: Noejin the Stormcaller has called for a vote in the Hall of Gales to ban lightning on feast days. The motion passes. A single flash, in the corner, objects, and is voted down. The flash hangs in the air and sulks. The Throne turns to you for a ruling on whether a vote can be sulked at.

choices.text: Rule it can be sulked at

effects.log: The flash is allowed one sulk a year, in a corner, in silence. It takes the offer with a minor, dignified crackle.
The ruling is read out in a clear, cold voice. The flash goes out. The Hall is darker, and the feast is quieter, and nobody mentions the flash again.

events.text: Gaksan Who Holds the Peaks is, as his name suggests, immovable.
