He has been sitting in the same chair in the Hall of Gales for nine hundred years, and the chair has begun to merge with him. The Throne would like him to attend the council. A small delegation has been sent to ask politely whether he can be lifted.

effects.log: You ask. Gaksan thinks about it for eleven years and then rises, with a sound like a landslide. The chair comes with him. The council makes room.
You bring the council to his chair. It is the most patient meeting in memory. Gaksan says one sentence, and everyone agrees with it.

events.text: A tidal wave has been promised to a coastal city by an accident of the Weather Table, and cannot be recalled without a god's signature. The Throne is stalled: a signature costs, and nobody wants to be the one who signed a drowning or unsigned a promise. The wave waits offshore, patient and enormous.

effects.log: You sign. The wave folds like a hand, and the city never knows. The Throne records an unusual mercy and a quiet debit against your name.
You divert it to a sea with no shore. It rises, and falls, and is gone. Haeryong sends a polite note of admiration for the arithmetic.

choices.text: Let it fall and warn the city

effects.log: You warn the city in a dream, and every soul climbs to high ground. The wave takes the empty streets. The Throne rules this a clean outcome and not a kind one.

events.text: It is the Turning of the Gale, the Throne's great feast, when every wind in the cosmos is invited to dinner. The seating is a nightmare. The East Wind will not sit by the West, and the North has lost its voice. A minor breeze, hurt at its place near the door, is being quietly blown about the room.

effects.log: The breeze, astonished, settles in your sleeve. For the rest of the dinner it carries your words to the other end of the table, softly, and the feast is a triumph.
You reseat everyone in a spiral. The winds, intrigued, sit where they are put. It is the best Turning in a thousand years.

events.text: A small storm-spirit has fallen in love with a mountain, and cannot stop circling it. Gaksan has been patient, and unmoved, as he is. The spirit's brothers have begged the Throne to intervene. The mountain, asked, says only that he has noticed the weather has been nice.

effects.log: You advise the spirit to land. It settles in a high valley and becomes a gentle fog that clings to the peak each dawn. Gaksan says nothing, but the snow melts a week early.
You advise the spirit to move on, kindly. It drifts away, grieving, and the mountain stands unchanged. There is a cold patch on the summit for a century.

events.text: The Throne of Storms keeps a Court of Complaints where mortals' curses against the weather are heard on the first of each month. Most are petty. This month's include a baker who curses a rainstorm for ruining a wedding cake, a bride who thanks it for the same, and a cat who is merely loud.

effects.log: The baker is paid in a month of sunshine. The bride, sulking, is sent a rainbow. The cat is given a sunny windowsill. Everyone is mildly content.
The bride gets her rain and a dozen lucky omens. The baker, gently, is sent a new cake. The Court laughs for a week.
The cat is awarded a small thunderstorm of its own, in a bowl. It sits in it, purring. The Court, delighted, adjourns.

events.text: Noejin has decided to stop thunder entirely for a year, as a protest against being called loud. The skies are silent. Mortals far below creep around nervously. Lightning, unaccompanied, looks bare. The Throne begs Noejin to reconsider, and Noejin, sulking, asks for a quiet word with you.

effects.log: He tells you, for three nights, how tired he is of being feared. At the end you propose a gentler thunder, a roll, a purr. He tries it. It is lovely.

choices.text: Tell him he is a bully

effects.log: He roars. Then he laughs. 'Well,' he says, 'someone had to say it.' The thunder returns the next day, at three-quarters volume.

events.text: The sea gives up a drowned city that has lain on the floor for four thousand years. It rises, whole, into the sunlight, and the Throne of Storms is called upon to decide who owns it. The city's last inhabitants, a colony of very polite crabs, have already moved in.

effects.log: The crabs take possession with great gravity. The city of crabs flourishes for a thousand years, and their ambassador sends you a pearl every spring.
The city becomes a shrine to drowned things. Haeryong is quietly proud. Mortals sail to it in secret, and leave small boats in the doors.
You lower it back, gently. The crabs, grumbling, relocate. Haeryong thanks you, and the city is a little closer to the stars than it was.

events.text: A mountain-spirit of the Throne's smallest range is retiring, after nine thousand years, and has asked you to take on its peaks. It is not a grand office. It is a slope, a dozen goats, and a footpath that two old women walk each morning. The spirit's eyes shine.

effects.log: You take on the slope. The goats are rude and the footpath is long and the two old women, one morning, wave. It is the happiest of your offices.
You find a young cloud-spirit of the right temper. It takes the mountain with enormous solemnity. The old spirit, retiring, weeps and plants a tree.

events.text: The Weather Table, on which the Throne plans every storm, is cracked straight across the middle in the night, from the east coast to the west. The gods of the Throne stand round it. Haeryong says it was thunder. Noejin says it was the sea. Gaksan says nothing, since he is a mountain, and that is the loudest accusation of all.

effects.log: You mend it with a seam of gold, in the old way, and the crack becomes a feature. The Throne approves, wearily. It is a better table.
The hearing lasts a year and finds no one guilty and everyone sorry. The crack remains. The gods learn to plan around it, and the weather, for a while, has a curious bend.

events.text: The crack in the Weather Table has begun to leak: a thin steady drizzle falls from it onto the Hall's floor. The gods have put out basins. The drizzle, it turns out, is a small but real weather, and a mortal village far below has begun to depend on it for its crops. The Throne must decide whether to mend the leak.

effects.log: The drizzle stays. A village below calls it the Gift and builds a small shrine. Haeryong mutters about maintenance, then adds a drain and a flowerpot.

choices.text: Mend it and send rain instead

effects.log: You mend the leak and send the village a proper rain. They are grateful, a little less moved. The Table is whole again, and a little duller.

events.text: The village below the Weather Table's leak sends a deputation, as promised, to the Hall of Gales: three farmers and a nervous child, carrying a basket of eggs. They have come to say thank you. The child, awed, asks which god makes the rain. The Throne goes very still.

effects.log: You say the Table does, and the Table is mended with gold, and that it is nobody's fault. The child nods and gives you an egg. It is the most precious thing you have ever been given.
Noejin, enormous, kneels and tells the child he does, with a solemn rumble. The child, unafraid, tells him to be kind to the clouds. He says he will.

events.text: Haeryong King of the Tides keeps a drowned court beneath the Hall of Gales, where every ship ever lost is moored in a long quiet harbour. He invites you to sit in it for a night. The captains rise and bow, all of them, and not one of them has a face. He says it is the only place he can be understood.

effects.log: You sit through the night and hear the sea's long catalogue, each ship a sentence. At dawn Haeryong thanks you, in a voice like a closing door.
You decline. He nods, hurt, not offended, and the harbour dims. For a decade he is distant, and then, one day, sends a pearl.

events.text: Haeryong asks a favour: one of the drowned captains, a woman of the east coast, has been trying for nine hundred years to deliver a letter. The letter is still wet. The addressee is long dead. Haeryong asks whether you might deliver it to the addressee's descendants.

effects.log: You find the descendants in a coastal village, a family of fishers. You leave the letter on a doorstep. They weep and do not know why, and the captain is, at last, at rest.
It says only: 'I'm sorry I was late.' You close it, and deliver it, shaken.

events.text: Haeryong comes to the Hall of Gales one morning without his crown. The drowned court is quiet. He sits beside you and says the captain's letter has done what nothing else could: the harbour has begun, ship by ship, to sail. He has never been so lonely, or so glad.

effects.log: You sit with him till the last ship is gone. The harbour is empty, a long clean bay. Haeryong sleeps for a hundred years and wakes lighter.

choices.text: Offer him a ship of your own

effects.log: You give him a small boat, made of nothing but your regard. He sets it on the empty harbour, and it floats, and he sails it for a long time.

events.text: Gaksan Who Holds the Peaks has begun, for the first time in his existence, to speak, and the thing he says is a small, low, shocking song. The Throne of Storms assembles to listen. He sings for three days. It is about a stone that wanted to be a bird.

effects.log: The song ends, and Gaksan, embarrassed, turns his face to the wall. You tell him it was the finest thing you have heard. He does not move for a week, and then he hums.

choices.text: Ask him what the stone became

effects.log: He says it became a mountain, which is a bird that has decided to stay. It is the oldest joke in the Throne, and it is a good one.

events.text: Gaksan, to the Throne's astonishment, has asked for leave: he wishes to walk. A mountain walking is no small matter, and the lands below are alarmed. He has chosen the route, which is a long loop of the world, and the date, which is Tuesday. He asks only that someone go with him.

effects.log: You walk beside the mountain for a year, which is a step a day. He talks, a little. Villages watch him pass, and he is the gentlest cataclysm ever. At the end he sits, with a sigh, and is home.
You go ahead and warn the villages. They set out flowers on the road. He crosses a continent in a garland, and is, for once, speechless.

events.text: A young god of the Throne has discovered how to speak to the weather, and is using this to order it about. The weather, which is old and patient, tolerates it. The young god is sure he is a prodigy. The Throne looks to you to correct him gently, since you are the only one he would hear.

effects.log: You tell him that the weather is a conversation, and he has been shouting. He is mortified, then curious, then silent. A year later he is the best listener the Throne has had.
The weather, with great restraint, rains on him for a month. He learns. He thanks it. The Throne watches the entire episode with a pleasant, quiet satisfaction.

events.text: The Throne of Storms holds a trial, once an age, of a storm that has done wrong. This storm swept a village into the sea and has asked to be judged. It stands in the dock as a column of cloud, humming. Haeryong prosecutes; Noejin defends. You are asked to be the third judge.

effects.log: The storm is sentenced to a hundred years of calm. It nods, shrinks, and goes to lie in a high valley. It is, you hear, a model prisoner and writes poetry in the mist.
The storm is acquitted on the grounds that it is a storm. It leaves, and the village it swept is never rebuilt. You carry the verdict like a stone, and do not know if it was right.
The storm is bound to rebuild the village in dreams, every year, for a thousand years. It does, rather beautifully, and the village remembers.

events.text: A messenger from the Will of Heaven arrives at the Throne of Storms with a polite request that it cease its weather during a state ceremony. The Throne is affronted. Haeryong threatens a flood. Noejin proposes a tempest. Gaksan, quietly, proposes tea. The messenger waits, and perspires, and looks at you.

effects.log: You offer a sky of high thin cloud for the ceremony: calm, but unmistakably the Throne's. Both sides accept with offended dignity. The ceremony goes beautifully.
You agree, for peace. The Throne grumbles. A week later the ceremony is washed out by a freak, and unattributed, storm. Nobody can prove a thing.

choices.text: Side with Gaksan and bring tea

effects.log: You bring tea. The messenger, bewildered, drinks it, and the matter is resolved over three cups. The Will of Heaven sends a thank-you note.

events.text: A fisherman prays to the Throne every morning and has done so for sixty years. He asks only that the sea be kind to his boat. The sea has been, mostly. Today his prayer is different. He asks that it be kind to his son's boat, because his own is too old. The Throne goes quiet around the Table.

choices.text: Grant it, for the whole family

effects.log: You set a kindness over the family's coast for three generations. The sea there is the gentlest on the map. The fisherman's grandson names a boat after you.

choices.text: Grant it, for the one day

effects.log: You grant a day. The son returns with a full net and the old man weeps. The next day, the sea is the sea. The old man prays again anyway.

events.text: An argument at the Throne of Storms has gone on for three days and shows no sign of ending. Thunder shakes the Hall of Gales, rain falls in sheets from the ceiling, and the Weather Table is flooded. Nobody remembers what it was about. They are all, deeply, enjoying themselves.

effects.log: You hurl a cloud. Noejin cheers. By dawn you have forgotten the subject too, and the Throne is as one in its pleasure and its weariness.
You call for a break, and the Hall falls silent. The gods, panting, look at each other and laugh. The argument is not resumed, and nobody asks why.

events.text: The Throne of Storms is asked to lend a storm to a mortal wizard who wishes to power a great machine. The machine, he says, will bring light to a hundred towns. The Throne has qualms. Noejin is flattered. Haeryong thinks it will sink. The wizard stands in the Hall, wringing his hat.

effects.log: The storm is lent, with strings. The machine lights a hundred towns, and the wizard, grateful, sends a small thunderbolt every Midsummer, back up the road, as thanks.

choices.text: Refuse, but offer a gentler wind

effects.log: A gentler wind is lent. The machine works, but only on windy days. The wizard grumbles, then learns to love breezes.

events.text: A very small bird has flown all the way up the sea of clouds to the Hall of Gales, against the wind, for no reason it will give. It lands on the Weather Table and refuses to leave. It will not be fed, nor lifted. Noejin attempts to blow it away. The bird digs in its claws and looks at you.

effects.log: The bird stays, a small brown fixture on the Weather Table. The storms, bewildered, grow gentler. Within a year the Table is the calmest in the cosmos.

choices.text: Ask the bird what it wants

effects.log: It does not answer, but it looks at you with an enormous, calm, ordinary kindness. You offer it a seat on your shoulder. It accepts.

events.text: A storm that was born a thousand years ago and has never once broken is brought to the Hall by a pair of gods who cannot manage it. It is enormous, patient, and clearly unhappy. It has been holding its rain all this time. They ask you whether to let it go.

effects.log: You tell it that it may. It rains, over a barren plain, for nine years. The plain, afterwards, is a country. The storm, spent, is a clear sky, and sighs.

choices.text: Teach it to rain a little at a time

effects.log: You teach it a drizzle. It takes a century, and is a pleasure to watch. The storm, finally, is a gentle thing, and an old friend.

events.text: The Throne of Storms decides to hold a contest of winds, to settle once and for all which is the strongest. The contest is a disaster. The north wind is sore, the south wind is sullen, and the west wind refuses to enter on the grounds that it is not vain. The east wind wins by default and is miserable.

effects.log: You declare it a tie of the four. The winds, relieved, shake hands, and the world below has a very even year. The east wind sends you a mild breeze, in thanks.

choices.text: Award the west wind a prize for modesty

effects.log: The west wind is overwhelmed and blushes into a gentle gale. It becomes the favourite wind of poets, and of you.

events.text: At the edge of the Hall of Gales, on a balcony open to everything, an old god of the sea sits alone with a cup of something warm. He is nearly translucent. He has been telling the waves a story for three thousand years and has reached the part where he forgets how it ends.

effects.log: You sit with him. He tells the story from the beginning. You do not know how it ends either. He does not mind. It is a very good story.
You suggest an ending, off the cuff. He frowns, tries it, and finds that it fits. He weeps. The waves, below, go quiet and then roar.

events.text: The Throne of Storms has been asked, by the Green Assembly, for a tempest to scour a plague from a forest. The Throne considers this a favour and a risk. The forest is very old, and the tempest does not discriminate. The Assembly's envoy, a delicate faun, is white with strain.

choices.text: Grant a tempest, and watch the trees

effects.log: You grant a tempest, narrowly aimed. It scours the plague and spares the oaks. The faun kisses your hand, and the Assembly sends a thank-you of seeds.
You offer a long rain. It takes years, and the forest is saved slowly, and nobody can say it was the Throne. The faun is uncertain, and then grateful.

events.text: Haeryong, Noejin and Gaksan each claim a rainbow that appeared over a harbour in the dawn. None of them made it. It is a particularly good one, double, with a third faint bow inside. Each says it is the sign of their domain. They look at you, with the air of children who have each found a coin.

choices.text: Rule it belongs to the harbour

effects.log: You rule it the harbour's. The harbour-spirit, a little old man with a lantern, is so pleased he sits under it for a month. The three gods sulk, then laugh.

choices.text: Rule it belongs to all three

effects.log: You rule it belongs to all three, and they must visit it together. They do, and it is the first time in centuries they have shared a bench.

events.text: A boy far below has sworn to climb a mountain to petition the god who holds it. The mountain is Gaksan's, and Gaksan has no intention of being petitioned. He sits at the summit, immovable, as the boy climbs for three days, and then another three, and the Hall of Gales watches the whole affair with interest.

effects.log: You ask Gaksan to listen. He doesn't. But he moves a stone, very slightly, so that the boy's last step is easier. The boy never knows.
The boy reaches the top and simply sits down beside the god and says nothing. Gaksan, startled, says nothing too. They sit there for a week, and it is the best conversation either has had.

events.text: The Throne of Storms is in dispute with the Throne's own weathercock, an enormous bronze bird atop the Hall, which has begun to point in directions that do not exist. It spins and creaks. The gods have called a conference. The weathercock, offended, points at you.

effects.log: You follow where it points, a direction with no name, and find an odd small door, and behind it a snug room with a stove and a chair. The weathercock settles. You do not tell anyone where the room is.
You oil it, and it points where it should, sulking. A week later it spins to a fresh unmapped direction, and you hear it chuckle.

events.text: At the Hall of Gales, there is a custom: whoever speaks last in a council must say something that no one else would have. The last speaker is you, the council ends, and the silence fills the room. The Throne's gods wait, with the expectancy of a theatre, for your sentence.

choices.text: Say you are glad to be here

effects.log: A pause. Then, slowly, the room smiles. It is the one thing no one else would have said, and it is true, and the Throne goes to bed warmer.

choices.text: Tell a joke about the weather

effects.log: It is a very old joke about rain. Nobody laughs for a moment, and then Haeryong does, and the Hall rocks. The council ends in joy.

events.text: The Throne of Storms' youngest god has brought a stray cloud home from the lowlands and named it Pudding. It is a small, damp, lopsided thing that rains only on the god's shoes. The Throne has a rule against pets. The god looks up at you with brimming eyes.

effects.log: You rule that Pudding is not a pet but a colleague. The Throne, appalled, accepts. Pudding is given a desk, and rains on the paperwork.

choices.text: Rule that Pudding must be released

effects.log: You release Pudding in a high valley where it can rain freely. The young god weeps. A year later, a tiny, damp cloud follows them to the Hall and settles on their head.

events.text: A drought has gripped a mortal land for nine years, and its king has sacrificed to every god but the Throne of Storms, whom he fears. He comes at last on his knees to the Hall of Gales with a bowl of his own tears. He is no longer afraid. He is only tired.

effects.log: You send it. It falls for seven days, warm, steady, patient. The king looks up with his mouth open. The kingdom, afterwards, names its children after weather.

choices.text: Send the rain, and ask a price

effects.log: You send it, and ask the king to keep the river free for all. He agrees, and does, and the price is paid in better laws for a thousand years.

events.text: A small group of mortal weather-scholars far below has noticed that the Throne of Storms follows patterns, and has written to the Throne asking, respectfully, to be sent a copy of the Table. They have deduced half of it already. Noejin is incensed. Haeryong is intrigued. Gaksan is, as ever, silent.

effects.log: You send half the Table, truthfully. The scholars are delighted, and devote themselves to the other half. The world below gets its first accurate forecast in a thousand years.

choices.text: Send nothing and a polite note

effects.log: You send a note praising their diligence. They are encouraged, and in a century they have guessed the rest. The Throne is secretly proud.

events.text: A god of the Throne is dying of old age, and has asked to spend its last season as a small, ordinary breeze in a meadow. The Throne agrees. You are asked to arrange it. The god is gentle and tired, and takes your hand, and says only: 'Make sure it is a warm meadow.'

effects.log: You find a high green meadow in a mortal summer. The god becomes a breeze, and stirs the grass, and is gone by autumn. Children in the meadow say the wind has a lovely voice.
You carry them in your arms, and set them down in the grass, and stay a day. It is the quietest day you have had in a thousand years.

events.text: The Weather Table predicts a storm of epic proportions for a coast whose people are, by the Table's reckoning, wicked. The Table is never wrong. But the Throne has had its doubts about the Table's moral judgement for a while. A deputation of gods asks you to decide whether to send it.

effects.log: You send it. The coast is flattened, and is rebuilt kinder. You will never know if it needed to be done, and the Table says it did.

choices.text: Hold the storm, and test the coast

effects.log: You hold it for a year and send gentle trials. The coast passes, narrowly. The Table is outraged. The coast, unknowing, rebuilds a temple.
You overrule the Table. The Throne is shocked into silence, and the coast is spared. The Table sulks, and its next prediction is wrong, once, in a kinder direction.

events.text: The Throne of {b3_order} has a footstool, and the footstool has a history. It was a god once. It was demoted, politely, after an incident that nobody will describe, and has served as furniture ever since. It has opinions, which it expresses by creaking. You find, on your second day, that you have begun to ask it things.

effects.log: It creaks for an hour. The tale is shorter than the creak and much sadder. You promote it to a cushion, and it purrs, faintly, like old wood.

choices.text: Keep using it as a footstool

effects.log: You use it as a footstool with a consciously clear conscience. It creaks pleasantly. Neither of you mentions it again.

events.text: Each morning a herald reads out the prayers addressed to the seat of {b3_order}. Most are small. One, today, is addressed to {b3_oldhead}, who left the seat in a hurry, and is still being prayed to by a village that has not heard of the change. The herald pauses, pen raised.

effects.log: You send the village a warm, vague blessing in the old head's manner. The village is content. {b3_oldhead}, informed, sends you a dry note of thanks.
You send the blessing as yourself, and a dream explaining the change. The village is flustered, then fond, and adopts you with only minor protest.

events.text: A visiting god of the Green Assembly, ancient and genial, has been shown into the council chamber of {b3_order} and has fallen asleep in the chair. It is the chair you were going to sit in. The council of {b3_order} waits, hushed. Whoever disturbs a sleeping elder of the Green Assembly is cursed with weeds for a century.

effects.log: You sit on the arm of the chair. The council, relieved, follows your lead. The visitor sleeps through a three-hour meeting and wakes saying it was the best he has attended.
You hold a cup of tea under the visitor's nose. He wakes, delighted, and says that was exactly the right thing, and that you are, it appears, the right sort.

events.text: The seat of {b3_order} comes with a dream. Every night, for a year, you dream the same dream: a long corridor of closed doors, each marked with the name of a prayer you did not answer. {b3_elder} says every holder has had it. You are advised to open one door, and not to look behind it twice.

effects.log: Behind it is a woman in a kitchen, aged and tired, whose prayer was a small one. You answer it in the dream, at last. In the morning there is a loaf of bread on your pillow.
There are nine thousand. You stop at nine hundred. The count itself is the lesson, and a heavier one than any door.

events.text: {b3_peer} has been passed over for the seat, graciously, and with a speech, and is not taking it well. They send you a note each morning: a single line, pointed, exquisitely worded. This morning's reads: 'I trust the cushions are comfortable.' The note arrives with a cushion.

effects.log: You send it back with a note: 'Not as comfortable as yours.' {b3_peer} laughs, for the first time in decades. The notes continue, but gentler.
{b3_peer} is stunned, then insulted, then thorough. They are the best counsellor the seat has had, and never stop sending you cushions.

events.text: The heralds of {b3_order} have laid down their staves. They are not on strike, exactly, they say: they are 'pausing'. They want one thing: that prayers be answered in order of arrival, not of loudness. The Throne has never done it. The corridors are filling with undelivered dreams, and the lamps have begun to flicker.

effects.log: You decree answering in order of arrival. The first week is a catastrophe of small prayers and large silence. The heralds return, grim and triumphant.

choices.text: Refuse and offer a pay-rise in worship

effects.log: The heralds accept, glumly. A season later the loudest prayers are as loud as ever, and the heralds remember who bought them.

events.text: The order of arrival has worked better than anyone dared hope, and worse than anyone admitted. The loudest gods are furious, the quietest delighted, and a small god of lost buttons has, for the first time, received a hundred prayers answered in a week. The heralds ask what you intend next.

effects.log: You write it into the Throne's law. The loud gods grumble, and in time learn to wait. The heralds send you a banner embroidered with a button.
You allow exceptions. The heralds draw up the list with enormous care, and within a decade it has swallowed the rule. They are exhausted and proud.

events.text: A century on, the oldest herald of {b3_order} comes to you, bent as a root, and says the order of arrival is now the only law the mortals trust. The old herald asks for one reward: to hear, once, a prayer answered the way they would have wished it done when they were young. They sit down, and wait.

choices.text: Answer a prayer in front of them

effects.log: You choose a small prayer from a child, and answer it in the old herald's presence. They watch, and weep, and then fall quietly asleep with a smile.

choices.text: Give them a prayer to answer

effects.log: You hand the old herald a prayer and a pen. They answer it, shaking. It is the finest prayer ever answered in the Throne, and nobody ever reads it.

events.text: A god of a vanished domain, the god of a river that dried up, comes to the Throne of {b3_order} to request a pension. There is no such thing. The god sits on the step in the sun with a bundle of dry reeds and waits to be told no. The heralds hesitate. They have not, themselves, been told what to do.

effects.log: You invent one: a small daily ration of worship, drawn from the Throne's own. The god accepts, bewildered, and the river, a hundred years later, runs again in a dream.

choices.text: Offer the god a place on the staff

effects.log: The god becomes a gatekeeper and the best the Throne has had. The dry reeds are planted along the steps, and in spring they green.

events.text: The seat of {b3_order} receives a gift every year from a mortal woman in a country the pantheon has never governed: a pot of preserved plums, with a note. 'To the god who sits in the chair,' it reads. 'I do not know your name, but I think you might be tired.' This year's pot is dated with a woman's hand, shaking.

effects.log: You send a dream with a name and a thanks. She wakes and weeps and tells her granddaughter. The plums continue, and so do your visits.

choices.text: Send a blessing for her household

effects.log: You send a warm blessing to her house. Her family prospers quietly for a century, and never knows why the plums were so good.

events.text: A truce of fifty years between two domains is up in a week, and the seat of {b3_order} is expected to broker its renewal. Both sides have set out their terms in chests of paper. Both want the seat to read every one. You have a week, and a long, long reading list.

effects.log: You read for six days and part of the seventh. The terms are sixteen words, repeated. You sign the truce on the last afternoon, and it holds another fifty years.
You put both parties in a room with a pot of tea and no paper. By dusk they have agreed on eleven of the sixteen words, and find the rest do not matter.

events.text: In the library of {b3_order} you find that every holder of the seat before you has left a single sentence of advice in the margin of the Book of Seats. Most are banal. One is a drawing of a duck. One says only: 'Leave.' You are meant to add your own.

choices.text: Add a sentence of your own

effects.log: You write it in a firm hand: 'The heralds are the order.' It is remembered for ten thousand years, and followed, which surprises everyone but you.
You draw a duck. It is a better duck. It is quoted, solemnly, in the councils of every pantheon for the rest of the age.

events.text: A mortal comes to the temple of {b3_order} and asks to see the god in the seat. The priests, appalled, explain that it is not done. The mortal, a stout, determined woman with a basket, sits on the temple step and begins to knit. She will wait. She is quite prepared to wait for several years.

effects.log: You come down as a breath of warm air and a figure in the doorway. She looks up and says, 'Oh, there you are,' and shows you the scarf. It is for you.

choices.text: Send a dream and ask her to go home

effects.log: She wakes from a nap on the step, nods, and goes. She leaves the half-knitted scarf. In a hundred years the priests still keep it in a glass case.

events.text: {b3_elder}, the senior counsellor of {b3_order}, has been secretly writing the prayers that arrive, in the dead hours, to keep the lamps lit. They are polite, anonymous, and warm. Nobody has noticed because they are so well done. You find the stack by accident, in {b3_elder}'s desk, and sit down very quietly.

effects.log: You answer each one in turn. {b3_elder}, a century on, discovers the answers, and sits in the library for a long time, and says nothing, and smiles.
{b3_elder} blushes, a thing you did not think possible. The practice is made official, and a tradition: the dead hours are kept, in secret, with great tenderness.

events.text: The Throne of {b3_order} is traditionally warmed by an enormous brazier in winter. This year the brazier has gone out, and the god who tends it has fallen asleep. The Hall is cold, and the heralds are afraid to wake him. He is, by far, the oldest and grouchiest god in the Throne.

effects.log: You light it with a spark of your own worship. The old god wakes, scowls, and warms his hands, and says nothing. In spring he leaves a pot of honey on your desk.
You wake him with tea and an apology. He grumbles for an hour, and relights the brazier with a snap of his fingers. The Hall is warm by lunch.

events.text: A very young god, newly raised, comes to ask your advice on how to be a god. You have no idea how to answer. You have been one for four thousand years and still find the job surprising. The youngster waits with burning eyes, and a notebook already open.

effects.log: You say you do not know, and that the not knowing is most of it. They write that down, underline it, and become, in time, a kinder god than you.

choices.text: Tell them to eat well and sleep

effects.log: You say: eat, sleep, answer the smallest prayer first. They write that down. It is the best advice either of you ever receives.

events.text: An old enemy of {b3_order}, a god who has spent a thousand years sending storms against its temples, has sent you a letter of congratulation on taking the seat. The handwriting is shaky. The postscript says: 'I always hoped it would be somebody who read the mail.' It is signed with a tiny drawing of a hammer.

effects.log: You invite the old enemy to tea. They come, stiff as a plank, and stay for supper. The storms stop. The two of you are dreadful at conversation, and become friends.

choices.text: Keep the letter and stay wary

effects.log: You keep the letter, and your guard. The old enemy's storms do not return, but neither does the letter's warmth. You wonder, sometimes, what you missed.

events.text: Someone has sat in the Throne of {b3_order} while you were out. You can tell by the cushion, which has a dent in the wrong place, and by the tea, which is half-drunk and has too much honey. A note in a childlike hand reads, 'I only wanted to see.' Nobody on the staff will confess.

choices.text: Leave out another cup, and a second cushion

effects.log: The next morning the second cushion is dented, and the second cup drained. A small mortal ghost, perhaps, or a very shy god. You leave the cushion there, always.
The watch reveals a small stray spirit of dust, delighted to be noticed. It is installed as an unofficial mascot, and sits on the cushion in the sun for centuries.

events.text: The Book of Fates has a page for every holder of the seat of {b3_order}. Yours has been left blank, which is not unusual. What is unusual is that it is now slowly filling itself with a very small, careful handwriting that you recognise as your own, from a time you cannot place.

effects.log: It is a list of small kindnesses you have yet to do. You read them, and are afraid to do them, and do them anyway, one by one, over the years.
You close it. The writing continues, quietly, behind the cover. You can hear the pen. It is not hostile. It is just, unavoidably, there.

events.text: {b3_oldhead} has been spotted on the edge of the Hall of {b3_order}, in the guise of an old pilgrim, watching the proceedings. They are disguised, badly, in a straw hat. The heralds have been instructed not to see them. Everyone is straining to see anything else. The pilgrim leans on a stick and sniffs approvingly.

effects.log: You invite them to take the seat of honour. {b3_oldhead} refuses, then accepts, then orders the tea. They watch you for an hour and say only: 'Better than I was.'
You pretend not to see. The pilgrim goes home content, and sends a postcard the next day, signed with a straw-hat sketch. It is pinned to the wall.

events.text: At the end of your first age in the seat of {b3_order} the heralds present you with the ledger of everything you have done: three thousand pages, hand-bound. They have also, with great tact, appended a short list of what you did not. It is shorter than you expected, and worse.

choices.text: Read the list of what you did not

effects.log: It stays with you. In the next age you do, slowly, one of the things on it, and then another. The heralds take note, and do not say.

choices.text: Read the ledger of what you did

effects.log: You read what you did. It is a fine book. You keep it on the shelf where visitors can see it, and keep the other in your sleeve.

events.text: The Court of the Unlit Sun meets in the shadow behind the sun, in a hall with no ceiling and no walls, only a floor of cooled ash. A Night Herald hands you a candle that does not give light. 'You hold it,' the Herald says, 'so that you know what we do.' Its flame is a hole in the dark.

effects.log: You hold it, and the dark within it deepens. The Herald nods. The Court has found that you are patient, which is a rarer virtue than cruelty.
'What you would not say aloud,' the Herald murmurs. You find, to your surprise, that you can tell exactly how much that is.

events.text: Among the gods of what is eaten, hidden and owed, there is a ritual: each member of the Court gives up one secret per age, and writes it in the Book of the Unlit Sun, which no one reads. Yours is due. You consider what you hold. It is heavy, and small, and nameless.

effects.log: You write it down. The Book swallows it. You feel lighter, and slightly exposed, and the Court, which sees nothing and knows everything, hums.
You write something plausible and false. The Book swallows it too, and you feel a flicker of a laugh from the dark. It is not fooled, and does not mind.

events.text: A debtor of the Court, a minor god who borrowed worship at a ruinous rate, stands in the shadow with his head bowed. He cannot pay. The Court's custom is to take something he loves. He has nothing left but a small wooden bird, carved by his mother. The Court looks to you.

effects.log: You take it, and the debt is cleared. He leaves, hollow and free. In a century you return it in secret, and the debtor never learns who.

choices.text: Forgive the debt and pay it yourself

effects.log: You pay it from your own stores, and tell no one. The Court notes the loss, and the cost, and respects you in the particular way the dark respects things.

events.text: A pilgrim has come to the Unlit Sun's door asking not for power but for forgetting. They have done something they cannot bear, and they would like it taken. The Court deals in debts, and things hidden, and this is both. A Lamp-Snuffer looks at you. 'What do we ask,' they murmur, 'in return?'

effects.log: You ask for nothing. The pilgrim is made to forget, and is gentle ever after. The Court sighs: you have given a gift where it traded, and the dark, uneasily, approves.

choices.text: Ask for a memory of equal weight

effects.log: You ask for a memory of equal weight. The pilgrim gives one, a sweet one, and you carry it, with a small stab of unfairness, for centuries.

events.text: The Eclipse Lord of the Court has a pet, a very small star, extinguished, that sits on his shoulder and gutters faintly when he is angry. It has begun to flicker at you. The Eclipse Lord observes this and says, without turning his head: 'It has not done that for anyone in nine hundred years.'

effects.log: The star-ember settles on your finger, a cold small weight, and sighs. The Eclipse Lord says nothing for a long time, and then, in a dry voice, 'Good.'
'Always,' says the Eclipse Lord, 'a little.' It is the first personal thing he has said to anyone in years. You sit with him, and the ember, and the dark.

events.text: The Court of the Unlit Sun keeps a ledger of what is owed. It is as large as a mountain and written in tiny letters, and every god of the pantheons has an entry. You are given a day to look at your own. It is longer than you hoped, and the first entry is in a handwriting you know.

effects.log: It is a small debt, to a mortal you forgot, for a kindness never repaid. You find them in a dream, an old man, and say thank you. He says, 'You are welcome. It took you long enough.'
The last is blank, with a date: not yet. You close the ledger, and are quiet all week, and a little kinder than before.

events.text: A rival of the Court, a god of the Will of Heaven who despises the dark, comes to its door to complain about the shadows it casts across his temples at noon. He is genuinely furious and quite right. The Night Herald is unmoved. You are asked to see him out.

effects.log: You walk him out and apologise, truthfully. He is thrown. By the gate, he mutters that the shadows are, in fact, rather restful on a hot day.

choices.text: Walk him out and say nothing

effects.log: You walk him out in silence. He goes, glaring. The shadows lengthen a little that afternoon, and a temple in the sun is, briefly, cold.

events.text: On the night of the Long Dark, the Unlit Sun's members each light a candle of their own hiding. The shadows are thick as velvet and full of small sounds. A candle is lit in front of you by a hand you cannot see, and in its glow is a face, yours, younger and kinder, watching you with an expression of simple hope.

effects.log: You tell it, quietly, what has happened. It listens. When you finish, it nods once and fades. The candle burns down. You are lighter for the telling.
You snuff it. The dark swallows the face. It is the kind of thing the Court admires. You sleep badly for a month.

events.text: The Court has a custom of the Shared Meal: once an age, all the members dine on what the Court has taken in tribute, which is almost always grief. The grief is cooked, lovingly, by the oldest Ash-Bearer, with salt. It is the best meal you have ever tasted and you cannot bear to ask why.

effects.log: You eat it all. You weep through the pudding. The Court weeps with you, in a quiet, orderly way, and afterwards is cheerful.
The Ash-Bearer is astonished and eats your leftovers in silence. A bowl is left outside your door each night for a year. You do not ask what is in it.

events.text: A mortal sorcerer far below has been summoning the Court by name, with chalk and dried herbs, and mispronouncing it, so that the summons arrives garbled. The Court receives a half-formed invitation to tea. The Night Herald, vexed, asks who will answer. The summons is the sort of embarrassing thing that must be done.

effects.log: You appear in a chalk circle in a cottage kitchen. The sorcerer, an elderly woman with flour on her hands, is flustered, apologetic, and a delight. You stay for a pot of tea. She never asks for anything.

choices.text: Send a dream with the correct pronunciation

effects.log: You send the correct name in a dream. The sorcerer wakes and, thereafter, gets it right. The Court is both mildly impressed and mildly disappointed.

events.text: A god of the Will of Heaven, bright and desperate, comes to the Court of the Unlit Sun to borrow a thing it has never lent: dark. A little shadow, for a festival of the stars that needs contrast. The Court is amused. The Eclipse Lord names a price. The price is, quite plainly, a debt of light, to be called in at a time of the Court's choosing.

effects.log: You broker it. The god of the Will signs with a shaking hand. The festival is a triumph, and the debt is entered in the great Ledger in a hand that is not quite yours.

choices.text: Refuse the loan on the god's behalf

effects.log: You refuse. The god, bewildered, thanks you, and goes. The festival is a dim one. The Court, not offended, adds a small note: 'Prudent. Remember.'

events.text: The Court calls in its debt of light. The god of the Will comes to you, white, because the thing the Court asks is a single dawn, borrowed, from the god's own temple, on the day of its greatest festival. The god asks you to speak with the Court. You know the Court, and the Court knows you.

effects.log: The Eclipse Lord considers, and agrees to a smaller dawn: the first minute. The god of the Will gives it up with a trembling sigh and is, afterwards, a changed and humbler god.
You pay half from your own worship. The god pays the rest. The Court is satisfied, and you gain an unusual standing in the shadow: someone who pays for others.

events.text: A century later, the god of the Will comes to the door of the Unlit Sun carrying a lantern, and offers it freely, unasked. It holds the light of the dawn they once gave up, kept and kindled. 'Not repaying,' the god says. 'Giving.' The Court is hushed. The Eclipse Lord has not, in nine thousand years, been given anything.

choices.text: Accept the lantern for the Court

effects.log: The Eclipse Lord takes the lantern with both hands. The Court's hall, for the first time, has a small, steady light. It is not comfortable. They keep it.

choices.text: Ask the Court to accept it

effects.log: The Eclipse Lord does. His voice, as he says thank you, cracks. The god of the Will departs, lighter, and with a friend in the dark.

events.text: A Night Herald asks you, in confidence, to deliver an unsigned warning to a god of the Silent Hall who has begun to forget the names of the dead. The Court wants to help without appearing to. You are to leave the note on a doorstep and say nothing. It is the sort of kindness the Court cannot admit.

effects.log: You leave the note. The god of the Silent Hall finds it, reads it, and after a week begins to write names on the walls. The Court says nothing, and nothing is exactly right.
You sign it, which is not the Court's way. The god of the Silent Hall thanks you by name. The Herald scolds you, and then, in the corner, smiles.

events.text: A pair of Court initiates, twins of the eclipse, argue each night about which of them is the shadow and which the sun. You are the Court's judge of small disputes, a post of no honour. They come before you, glaring, hand in hand. Each says the other copies. Neither will let go.

choices.text: Rule that they are both shadows

effects.log: They stare at you. Then they laugh, and then they cry, and then they go away together, still holding hands, and cease to quarrel.

choices.text: Rule that neither is, and send them to the kitchens

effects.log: They scrub pots together for a decade. They emerge as the best-loved pair in the Court, and no one ever asks which is which.

events.text: The Court of the Unlit Sun is asked by the Throne of Storms to hide a thing: a fine, bright, terrible thing, a lightning-bolt that fell and never discharged. They want it kept in the dark until it forgets. The Court agrees. You are to be its keeper. It hums, and smells of ozone, and has begun to sulk.

effects.log: You keep it in a drawer lined with ash. It sulks for a decade, then dozes. When it is returned, it is a very ordinary spark, and the Throne is relieved.
You talk to it each night. It learns to listen. When it is returned, it discharges softly in the Throne of Storms, over the sea, and is gone like a sigh.

events.text: A famous Heavenly Court inquisitor has come to the door of the Unlit Sun with a warrant, searching for a stolen thing. The Court denies it. The inquisitor is polite and implacable. You know where the stolen thing is: in your sleeve, given to you by a desperate friend. The inquisitor looks at you.

effects.log: The inquisitor takes it with a small, pale smile. Your friend is exposed. The Court's regard for you is quiet, and cold, and then, after a decade, thaws.

ok.log: The inquisitor believes you, and leaves. The thing stays in your sleeve, warm, a secret and a weight. The Court sends a bowl of black plums.

fail.log: The inquisitor sees through you. You are fined a year of your standing, and the thing is taken.

events.text: The Hand of the Unlit Sun, the Court's chief, is dying. They have kept the Court from fraying for twenty thousand years by never telling anyone what they felt. At the last they ask you to stay beside the bed and not to speak. You sit. The silence is complete, and it is, you realise, a kind of love.

effects.log: The Hand dies at dusk, and the shadow across the room lifts, a little. You sit another hour, and then rise. The Court is a degree warmer.
You say, 'Thank you.' The Hand's eyes open. They say nothing, but their hand finds yours. The Court is told nothing, and all of it, by your face.

events.text: The Court of the Unlit Sun has a Hall of Masks, where the members wear whichever face the moment needs. You are asked to choose one for the next age. They are all lies, politely. One is blank. One is smiling. One, at the back, is yours, as it was in your first life, and it is very tired.

effects.log: You put it on. It fits too well. The Court, who sees, says nothing, and you walk out into the Hall with the oldest face you own, and are, for the first time in ages, plain.
You wear the blank. It is restful. It changes, slowly, to match whoever speaks to you, and the Court soon calls you the Mirror.

events.text: A dying mortal far below prays to the Unlit Sun for one last secret to be buried: a name that must not be spoken after death. The Court agrees. A Night Herald hands you the secret in a sealed jar, and asks you to keep it for a thousand years. It is warm, and it is trembling.

effects.log: You keep it on a shelf for a thousand years. Every night it trembles, and every night you leave it be. When the time comes you bury it in the ash, and the Court sighs.
A single word slips out, soft and kind, a mortal's name. You close it again. You will never speak it, but you will hear it, always, at the edge of sleep.

events.text: A very small god of what is lost under couches has joined the Court, and is thrilled. Their domain is buttons, coins and the left sock. They trot into the Unlit Sun's hall with a tray of lost things, humbly, to present as tribute. The Court is moved. The Eclipse Lord eyes a particularly fine button.

effects.log: You praise it with great seriousness. The Court accepts the button with a courtly bow. The little god glows, and is the Court's favourite from that day.
You establish a small service for the matching of lost socks. It is the Court's most useful work in ten thousand years, and nobody dares say so.

events.text: The shadow behind the sun has a draught, and you have found where it comes from: a hole in the world, small and round, no bigger than a cup, through which a faint, cold wind blows. Someone has set a cup on it. The cup is full of something that glints. You are, plainly, supposed to find it.

effects.log: You see a quiet kitchen, a long way off, with a woman at a table who is, by all appearances, waiting for you. You close your eyes. When you open them the hole is a cup again.
You cover it with a saucer. The wind stops. The cup, under the saucer, hums a little, and the Court puts a candle on it, for the draught.

events.text: A young god of the Unlit Sun, newly sworn, comes to you in tears. They have done something the Court asks of them, and they cannot sleep. A mortal woman begged, and they refused, as the Court requires. They ask if it is right. You are not sure the Court would approve of the answer you want to give.

effects.log: You tell them so, plainly. They weep harder, then stop, then go down to the woman's house in a dream and make it right. The Court looks away, and lets it stand.

choices.text: Tell them it was the Court's law

effects.log: You tell them the law. They nod, hollow, and go back to their duty. You watch them go and wonder what you have done.

events.text: A star in the sky of the world below has been dying for a million years and has finally asked to be given to the Unlit Sun. It is a gentle old star, and does not want a funeral. It would like to go quietly, behind the sun, where it will not be seen. The Court's custom is clear: the dying come here.

effects.log: You receive it in the shadow behind the sun. It settles, dims, sighs, and is gone, leaving a warmth in the ash. The Court keeps it, always, as a hearth.
You sit with it, as with a dying friend, for a thousand years. When it goes you carry its last light in your sleeve, and it makes you gentler.

events.text: A rumour has reached the Court that someone far above is trying to light the Unlit Sun. A zealot of the Will of Heaven has found a way. The Court is divided: some members would welcome the light, some would be undone by it. The Night Herald asks for your vote, and the Herald's eyes are wet.

effects.log: The vote carries narrowly. The zealot lights the Sun for an hour, and the Court stands, blinking, and some of its members weep. It does not last. It is not forgotten.
The vote carries. The Sun remains unlit. The zealot leaves, rebuffed, and the Court is darker, and safe, and a little less than it was.

events.text: The Court of the Unlit Sun has a long and hallowed tradition of stealing small things from the other pantheons: a spoon, a hat, a half-finished poem. The thefts are never malicious. They are returned a century later, with interest. It is your turn to choose what is stolen. You think carefully.

effects.log: You take a famous god's first prayer, a faded scrap. A century later you return it, framed. The god sits with it all day, and sends the Court a basket of apricots.
A spoon is stolen. A century later it is returned with a tiny spoon beside it, and a note. The pantheon in question is baffled and, privately, thrilled.

events.text: A small wounded spirit crawls into the hall of the Unlit Sun and collapses before the Eclipse Lord. It is a spirit of the dawn, wrecked by a dispute with its own pantheon. It has come here because the Court is the only place where no one will ask it to be bright. The Eclipse Lord looks at you.

effects.log: You take it in, and tend it. It sleeps for a year in the shade. When it wakes, it is grey and small and cheerful, and refuses to be bright again, and is loved.

choices.text: Send it to the Green Assembly

effects.log: You send it to the Green Assembly's garden, where there is shade and no questions. It is happy there. It sends a seed each spring, and it blooms by your door.

events.text: A god of the Court has been caught in the act of an unexpected mercy: they spared a debtor, quietly, and then lied about it. The Court has an interest in the lie, not the mercy. A tribunal is convened in the dark. You are one of three. The accused stands very straight, and is shaking.

effects.log: You acquit, citing a clerical error. The Court mutters. The accused weeps in the corridor, and is thereafter the most loyal member of the dark.

choices.text: Convict, and sentence to a quiet year

effects.log: You convict, and sentence them to a quiet year, in the care of the oldest Ash-Bearer. They return changed, deeper, kinder, still lying a little.

events.text: On the shortest day, the Court of the Unlit Sun holds a vigil for the sun, in which all the members sit in the dark and wait for the light to return. It is a joke the Court makes against itself. This year the sun is late. The members shift. A very old voice from the back says, quite calmly: 'Perhaps this time.'

effects.log: You wait. The sun is a few minutes late, and the Court holds its breath, and when it comes, a small gold bar across the ash, the Court exhales in one long sigh. It is the best moment of the age.

choices.text: Tell a joke to pass the time

effects.log: You tell a joke about eclipses. It is dreadful, and the Court roars, and the sun, to its astonishment, finds the whole Court laughing at the dawn.

events.text: In a dream, an old mortal sits at your table and eats your bread and says nothing. You do not know them. They look at your bread with great love. They weep a little, and leave. In the morning there is a small cut loaf on the table. It tastes of a house you used to live in, in a life you do not remember.

effects.log: You eat it. The taste fills you with a sad, deep warmth. The Court, passing, says only: 'We all have one.'

choices.text: Leave the loaf for the Court

effects.log: You share it among the Ash-Bearers. They eat in solemn silence, and for a week the Court is quiet with remembering, and you are well loved.

events.text: The Court of the Unlit Sun has a famous rule: no member may ever refuse a request made at midnight by the light of a single candle. A small child, seven or so, mortal, a prayer-ghost, has appeared at the door at midnight with a candle and a toy horse. It asks you, in a very small voice, to find its mother.

effects.log: You search through the ledger of the dead, and the ledger of the living, and find her, an old woman, in a far country, waiting. You carry the child to her door. She opens it, and does not speak.

choices.text: Walk the child to the Silent Hall

effects.log: You walk the child to the Silent Hall and place it in the care of the Ferryman. He takes the toy horse and the candle with a solemn nod. The child sleeps.

events.text: The most dangerous debt the Court holds is a debt of silence, owed by a god who knows the true name of the world and swore never to speak it. They are dying, slowly, of holding it in. The Court has decided that someone must hear it, to relieve them. It will be you, if you will take it.

effects.log: The name is quiet, and ordinary, and unbearable. You carry it ever after. It is a kind of loneliness, and a kind of company, and the Court salutes you.
You decline, honestly. The god sighs and chooses another, a quiet scribe, who bears it with good grace. The Court does not hold your refusal against you, and nor, quite, does the scribe.

events.text: A mortal prayer reaches the Court that is not for a favour but for company: someone, in a dark house, alone at night, praying to the shadows because the shadows seem friendlier than the day. The Court has a rule about prayers like these. They are answered by whichever member happens to be nearest. Tonight it is you.

choices.text: Sit with them in the dark

effects.log: You sit beside the bed for a night, unseen, and breathe quietly, and by dawn they are asleep. You do it again, every year, on the same night.
You send a dream of a lit window and a kettle singing. The sleeper wakes with an odd contentment, and the shadows, in that house, are kind for the rest of their life.

events.text: A god of the Court of the Unlit Sun has gone missing. They left a note: 'Gone to see what the light is like.' The Court is outraged, delighted, and afraid. A search party of one is assembled, and you are it. Behind you, the Night Herald says, quietly, 'Tell them we are not angry.'

effects.log: You find them on a hillside at dawn, squinting in the sun, with their hands out. They look at you, and laugh. They return in a year, brown and humbled, and the Court never speaks of it.
You report that you could not find them. The Court knows. A year on, a postcard arrives from a sunny country, with a small, blurry sketch of a sunrise.

events.text: The Concord of Domains meets in a ring of empty chairs, one for every god who has ever slept, and the oath is sworn aloud: that no domain shall be taken while its god sleeps. A Concord Warden hands you a cup of water. 'Drink,' they say, 'and mean it.' The water tastes of every domain at once.

effects.log: You swear, and the ring of empty chairs creaks softly, each in turn. You feel, for a moment, the sleeping gods' regard like a warm hand on your shoulder.

choices.text: Drink and ask what it means

effects.log: The Warden smiles. 'It means you have no domain of your own that is safe,' they say. 'That is the point.' You swear anyway, a little more soberly.

events.text: A god of the Throne of Storms lies sleeping in a high valley. His domain, the Sea of Eastern Gales, is being quietly annexed by a god of the Will of Heaven, who is a good deal more awake. The Concord has been informed. A Concord Envoy asks you to go and tell the annexing god, politely, to stop.

effects.log: You go. The annexing god is cordial and unrepentant. You spend a week in a negotiation of hats, in which he gives back the Sea but keeps, as a trophy, a gale.
The letter is read. The annexing god is deeply embarrassed, since the Concord is never to be provoked. The Sea is returned by dawn, with a bowl of apologetic plums.

events.text: A sleeping god of Dreams in the Silent Hall has been robbed. Not of his domain, but of a single dream, a very old one he was saving. The Concord, bound to protect, takes the theft as an attack. The thief, a small mortal ghost with a pillow, is caught and shaking. She says she only wanted to see what it was.

choices.text: Return the dream, and keep the ghost

effects.log: You return the dream, and take the ghost on as a clerk of the Concord. She is a diligent, dreamy filing-clerk, and sleeps with her head on the ledger.
You punish her with a century of silence. The ghost accepts it with a nod. The dream is returned, slightly worn at the edges.

events.text: The Concord's Keeper asks you to count the sleeping gods. It is a simple task: walk the ring of chairs and tally those with someone in them. You count nine hundred and twelve. The Keeper looks at your tally and says there should be nine hundred and thirteen. There is a chair you did not see, and it is yours.

effects.log: You sit. It fits. A small tally is added. The Keeper nods. 'Not asleep yet,' they say, 'but the chair is patient.' You rise with a very odd feeling, as of having been measured.
You leave it, and the Keeper writes it in the margin as 'reserved'. It sits there for ten thousand years, polished weekly.

events.text: A god in the Concord's ring has woken after five thousand years of sleep. They sit up in the chair, blink, and ask what has changed. Nobody quite has the heart to tell them: their domain has, in the interval, been divided, renamed, and in one case turned into a pub. You are the first to speak to them.

effects.log: You tell them. It takes the afternoon, with a pot of tea. They listen, and nod, and ask about the pub. By evening they are laughing, a thin, stunned, bright sound.

choices.text: Say only that the world is well

effects.log: You say the world is well. It is true, in a way. They nod, and rest, and ask no more. You tell yourself it was a kindness, and the Concord does not enquire.

events.text: The woken god has taken up their domain: the weather of one particular hill, and the songs sung on it. The hill has changed; so have the songs. They ask the Concord's help to learn them again. Every evening they sit on the hill, in the dusk, and a handful of mortal children, who have heard, sit with them and teach.

choices.text: Join the evenings on the hill

effects.log: You sit with them and the children. By the third month the god has learned seven songs, and written one. The hill is greener than it has been in an age.
You send a teacher, a retired bard of the Green Assembly. The god and the bard become inseparable. The hill's songs are sung in two accents ever after.

events.text: A thousand years later, the woken god stands for the seat of Keeper of the Concord. They are a surprising candidate: shy, patient, and wildly out of date. The Concord debates for a year. The votes are tied, and the deciding vote falls to you. The god looks at you across the ring, hopeful and afraid.

effects.log: The god takes the chair. In a year, the Concord's oath is rewritten, simply, in the old style, and it is the most beloved version yet.

choices.text: Vote for the other, and say why

effects.log: You vote against, honestly, and explain. The woken god takes it well, and returns to the hill, and writes you a song. The Concord remembers your candour.

events.text: A god of the Harvest sleeps under a field in the country of mortals, and the farmers above have just begun to dig a well in the same spot. The well will wake him. It will be the end of the field, and the farm, and perhaps a great deal else. The Concord's duty is to stop it. The farmers are not wicked. They are thirsty.

choices.text: Divert the well to a nearby spring

effects.log: You nudge the farmers' spade a hundred paces east. Water is struck at once, sweet and clear. The sleeping god turns over, content, and the field grows richer for a century.
You wake him with a cup of cold water and a murmur. He yawns, and says the field is welcome to the well. The farmers, who dream of a kind old man, name the well after him.

events.text: A junior Concord Witness named Min, bright and over-eager, files a report of a hundred and twenty pages on a minor infringement: a god of the Mountains has added a pebble to a slope without consulting the sleeper below. The pebble is real. So is the report. Min waits by your desk, trembling with importance.

effects.log: You read it. It is meticulous, and sweet, and at the end, in a footnote, Min writes: 'It was a very nice pebble.' You rule it a lesson, and Min a treasure.
You dismiss it with a smile. Min deflates, then straightens. 'Quite right,' they say. 'I was getting carried away.' They become, in time, the Concord's best judge of proportion.

events.text: The Concord holds a trial: a god of Fire is accused of stealing a dream of Fate, which sleeps. The god of Fire says he borrowed it to light a lamp. The dream, a bright wounded thing in a jar, hums. The Concord looks to you for a ruling. The god of Fire stares at his feet.

effects.log: You rule it theft. The god of Fire pays the sleeper's priests in a hundred lamps. The dream is returned, and the lamps, strangely, burn with a kind of grief.

choices.text: Rule it borrowing, and set a rate

effects.log: You rule it a loan, and set a term. The sleeper's dream is lent a thousand nights to the lamp and then returned. The god of Fire is chastened and the dream, rested, hums contentedly.

events.text: At the Concord's yearly vigil, the members sit by the beds of sleeping gods in turn, and tell them the news. It is a custom of tenderness. This year you are assigned a very old god of the Sea who has slept for six thousand years. You tell him the news. His eyelid twitches, as if to say: go on.

effects.log: You tell him for a whole night, small things and large. At dawn his hand moves, very slightly, and the tide below, for a moment, runs backward.

choices.text: Tell him only the good news

effects.log: You tell him the good news, and there is more than you thought. By dawn you are smiling, and so, you could swear, is the sleeper.

events.text: A god of the Beasts sleeps in a cave. A bear, his oldest friend, has been guarding the entrance for four thousand years. The bear has grown thin and slow and tired, and is not allowed to leave. He growls at you as you approach, and then sits down, because he is too tired to stand. The Concord's rule is that no sleeper's guard may be relieved without consent.

effects.log: You enter the cave and whisper. The sleeper, deep in sleep, moves his hand, once. It is enough. The bear is relieved, and sleeps for a year at the mouth of the cave, content.

choices.text: Guard the cave for a night yourself

effects.log: You sit at the cave's mouth while the bear goes to the river. He comes back quiet and washed and grateful, and growls at you, once, in a friendly way.

events.text: The Concord's court is asked to rule on an old puzzle: if a god sleeps for ten thousand years, and a mortal prays to them each day, and the prayers pile up unanswered, to whom do the prayers belong? A deputation of lawyers has been preparing the argument for three centuries. You are asked to give the first view.

choices.text: The prayers belong to the sleeper

effects.log: You rule that the prayers wait. The lawyers sigh with joy and begin to write, and a library of prayers grows at the foot of the sleeper's bed, quiet and unharvested.

choices.text: The prayers belong to the one who prays

effects.log: You rule the prayers return, in time, to the one who prayed them, as a blessing. The lawyers are shocked, and a tradition begins that is kinder than the law.

events.text: A Concord Warden is found sleeping at their post, and the Concord, which exists to protect the sleeping, is thrown into confusion: is it a crime? The Warden wakes, appalled, apologises, and is asked to explain. They say they had not slept in four hundred years. A hush falls. They look at you for support.

effects.log: You defend them: a sleeping Warden is no worse than a waking one, and perhaps more honest. The Concord, after a pause, laughs, and the Warden is excused and sent on a long, deserved holiday.
You insist, gently. The Warden accepts a light reprimand. They sleep, afterwards, at a decent hour, and the Concord thinks well of your fairness.

events.text: A god of the Mountains comes to the Concord in a rage: a sleeping god of the Harvest has been, he claims, 'growing in his sleep'. The god of the Mountains says the harvest is spreading up his slope. The field has crept a hand's breadth. The Harvest, asleep, is blameless. The Mountains, awake, is furious.

effects.log: You walk the slope with both domains, and agree on a fence of stones. The sleeper's field stops. The god of the Mountains leaves a handful of wild flowers on it as a peace-offering.
You rule for the Harvest, citing the Concord. The god of the Mountains is stung, and sulks, and a year later sends an apology of dry stone walls.

events.text: A mortal prophet has found the entrance to a sleeping god's chamber, and means to wake them with a bell. The Concord is alerted. The prophet is not wicked, only certain: the god, they believe, will save a drowning country. A Concord Envoy is dispatched. You are told the prophet cannot be harmed.

effects.log: You speak with the prophet for three days. In the end the prophet sets the bell aside, and rings it instead in a field, for the drowning country, and all the villagers come.
You take it. The prophet weeps, and curses, and goes to find another bell. The sleeper sleeps on. The country, in time, learns to swim.

events.text: The Concord has a Book of Dormancies, in which every sleeping god's domain is described, so that nobody shall mistake it for abandoned. It has one blank page, which is yours. A clerk asks, delicately, whether you would like to fill in your domain now, in case you are ever, as it were, unavailable.

effects.log: You write it in plain words, and sign. The clerk blots it and closes the book gently. You feel, for the first time, a kind of plain, quiet security.

choices.text: Leave it blank, with a smile

effects.log: You leave it blank. The clerk makes a note: 'to be filled in when needed.' It stays there, a white page, with something almost like a promise.

events.text: In the Concord's ring, a sleeping god's chair is found empty, the cushion dented, a warm cup beside it. The sleeper has gone, mid-sleep, on some errand of their own. The Concord is aghast: can a sleeper walk? A search of the cosmos is called. You are put in charge of finding a god who isn't, technically, awake.

effects.log: They lead to a mortal bedroom. The sleeper is sitting by a sick child, holding its hand, fast asleep. You stay with them till the fever breaks, and the sleeper walks home, unknowing.

choices.text: Wait for them to come back

effects.log: You wait. They return at dawn, and slide into the chair, and sleep on. You never learn where they went, and the cup is, on the table, still warm.

events.text: An envoy of the Court of the Unlit Sun comes to the Concord with a polite proposal: that the dark pantheon be admitted to the oath as an equal. The Concord is aghast. The envoy is courteous and unsmiling and holds out a sealed paper. 'They would like to be protected as well,' the envoy says. 'Quietly. Sleep is sleep.'

effects.log: You argue it for three nights. The Concord yields, narrowly. The Unlit Sun swears the oath in a dark corner with a small, shy candle. The Concord is a little stronger.
You argue against. The envoy bows, unoffended. 'We shall ask again in an age,' they say. The Concord is safe, and a little smaller.

events.text: The Concord has declared a Day of Waking, to remind its members what they protect. They each wake one sleeper at random for an hour, just to say hello. You draw a very old god of the Mountains, whom you have never met. They open one eye. 'Ah,' they say. 'You. I was hoping it would be you.' They don't say why.

choices.text: Sit with them for the hour

effects.log: You sit with them for the hour. They say very little. At the end they say, 'Thank you,' and sleep on. You have never felt so honoured.
'You were kind to a pebble once,' says the god. 'I remember.' The eye closes. You cannot remember the pebble. You decide that, from now on, you will be kind to all of them.

events.text: A god of Thunder has been accused of snoring. It is a minor charge, but it has rattled the windows of three mortal villages and the Concord's own tea-cups. The sleeper is blameless; the villages are cross. A petition arrives, signed by a goat. You are asked to find a compromise that disturbs neither.

choices.text: Build a hush around the sleeper

effects.log: You build a ring of wool-clouds around the sleeper. The snoring becomes a distant purr. The villages are grateful, and the goat sends another petition, in thanks.

choices.text: Teach the villages to like it

effects.log: You send a dream to each village that thunder-snoring is a lullaby. By spring they are sleeping better than ever, and name their children after the rumble.

events.text: The Concord's archive holds the last words of every god who died in their sleep. They are almost always trivial: a request for a blanket, the name of a dog, a grievance about soup. The archivist, very old, reads them aloud on the quiet evenings. Tonight she reads a line that is addressed to you. It says: 'Tell them it was fine.'

effects.log: The archivist consults the register. 'A god you never met,' she says. 'She left it for whoever sat in your chair.' You sit for a long time, and then say, aloud, 'It was fine.'

choices.text: Copy it to carry with you

effects.log: You copy the line onto a scrap and fold it into your sleeve. In the years to come, when things are bad, you take it out. It always works, a little.

events.text: A very old Concord oath is nearly forgotten: that the Concord's members must, once every thousand years, trade places with a sleeper for a night, and dream what they dream. The Concord has let it slide. A young Witness reminds the Keeper. The Keeper, aghast, turns to the oldest member. That is you.

effects.log: You lie in a sleeper's chair and dream a dream of a tall quiet city that has no people, only lights. You wake lighter and not entirely certain which of you was dreaming.
A younger member volunteers, grinning. They return changed, and refuse to speak of it, and are never again afraid of the dark.

events.text: At the Concord's gate, an old, shabby, dignified god in a threadbare robe asks for admission. He has no domain left. It was taken from him, while he slept, a very long time ago, and the Concord was not yet founded. He has been looking for the oath ever since. He says he does not want it back. He only wants the oath to exist.

effects.log: You open the gate, and give him a chair in the ring. He sits, and the ring, which had held nine hundred and thirteen, holds nine hundred and fourteen, and the oath, for a moment, is whole.

You offer to return it, what remains. He shakes his head, smiling. 'Keep it,' he says. 'Someone should.' He sits in the ring, and you look after the domain, which turns out to be a very small, very fine pond.

events.text: An embassy from the mortal world, led by a gruff old farmer, presents the Concord with a petition: that the sleeping gods be allowed to wake for the harvest festival, once a year, to see what they are protecting. The Concord has never been asked anything so sweet. The farmer stands, hat in hands, and the Concord falls silent.

effects.log: You grant it. Once a year, in the autumn, the sleeping gods stir for a day. Mortals gather in the fields and sing, and the gods wake, and smile, and sleep again. The Concord has never been more loved.

choices.text: Grant it on a smaller scale

effects.log: You grant it for one god, chosen by lot. The farmer's village is the lucky one. The god of the Harvest sits among them at the festival, and cries quietly into his beer.

events.text: A sleeping goddess of Life sighs in her sleep and, in the room where she lies, a flower unfolds. The Concord Wardens on duty are alarmed: is it a stirring? An alarm has been raised. Her bedside is thronged with anxious officials. The flower opens fully. It is a plain, small, white one. It smells of cold milk and early morning.

effects.log: You stay until it fades. She does not wake. But the room is a little warmer, and the Wardens, standing round, one by one find themselves smiling.

choices.text: Press the flower in a book

effects.log: You press it in the Book of Dormancies, at her page. In a thousand years she will wake, find it, and know that someone looked after her.

events.text: The Concord's oath is read aloud at every meeting, and every meeting someone, somewhere, mishears a word. Tonight it is 'no domain is taken while its god sleeps' that comes out, from a nervous initiate, as 'no domain is baked while its god sleeps'. A silence. Then the whole Concord begins, helplessly, to laugh.

effects.log: You laugh until you cry. The initiate, mortified, is rescued by the Keeper, who says it is the first time in a thousand years the oath has been enjoyed. 'Baked' becomes the Concord's private word for the sweetest ones.

choices.text: Adopt the misreading as an honorary amendment

effects.log: You propose an amendment to protect baked domains too. It carries with a roar. A shrine to the cooking of pies is built in the corner of the ring.

events.text: At the long night of the Concord, a younger member asks you what you are protecting. You hesitate. You have the oath, the chairs, the sleeping gods, the empty rooms. You say 'domains', and the youngster looks politely unconvinced. They ask again, gently. They are not trying to catch you. They really want to know.

effects.log: You say you are protecting the right of anyone to rest, safely, without waking to find that the world has been taken from them. It is the first time you have said it aloud, and it is true.
They think for a moment. 'The dreams,' they say. 'Not the domains. The dreams.' You nod slowly. The youngster is, on the whole, a better Warden than you.

events.text: The Hall of Gales has a rafter that creaks in a particular key whenever somebody in the room is lying. It has been creaking for a week at the council. No one admits to anything. Haeryong stares at the ceiling. Noejin stares at his boots. Gaksan, asleep, is making the loudest creak of all.

choices.text: Own up to a small lie

effects.log: You admit one, aloud, a trivial one. The creak stops. The Hall releases a breath, and three other gods confess to smaller ones, and the rafter is silent for a decade.
