Gaksan wakes with a rumble and says he was dreaming of a lie he told in the last age. He tells it. It is dazzling. The creak ceases, in awe.

events.text: {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} have fallen out over a hymn. Each claims it as the order's own, and each sings it a different way. The two have been interrupting each other's services for a week, in perfect pitch, to the delight of the worshippers, who have begun to take sides.

effects.log: You rule for {b3_elder}. {b3_peer} stalks out and composes a rival hymn within the month, which is, annoyingly, better.
You rule for {b3_peer}. {b3_elder} accepts it with a tight smile, and sings the old way, very quietly, in the bath.
They sing it together, grimly, in two keys. By the third verse they have found a third, and the worshippers weep. The hymn is theirs jointly forever.

events.text: {b3_elder} accuses {b3_peer} of stealing a small miracle: a rain that fell on a village in {b3_elder}'s domain and was credited to {b3_peer}. The village, asked, says it was a very nice rain and cannot say whose. Both gods look at you, offended in two directions.

effects.log: You ask the village again, in a dream. They say: 'Both?' The answer is accepted with deep disappointment on both sides, and a little relief.
You split the rain's credit by half, to the drop. The two gods split the offering likewise. They are equally unhappy, which is, in a pantheon, a kind of peace.
You claim the rain as a ruling of the order. Both gods are silenced, and mutter about favouritism for a century.

events.text: It has come out that {b3_peer} told a worshipper something unkind about {b3_elder}'s domain: that it is dull. {b3_elder} has taken to wearing black. The worshipper, a pig-farmer, is appalled, and wishes to apologise to both. {b3_peer} is unrepentant. 'It is dull,' they say. 'I love it.'

effects.log: {b3_peer} apologises, loudly and graciously, in a speech so long it becomes a compliment. {b3_elder} is mollified and then, to everyone's surprise, flattered.

choices.text: Agree it is dull, and have the dullness defended

effects.log: You make a stand for dullness. It becomes the order's motto: Steadfast, Dull, True. {b3_elder} stops wearing black, and starts wearing grey, with relish.
You say nothing. The feud simmers, and the pig-farmer, in the end, makes the peace by sending both of them a pie.

events.text: {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} each believe the other has been sending them anonymous poems about their failings. The poems are quite good. Each poet is certain the other is the author. The author is neither. The author is the order's door-keeper, a tired god of thresholds with an ear for iambs.

effects.log: You find the door-keeper in the attic with a lamp and a stack of rhymes. The poems are put into a volume, and the door-keeper is made the order's poet laureate. {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} sit through the reading in a sort of shocked amity.
You let it run. The poems keep coming. By the fifth year both gods are secretly writing replies, and the two are, in all but name, in conversation.

events.text: {b3_peer} has been accused by {b3_elder} of watering the order's wine. It is true, and was an act of kindness: the wine was too strong for the youngest gods. {b3_elder}, who made it, is mortified and furious. The hall gathers round to see the verdict. The cup is passed to you.

effects.log: You taste it. It is perfect. You announce so, and the matter dissolves in the mild surprise of the hall. The recipe is, thereafter, 'the watered' and a classic.
You rule against the watering. {b3_peer} bows, holds the cup high, and drains it, to the last drop, and is carried out, merry and defiant.
You rule for the watering, on grounds of mercy. {b3_elder} sulks, and brews a new vintage at four times the strength, as a statement, and the youngest gods give it a wide berth.

events.text: {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} have both been promised the same corner of a shrine, in a village that likes them equally. The villagers cannot choose, and have built a shrine with two doors and one altar. Each god insists on the other door being bricked up. The villagers are sad, and politely persistent.

effects.log: You rule that both doors stay. The gods enter by opposite ends and meet at the altar, scowling. The villagers deliver tea. By evening they are comparing offerings.
You brick one door. The god thereby displaced goes sulking to another village, which is delighted, and the shrine thrives with one god and one door.

events.text: A great festival is ruined: {b3_elder} and {b3_peer}, both asked to light the first lamp, each insisted on the privilege and lit it at the same moment, from opposite sides. The lamp went out in the crossfire. A dark pause fell across the whole of the worship, and then the worshippers laughed.

effects.log: You relight it. The worshippers cheer. {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} each glare at you for taking their glory, and then at each other for causing the need.

choices.text: Have them light it together, hands on one taper

effects.log: They do, stiffly. The lamp takes, and burns all night. A rumour starts that they are secretly the best of friends.

events.text: Among the gods of the order, it is rumoured that {b3_peer} has been recruiting. Not a rival order: the worshippers of {b3_elder}, one at a time, by being kinder to them in dreams. {b3_elder} has noticed the attendance at their shrine falling. They are bewildered and bitter, and have come to you for a ruling on 'kindness as theft'.

choices.text: Rule there is no such crime

effects.log: You rule against. {b3_elder} stares. Then, grimly, begins to be kinder in dreams themselves. Within a decade the order is the warmest in the cosmos, and nobody mentions how it began.
You rule it so. {b3_peer} is fined a season of dreams. The worshippers, in the interim, feel strangely cold, and many return in secret to {b3_peer}'s door.

events.text: {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} have always sat together at the hall's long table, side by side, in hostile harmony. This week, for the first time in nine hundred years, one chair is empty. {b3_peer} has not turned up. {b3_elder} sits stiff and white-faced beside the gap, pretending to read, and finally asks, in a dry voice, if you know where they are.

effects.log: You find them at the bedside of a dying mortal, unnoticed, holding a hand. You do not disturb them. You tell {b3_elder} only: 'They are doing something decent.' {b3_elder} nods, relieved.
{b3_elder} goes, with an air of great irritation, and returns two days later in a very odd mood, carrying a basket of eggs that is not theirs.

events.text: {b3_peer} has been invited to dinner by a rival pantheon, and {b3_elder} has taken it as treason. The invitation was in fact addressed to both, and the rival pantheon cannot understand the fuss. The two gods stand at your door with identical cards in identical envelopes, glaring at each other.

effects.log: You send them together, in a carriage, with a flask. They return, three days later, arm in arm, singing. The rival pantheon sends a thank-you note, and an enormous cheese.
You send {b3_peer}. {b3_elder} sulks. The rival pantheon is baffled, and {b3_peer} is the toast of the feast, and the quarrel is now on a larger stage.

events.text: A prayer arrived last week addressed to 'the god who is not {b3_elder}.' It was a joke, a mortal pun on an old phrase, but {b3_elder} has taken it to heart, and has been brooding. {b3_peer} makes it worse by answering the prayer. The hall has taken to calling {b3_peer} 'the other one.'

effects.log: You rule that all gods are, in some sense, not each other. The hall breaks into a muddle of philosophy. {b3_elder} is, by evening, strangely comforted.
You say a prayer is a prayer. {b3_peer} is vindicated, {b3_elder} stung. {b3_elder} writes a long, careful treatise on the nature of pronouns.

events.text: {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} each took a different side in a minor war between two worshipper villages, and now each village has been praying to them to destroy the other. Neither god will relent. Both are at your door, with a village's worth of grievance in each hand. The villages are, in all fairness, exhausted.

effects.log: You send dreams to the villages. They meet in the middle, at a ford, with cheese. The war ends over a pot of soup. {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} take the credit for it jointly, in silence.

choices.text: Let the gods fight it out

effects.log: The gods quarrel for a decade. The villages, tired of waiting for a war, go to market instead. The gods look up and find themselves without a cause.
You order a withdrawal. Both obey, in furious silence. The villages feel it as a drop in the air, a missing weight, and the war stops of its own accord.

events.text: {b3_peer} has painted a mural in the order's hall that shows {b3_elder}, unflatteringly, as a goat. It is a good mural. It is very much a goat. It is also, unfortunately, very like. {b3_elder} has asked you to have it taken down. A crowd has gathered to admire it. Some are taking notes.

effects.log: You leave it up. {b3_elder} wears the goat as a badge from that day on, with a defiant dignity, and the mural becomes the order's most beloved work.
It is painted over, with a landscape. {b3_peer} paints another, in secret, in a cellar, and in a hundred years it is found and revered.

events.text: It is the anniversary of the day {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} first quarrelled. Nobody remembers what about. The hall has put out a cake. Both gods have been invited to cut it. They have been standing on either side of it, knife in hand, for forty minutes, each waiting for the other to begin.

effects.log: You cut the cake. They each take a slice with a stately nod, and eat in silence, and then, simultaneously, ask for more. The quarrel is declared, formally, a tradition.
You take both knives. 'You may eat with your hands,' you say. They do. The room, shocked, bursts into laughter, and the anniversary is thereafter celebrated with fingers.

events.text: {b3_elder}, usually cool, has lost their temper in public and called {b3_peer} something unspeakable, a god of hangnails. It is the most devastating insult the order has ever heard. {b3_peer} has gone white. Silence has fallen, and in it everyone can hear someone quietly sob. It is {b3_elder}, appalled at themselves.

effects.log: You sit with {b3_elder} until the hiccups stop. In the morning they present {b3_peer} with a formal apology and a pot of salve, for hangnails. {b3_peer} laughs till they weep.
You sit with {b3_peer}, who is taking it, you find, very well. It is {b3_elder} who is in tatters. By nightfall both have come to you, separately, with the same request: please make them stop.

events.text: A summons arrives from the Heavenly Court: {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} are to give evidence in a case against a rogue god, and their testimonies disagree on every point. They have been briefed to cooperate. They have been in a room together for an hour, and neither has spoken a word. The Court is waiting. The room is very cold.

effects.log: You sit between them and ask them to tell it as a story, together. The account that results is full of the same details and none of the same words, and it convicts the rogue god.
You brief them apart. Their evidence is solid and entirely contradictory, and the Court dismisses the case. The rogue god, free, sends you a plain wooden clock.

events.text: {b3_peer} has been discovered keeping a secret garden, hidden in the hall's walls, of plants that {b3_elder} once said could not grow in the order's climate. They are thriving. {b3_elder} was right about the climate and wrong about the wall. The garden is beautiful. {b3_elder} is staring at it in a daze, and {b3_peer} is looking for the nearest exit.

effects.log: You praise it extravagantly. {b3_peer} blushes, {b3_elder} grudgingly agrees, and by spring the garden is open to all, with a bench labelled, by both, 'To a fine mistake.'
The garden is dismantled. {b3_peer} complies in cold dignity and, a century later, quietly plants a single seed in each of {b3_elder}'s flowerpots.

events.text: The long-running feud between {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} has been made the subject of a play, performed at the hall's great feast by a troupe of minor gods. The play is cruel and funny and exactly right. Both gods are in the front row, white-knuckled. The audience is howling. At the climax, the actors turn and bow to the two real gods.

effects.log: You start the applause. The hall roars. {b3_elder} and {b3_peer}, caught between pride and fury, stand and take a bow. The feud is, for a night, a national treasure.
You hush it. The gods sit in silence, and the actors, ashamed, bow out. The feud resumes in a lower, uglier key.

events.text: {b3_elder} has asked to resign the hall's third chair, in protest at {b3_peer}'s promotion to it. The resignation is written in an elegant, furious hand on a scroll the length of a river. {b3_peer} has asked to resign the chair in turn, from embarrassment. The chair, which is a rather good chair, sits empty between them.

effects.log: You refuse both. The chair is shared, a week on, a week off, and the two have to leave notes on the cushion. The notes are the best prose in the pantheon.

choices.text: Accept both and seat a third

effects.log: You seat a young god of lost keys. The older two are mortified, then relieved, then sulkily proud. The young god is the best chairperson the hall has had.

events.text: A visiting god, a stranger, has been quietly watching the quarrel between {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} from the back of the hall for a week, taking notes. The stranger is a scholar of feuds. They think it is the most beautifully sustained example in the cosmos. They ask for an interview with both parties and an hour of your time.

effects.log: The scholar publishes: 'A Textbook Quarrel,' two volumes. It is adopted by the cosmos's schools. {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} are both quoted. Both claim to be the victim.
The scholar leaves, disappointed, and writes the book anyway, from memory, with errors. The two gods are mortified, and united for the first time in a decade, in their hatred of the book.

events.text: {b3_peer} is dying, in the slow, grand way that gods do. {b3_elder}, who has quarrelled with them for four thousand years, has not come to the bedside. The hall watches the door. Evening falls. At the last moment, in the dark, {b3_elder} slips in, wearing an old cloak, and takes the empty chair.

effects.log: You leave. In the morning {b3_peer} is gone, peacefully, and {b3_elder} is still in the chair, holding a hand that is no longer warm, and weeping like a child.
You sit with {b3_elder} until dawn. Nothing is said. The hall is silent for a year after, and the quarrel is quietly closed in the books.

events.text: {b3_peer} has sent {b3_elder} a gift, a very old jar of honey with a note: 'For the bitterness.' {b3_elder} thinks it is an insult. The hall suspects it is a kindness. The honey is excellent. {b3_elder} has asked for a ruling on whether it is polite to eat a gift one suspects of being an insult.

choices.text: Rule it is polite to eat it

effects.log: You rule the gift edible. {b3_elder} eats it, grimly, on bread, and reports, in a tone of astonishment, that it is the best honey they have ever had.
{b3_elder} sends it back with a note: 'Thank you for the sweetness.' The two exchange the jar for several centuries, each a little sweeter than before.

events.text: {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} were once apprentices of the same god. The teacher has died and left a will, in which each is bequeathed one half of an unfinished work: a sacred drum. Neither can play it alone. The will does not say whether this is a trick. Both have come to you to ask what the teacher meant.

effects.log: They play it together, awkward, off the beat. The drum speaks. It is the voice of the teacher, humming a lullaby. They weep, and play on, and the feud is over.
You declare it a relic. It is laid in a shrine. The two visit it each year, separately, and each leaves a note. The notes agree.

events.text: A rumour reaches the hall that {b3_elder} is quietly funding a charity for the orphans of {b3_peer}'s worshippers. {b3_elder} denies it with great ferocity. {b3_peer} has heard, and, although they say nothing, the corridors of the hall have grown noticeably gentler.

effects.log: You praise it in the hall. {b3_elder} goes the colour of a plum and says they were passing and dropped some coins. The hall applauds the lie.
You keep it, and let the charity run. {b3_elder} never knows you know. It is the best-kept open secret of the age.

events.text: The hall has been asked to decide which of two gods, {b3_elder} or {b3_peer}, shall receive the title 'Elder of Hearths.' Both are suitable. Both are horrified by the idea of the other getting it. Both have put themselves forward and quietly voted for the other. The tally is a perfect tie, and both are embarrassed.

effects.log: The title is shared, which has never been done. They accept with the rigid courtesy of those who have outplayed each other, and the Elders of Hearths is, in future, always a pair.

choices.text: Give the title to a third

effects.log: You give it to a quiet god of kettles, who is overjoyed and overwhelmed, and the two older gods, relieved, retire to a corner and begin to quarrel about the kettle.

events.text: {b3_elder}, a stern disciplinarian, has caught {b3_peer} teaching the junior gods a rather scandalous drinking-song. {b3_peer} claims it is a traditional hymn. The juniors sing it again, in unison, with gestures. {b3_elder}'s mouth twitches. They ask you to rule on whether it is blasphemy.

effects.log: You rule it a hymn, on technical grounds. {b3_elder} unbends by a degree and requests the second verse. The song is sung at every feast for ten thousand years.

choices.text: Rule it blasphemy, and learn it

effects.log: You rule it blasphemy, and learn it that very night. The juniors catch you humming in the corridor. You are never, thereafter, entirely respected, and entirely loved.

events.text: A shipment of incense meant for {b3_elder}'s temples was delivered, by mistake, to {b3_peer}'s, and {b3_peer} used it, thinking it a gift. {b3_elder} has made a formal complaint, which is a perfectly reasonable complaint and a perfectly absurd one. The incense, on its own account, smells like a rose and a dispute.

effects.log: You order {b3_peer} to pay in kind. A box of fine incense arrives at {b3_elder}'s temples, with a note: 'It smelled of you.' {b3_elder} reads it three times.
You order the incense burnt at both temples simultaneously. The air above the order is sweet for a month. The two gods look at each other across the clouds and say nothing.

events.text: Both {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} have been invited to be godparents to a new god's first festival. They have been asked to stand either side of the cradle. The new god, tiny, glowing, is looking up at them with the unfocused interest of the very young. The two stand rigid, hating each other, while the baby grips a finger of each.

effects.log: You let it be. The baby gurgles. {b3_elder} and {b3_peer}, helplessly, begin to smile, at the baby, and then, awkwardly, at each other.
You commission a portrait. The two scowl at the painter. In the finished work, they are both smiling. The painter swears this was an accident.

events.text: {b3_elder} wishes to dissolve a shrine of {b3_peer}'s on the grounds that it is near their own, and the incense is clashing. {b3_peer}, furious, has brought in a crowd of worshippers, who sit down in the street. A herald is attempting to read the injunction, and the worshippers, very polite, are singing over him.

effects.log: You uphold the shrine. The crowd cheers, the herald sags, {b3_elder} sulks. The incense clashes for centuries, and the smell of it is, in time, a kind of music.
You rule that the incenses be burned on alternate days. Both gods grumble. The street has a calendar of sweet smells, and the crowd goes home, singing.

events.text: {b3_peer} claims that a certain star in the evening sky is theirs. {b3_elder} says it is theirs. The star, a minor one, would very much like not to be involved. It has been blinking nervously for a week. A delegation of astronomers from below is awaiting your ruling, and the star's.

effects.log: You ask. The star flickers once, in a way that could be read either way. It goes on shining, and the two gods agree, grumbling, to share it on alternate evenings.
You declare the star its own. The star, thrilled, glows a shade brighter. The astronomers record it with delight, and name it 'The Neutral.'

events.text: The quarrel between {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} has entered its second millennium. The hall has taken to guessing at its end, paid out in cakes, and a pile of them has accumulated outside your door. You are, by general consensus, the only one with the power to end it. The cakes are very good.

effects.log: You issue a ruling. It is long and detailed and entirely evenhanded. The quarrel ends, with a quiet, reluctant sigh from both, and the cakes are distributed among the poor.

choices.text: Let it run another thousand years

effects.log: You let it run. The cakes pile up. The feud becomes a landmark, and the cakes a custom, and the hall is, on the whole, happier for it.

events.text: {b3_elder} has been quietly teaching {b3_peer}'s daughter, a young goddess of tides, how to read. {b3_peer} has just found out, and is torn between fury and a terrible gratitude. The daughter, between them, holds a picture book and a pencil and looks from one to the other with enormous, interested eyes.

effects.log: You say it quietly. {b3_peer} does, stiffly. The daughter reads her first sentence aloud to both, and it is: 'Please stop.' They do.
The daughter picks a book. It is one {b3_elder} wrote. {b3_peer} sighs, and sits down, and listens to it read, and cries a little.

events.text: A very small god has been caught in the crossfire of {b3_elder} and {b3_peer}'s argument: a god of lost threads, who has been sent back and forth between them as a messenger for a hundred years. The poor thing has worn a groove in the floor, and has begun to rattle. It has come to you at last, in tears.

choices.text: Give the little god a desk

effects.log: You give it a desk at your side. It sits, trembling, and is soon the happiest clerk in the order. {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} send letters of apology, each in a separate envelope, the same day.

choices.text: Order the two to deliver their own messages

effects.log: You rule it. The two are forced to meet daily, in the corridor. Their quarrel, thereafter, takes place in person, and loses half its venom.

events.text: It is raining in the hall again. This happens whenever {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} meet, and has done for centuries. The rain is a small private weather, falling between them, and no one else is wet. It is entirely comfortable. The order has named it, fondly, 'The Quarrel.' Today it is a snowstorm.

effects.log: You stand in the snowstorm between them. They stop, stunned. The snow, melting on your hair, makes the rest of the hall laugh, and the weather clears.
You keep out of it. The snow thickens, the two gods continue to argue knee-deep, and the hall prepares hot soup. It is the most peaceful winter the order has known.

events.text: {b3_peer} has just done something remarkably kind for {b3_elder}, anonymously, and {b3_elder} has found out. They are furious, because it was done so well. They ask you to find a way to be kinder in return, but meaner, so that it cancels out. The logic is impeccable, and mad.

effects.log: You help them plot a kind of revenge: a favour so large that it must be repaid. {b3_peer} is baffled. The two, in the end, are in each other's debt for a thousand years.
'That would be worse,' says {b3_elder}. But they do it, and {b3_peer} goes pink, and the feud, which has been losing air for centuries, collapses with a small, embarrassed sigh.

events.text: {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} have been given the job of choosing the order's new emblem together, on the grounds that nothing else would force them to speak. The meetings have lasted three years. They have designed fourteen emblems, each worse than the last, and have now begun to argue about whether to stop.

effects.log: You choose the sixth, a lopsided sun. The hall adopts it. Both gods are insulted and relieved, and their long meetings, deprived of an object, taper off into tea.
You give them a week. They produce the fifteenth emblem in a night: a plain circle, with two small handprints in the corner. It is perfect.

events.text: {b3_peer} has been teaching the order's apprentices to ignore {b3_elder}'s orders, on principle. The apprentices have taken to it with relish. {b3_elder} gives an instruction and the whole hall obeys, ostentatiously late. The effect is that nothing in the order is done, and everything is a game.

effects.log: You back {b3_elder}'s authority. The apprentices straighten. {b3_peer} bows, with an expression of complete innocence, and tries another game the following year.
You grant a day a week for ignoring orders, by custom. The hall calls it the Day of Delay. It is the most productive day of the week.

events.text: A pair of heralds bring you the hall's records: in four thousand years, {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} have between them been right fifty-fifty, and wrong fifty-fifty, and have never once been wrong at the same time. The heralds read this aloud, solemnly, in the hall. The two gods listen. The silence stretches.

effects.log: You have the record framed. It hangs in the hall's main corridor. The two, passing it daily, find that it is the one thing they agree on.
'Luck,' says {b3_elder}. 'Skill,' says {b3_peer}. The heralds sigh. You write in the margin: 'Both.'

events.text: In the middle of a council, {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} both stand to make the same objection, in the same words, at the same moment. A stunned silence falls. They look at each other. They sit down. Both turn, simultaneously, to look at you, with the unspoken request: please do not mention this.

effects.log: You mention it, with a grin. The hall erupts. The two gods, scarlet, spend the rest of the council fighting for the opposite side of everything.
You say nothing. They owe you. Months later, when you need an ally in a vote, both of them rise, in unison, to speak in your favour.

events.text: {b3_elder}, annoyed at being outvoted, has taken to hiding {b3_peer}'s spectacles. {b3_peer} has taken to hiding {b3_elder}'s shoes. Both are playing it, with a ferocity, as a game of honour. The hall is full of half-blind gods in socks. They ask, at the same moment, for your help locating their things.

effects.log: You find both, in the same cupboard, where the junior gods have hidden them, for a laugh. The three of you return the items together. A truce, of sorts, is called.
You find the shoes. {b3_peer} stumbles about in a blur until {b3_elder}, grudgingly, returns the glasses. A sock is left behind as a memento.

events.text: {b3_peer} has proposed a new law for the order, which {b3_elder} has opposed in a speech that lasted nine hours. When the vote is called, {b3_elder} votes for it. The hall gasps. 'I wanted to be thorough,' {b3_elder} says. 'Now that I understand it, it is a good law.' {b3_peer} has been rendered speechless.

effects.log: You applaud. The hall joins in. The law passes, and {b3_peer} is, for once, struck with an affection so strong it is nearly embarrassing.

choices.text: Ask {b3_elder} to speak on the next law

effects.log: 'Gladly,' says {b3_elder}. 'Though I may change my mind.' The hall laughs. It becomes a custom: nine hours of opposition, then the vote.

events.text: A strangely beautiful accident has occurred: {b3_elder} and {b3_peer}, fighting over the same cloud, fell through it together and landed in a small, startled, mortal town. They are now standing in the market-square, covered in flour, in front of a baker who has mistaken them for a pair of travelling actors. Both are completely out of their depth.

effects.log: You arrive to find them handing out loaves to the crowd, red-faced, laughing. They return, a day later, covered in flour and arm in arm, with a basket of pastries.
You let them manage. They return in a week, humbler, and have been known to say the word 'bakery' in an odd voice ever since.

events.text: The order's most ancient rule is that two gods in quarrel must share a single cup of wine until it is settled. {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} have been sharing a cup for a hundred years. It is a very small cup. They have grown strangely close. Both ask you to rule that the quarrel is over, in a tone of immense, reluctant fatigue.

effects.log: You end it. They surrender the cup, with a little ceremony, and sit, awkward, on either side of the room. In a month they have reconvened for tea.
You let it go on. They grumble, and share it still. The cup is a legend, and the quarrel, by every measure, is a marriage in all but name.

events.text: {b3_peer} has composed a eulogy for {b3_elder}, to be read at their eventual funeral, and has accidentally read it aloud, to a full hall, thinking {b3_elder} was elsewhere. {b3_elder} was not elsewhere. {b3_elder} is sitting in the front row, in tears. It was a very good eulogy.

effects.log: You begin to applaud. The hall follows. {b3_peer} flees. {b3_elder}, drying their eyes, calls after them: 'It was too short.'
You request a second reading. {b3_peer}, scarlet, gives it. It is even better. {b3_elder} asks for a copy for their own records.

events.text: {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} have each filed a motion to ban the other from the library, on the grounds of noise. Both are in the library as the motions are read. Both are whispering. The librarian, a tiny and terrible god of silence, has gone pale. She raises one hand. Everyone in the hall freezes.

effects.log: The librarian rules for the library: both are banned, for a week. They go, humbled and silent. When they return, they have been reading the same book in two copies, and discuss it softly.

choices.text: Ask the librarian to be merciful

effects.log: She considers you with enormous gravity, then waves a hand. The two are admitted on probation, and are, thereafter, models of quiet.

events.text: Both {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} claim that it was they who first thought of the order's famous lantern festival. The festival has been going for ten thousand years. Neither can prove it. The records burned. Each has a witness: a very old tortoise, and an even older moth. The two witnesses disagree entirely, and slowly.

effects.log: You rule that the festival was invented by the worshippers, who asked for it. The two gods look at each other and agree, in a flat voice, that this is probably true.
You rule for the tortoise's account, for its patience. {b3_elder} is vindicated, {b3_peer} sulky, and the moth, offended, flits out of the window and does not return.

events.text: It is a small thing, but it has become large: {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} each want the window seat in the council hall. Neither will take the other. A rota has been drawn up and torn up three times. The window, which is a very ordinary window, looks out on a very ordinary courtyard, in which a cat sleeps.

effects.log: You install a second window. The two gods sit in them, side by side, looking at the same cat, in a companionable silence that lasts, according to the hall, several centuries.
You remove the seat. They stand. The council, standing, is the shortest in the order's history. A rumour starts that the window seat was haunted.

events.text: {b3_peer} has been going about the hall for a week, with a rather smug look, whispering to everyone that they know a secret about {b3_elder}. {b3_elder} is deeply uneasy. The secret is, in fact, that {b3_elder} has a soft spot for stray cats, and feeds them at night in the courtyard. It is not a bad secret. It will be a bad week.

effects.log: You tell the hall, with warmth. The hall is delighted. By evening, a dozen gods are putting out milk. {b3_elder} is mortified, then relieved, then tender.
You warn them. {b3_elder} shrugs, with an air of enormous dignity, and when {b3_peer} makes the revelation at dinner, answers: 'Yes. I know. They are lovely cats.'

events.text: Over four thousand years of quarrel, {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} have written one another seven thousand letters. They are a magnificent body of literature. A scholar from the Silent Hall has asked to publish them. The two, appalled, have been consulted. 'Not a word,' says {b3_elder}. 'Every word,' says {b3_peer}, with a quiet pride.

effects.log: The letters are published, with a preface by you. They become the most beloved correspondence in the cosmos. {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} deny any affection, with growing hysteria.
You seal them in a vault, to be opened in ten thousand years. The two gods, a little disappointed, begin to write another letter, a thick one, to be added to the pile.

events.text: {b3_elder} has called {b3_peer} a coward, in public, for refusing a duel. {b3_peer} has in fact refused because their opponent is a very young god of puddles who would be crushed. They cannot say so. The hall watches {b3_peer} take the insult, unspeaking, in a bow so deep it looks like a collapse.

effects.log: You say the truth, quietly, to {b3_elder}. {b3_elder} goes white, then grey, then offers {b3_peer} an apology so profound that the hall has to look away.
You let it stand, since it is not your quarrel. {b3_peer} bears it. A century later, {b3_elder} learns the truth, and visits {b3_peer}'s door with a very large pot of tea, unannounced.

events.text: A flood of prayers arrives at the hall from a single village, all of them addressed to 'whichever of you two is winning.' The village has a complicated reason. It involves a long-standing contest of guesses about the feud, with a pig as the prize. {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} are both rather moved by the loyalty, and a little horrified.

choices.text: Declare a draw, sparing the pig

effects.log: You declare a draw. The pig is spared. The village sends a tray of fruit buns and an apology to the pig.
You rule it a superstition. The village is crestfallen, and then cheerful, and the pig, from then on, is known as Judge.

events.text: The Kin of {b3_kin} hold their table in a room with no windows, under a ceiling of stored shadow, and every dish is a debt. You are served a modest pudding. The eldest Kin watches you eat. 'You owe us a pudding,' they say, with courtesy. 'We shall let you know what it costs.'

effects.log: You finish it. It was very good. Somewhere a ledger is amended, in small neat script, to your credit and your cost.
You leave the last bite. The Kin approves with a nod. 'Leave the last bite for the one who owes you,' they say. 'It is the first rule of the house.'

events.text: A child of {b3_kin}, small and solemn, has been told to teach you the house's secret handshake. It is eleven steps long. The child performs it, with great gravity, and then wipes its nose on its sleeve. You are expected to produce the same, without error, in front of the house, tomorrow.

effects.log: You practise until dawn, and the child, bleary, corrects you twice. At the hall you perform it flawlessly. The house is silent. The child beams.

choices.text: Ask the child to do it slowly

effects.log: The child does it slowly, delighted to be a teacher. You perform it with one forgivable wobble. The house says it is the best first attempt in a century.

events.text: In the great hall of {b3_kin} there hangs a portrait of every Kin who has died owing. They are the largest group. A new portrait is being hung. It is of an old, tired, cheerful god, a debtor to the end. The house has asked you, as the newest member, to say a few words over the frame.

effects.log: You speak of the debt as a kind of love. The house is moved. It is not a typical thing for a Kin to say, and it will be remembered as the moment you became one of them.
You speak of the god himself, of his jokes and his habit of humming. The house weeps, quietly. 'We rarely hear him mentioned,' says the eldest. 'We keep the debt, not the man.'

events.text: The Kin of {b3_kin} will lie to you twice in your first year, as a courtesy, to see whether you notice. You have noticed one. The second is still out there, somewhere, a small clean untruth in a drawer of otherwise honest talk. You catch the eldest Kin looking at you, with the faint smile of a sleeping cat.

effects.log: You name the first lie, and say there is a second. The eldest laughs, at length, and tells you what it was. It was, in fact, a rather good one.

choices.text: Wait for the second to turn up

effects.log: You wait. It turns up in your fourth year, at breakfast, in a casual remark about the weather. You remember it with respect.

events.text: A member of {b3_kin} has fallen ill, and the house will not call a healer, because a healer would be owed. The sick Kin lies in a bed of black blankets, pale and polite, and refuses all comfort. The house watches, helpless in its own rules. Someone will have to break them. They look at you, the newest, the least bound.

effects.log: You call the healer, and take the debt on yourself. The Kin recovers. The house says nothing, and the eldest pays your debt, quietly, in secret, in the old coin.
You sit by the bed and tell stories. The fever breaks in the small hours. The house, finding you there at dawn, makes a place for you at the table's warmer end.

events.text: The Kin of {b3_kin} have a custom: at the turn of the age every member must burn a letter they never sent. The pyre is lit in the hall, and the members file past with their small white envelopes. You find you have one. You do not remember writing it. It is in your own hand, and it is addressed to someone you cannot place.

effects.log: You burn it unread. The smoke smells of cut grass and cold rain. The house nods, solemn. A weight you had not known you carried is, for a night, absent.
You read it. It is two lines, kind and wretched, to a person you will never meet. You burn it. The ash is warm for a long time.

events.text: An outsider has come to the door of {b3_kin} asking to be taken in. They have nothing to offer but a very good story. The house does not admit strangers, but the story is true, and tells of a debt the house itself once failed to pay. The eldest looks round the table. 'Newest voice first,' they say.

effects.log: The house admits the stranger, with a few formalities. The stranger turns out to be a quiet god of lost things, and finds, over the years, three things the house had given up for gone.
The house refuses. The stranger bows and goes, with dignity. You think of them in the following years, and send, in secret, a loaf of bread to wherever they are.

events.text: There is a room in the house of {b3_kin} that is always locked. Each member has been told not to open it. You are the only one who has found the key, lying in a bowl of pickled cherries. You hold it up. Two members have noticed. They do not speak. They merely look at the door, and then at you, and wait.

effects.log: It opens onto a small bright kitchen with a stove and a kettle, where the house's founder sits, eternally, waiting for someone to ask if they want tea. You do. You sit. It is the best hour of the age.

choices.text: Return the key to the cherries

effects.log: You put it back, among the cherries. The two members exhale. Years later, the door is open, and nobody can say who opened it, and the kettle is singing.

events.text: The house of {b3_kin} has a debt it cannot pay: a hundred thousand years old, to a god of the Sea who vanished. The eldest has asked for a volunteer to go and look for the creditor. It is a thankless journey. Nobody has volunteered in three centuries. The eldest looks at the newest member with an air of weary hope.

effects.log: You go. It takes you a century. You find the creditor in a rock pool, half-asleep and wholly content. You tell the story. They say: 'Oh, that. I forgot. Keep it.' You carry the pardon home, rather stunned.

choices.text: Offer to pay a part of it

effects.log: You offer a modest, sincere instalment, from your own stores. The house is quietly appalled and quietly moved, and the debt, for the first time in an age, goes down.

events.text: A pair of rival Kin are fighting for the head of {b3_kin}'s table. The seat is a plain wooden chair. Each has gathered votes. Each has a long speech. You have been quietly approached by both, with gifts, which you cannot refuse without offence. You hold two identical silver spoons.

effects.log: You back the elder, a stern and honest god of unpaid debts. They win by one vote. They remember it, and are fair to you for a thousand years.
You back the younger, restless and warm. They win by one vote. The house changes, over a century, into something less afraid.
You use neither spoon, and eat soup with your hands. The house is aghast. Both candidates withdraw in confusion. A third is found, a quiet god of cutlery, who wins by acclaim.

events.text: One of the Kin of {b3_kin}, a thin old god who is mostly beard, has taken to following you about the house, holding a tray of tea. They do not speak. They offer the tea at each meeting, quietly, with a bow. You have refused it three times without causing offence. Another refusal might.

effects.log: You accept. It is the best tea you have had. The old god nods, and withdraws, and thereafter the tea appears, unasked, in each room you enter, and you are slowly, mysteriously, taller in the house's estimation.
They sit, astonished, on the edge of a chair. You pour. It is the first time in a century they have been served. They are overwhelmed, and tell you everything.

events.text: On the Night of Unpaid Things, the Kin of {b3_kin} leave their doors open and lay out a place for every debt they owe. There are a great many places. You are put to count them. At the thirty-thousandth, you find one with your own name on a card. It is not a debt. It is a welcome.

effects.log: You sit. The house, turning, finds you there, and does not speak. The food comes. It is the first Night of Unpaid Things at which every place is filled.

choices.text: Take the card as a keepsake

effects.log: You pocket the card. It is the plainest thing you own, and the one you will keep longest. The house says nothing, and the next year, the place is laid again.

events.text: The Kin of {b3_kin} play a game at table in which each member names a thing they have lost and the others must say who found it. The game is played in perfect seriousness and has no winners. Your turn comes. You name a thing you have lost. The others say, one by one, that they found it.

effects.log: They hand you, in turn, a laugh, a rule of thumb, a name, and a small warm stone. You carry them for centuries, and each, in turn, saves you.
You play on. The game does not end. The rest of the evening you are kindly handed things, and at the end you leave with the odd sense of having been given a great deal and having lost nothing.

events.text: There is a lie that the Kin of {b3_kin} tell the world, a very old one, that they are fearsome. In truth they are shy, tender, and owed a great many favours. A visiting god of the Will of Heaven, bold and radiant, has seen through it, and is laughing at the dinner table. The house has gone very still. They look at you.

effects.log: You rise and defend them with a speech so earnest that the visitor stops laughing. 'I see,' says the visitor, 'I shall tell no one.' They keep their word.
You laugh. The house is stunned, and then, helplessly, joins. The secret is out, and nothing is lost, and the Kin become, in time, rather popular.

events.text: The Kin of {b3_kin} are sending a letter to the Silent Hall, to be delivered by hand, a letter of apology for a quarrel eight thousand years old. Nobody can bear to take it. It is a thin letter, sealed with black wax, and somewhat damp. The eldest asks if you would go. You are, after all, no one's idea of a threat.

effects.log: You carry it to the Silent Hall, and place it in a pale hand. The god reads it and goes out into the rain. The next morning there is a reply, a single line: 'Yes.'

choices.text: Ask the eldest to carry it themself

effects.log: The eldest balks, and then, trembling, goes. They are back in a day, wet through and shaking with relief. The house throws them a party, which they do not enjoy.

events.text: A thief has been in the house of {b3_kin}, stealing nothing but crumbs. The Kin, who keep exact account of everything, are scandalised: it is the most insulting kind of burglary. They set a trap. The trap catches, after a fortnight, a small, hungry, mortal child who has crept up a drainpipe from the world below. The child gazes at the Kin with enormous eyes.

effects.log: The house feeds the child. The child stays three days, and is sent home with a pocketful of buns. The Kin say they are owed a thank-you. A drawing arrives a week later, in crayon: it is of the house, smiling.

choices.text: Send the child home at once

effects.log: You send the child home, with a note to its mother. The house is stung. A basket of buns is later sent down by an anonymous god, with a note: 'For the drainpipe.'

events.text: The Kin of {b3_kin} have learned that you are an excellent listener and have begun to unburden themselves to you in the corridors. You have heard nine hundred confessions this year, and each is a tiny, bright, sad thing. Your own heart is full to the brim. The eldest, passing, says: 'You will need somewhere to put them.'

effects.log: You keep a ledger, a secret one, of all you have heard. It is the saddest and most beautiful book in the house. You burn it, in a century, and the smoke smells of bread.
You walk to the edge of the world and tell the confessions, one by one, to the sea. It listens. When you return you are lighter, and the Kin, who cannot say why, are kinder.

events.text: At the end of your first year in {b3_kin}, the house gives you your Debt: a small black stone, with a symbol cut in it, and a number. The number is how much you owe. It is surprisingly low. The eldest says it is not the number that matters but the day it is called. 'Keep it by your bed,' they say. 'It will let you know.'

effects.log: You keep it. It is, in the mornings, faintly warm. On the day it grows cold, years later, you know at once what is owed, and pay it, gladly.
You carry it. It clinks against your keys. It gives you, in strange hours, a small sense of being held, and of being accountable, and you do not mind it at all.

events.text: The Academy of {b3_acad} teaches divinity in the way a river teaches a stone: slowly, and mostly by being there. The first lesson is how to be looked at. The master of the class, an elderly god of mirrors, sits you in front of a lamp and tells you to be admired for an hour without moving.

effects.log: An hour is long. By the end your face has learned a patience it did not have. The master of mirrors says you will do, and that is the most they ever say.
You study the lamp, and the master, who had never seen a student reverse the exercise, lowers their glass and says it is the right answer to the wrong question.

events.text: In the second year at {b3_acad} students are given a prayer to answer, a real one, to be marked. Yours comes from a mother, in a bad winter, who asks for firewood. The examiners watch to see if you will conjure a forest. They are not looking for a forest.

choices.text: Send a neighbour with a cart

effects.log: A neighbour wakes with a thought and a cart of logs. The examiners mark you well: you used the world, not a miracle. The mother never knows you were there.
You warm the walls for the winter. It is lovely, and beyond the brief. The examiners mark you down and then, in the margin, write 'unfairly good.'

events.text: Your tutor at {b3_acad} is a god of dust, ancient and sneezy, who tells the same joke every lecture and is delighted every time. The students have learned to laugh in the right place. This term, you are the only one in the class who has not, and the tutor has noticed. The joke begins.

effects.log: You laugh. The tutor, relieved, claps. It is the shared lie of a happy classroom, and you take your small part in it with a sense of obscure well-being.
The tutor is stunned. After a week of silence, they produce a second joke, which is much worse. The class is in tears. It becomes the term's best-loved failure.

events.text: The Academy of {b3_acad} runs on a rule: no student may ask for help before they have been stuck for a full day. The rule is cruel and invisible. In the library you find a young god, red-eyed, who has been stuck for six hours and cannot bear to ask. They look up at you, hopeful, and then at the clock.

effects.log: You help them with the problem. It is not allowed, and it is unnoticed, and the young one passes. They remember. A century later they save you from an embarrassing mistake.

choices.text: Sit with them till the full day is up

effects.log: You sit with them, saying nothing, until the clock strikes. Then you help. It is the rule, and the kindness, and neither is broken.

events.text: {b3_acad} keeps a stuffed hawk in the lecture hall. It is a real hawk, long dead, who was once a messenger of the Sky. The students call it the Examiner and bow to it before tests. This term, mysteriously, the hawk has moved a foot to the left. Nobody admits to it. The test is tomorrow.

effects.log: You move it back, with some ceremony. The test goes badly for everyone but you. The hawk, you swear, has a faintly approving expression.
You leave it. The class passes, to a student. The hawk, somehow, is back in its first position by the next morning. Nobody asks.

events.text: A visiting god of the Silent Hall lectures at {b3_acad} on the art of forgetting. The lecture is memorable. The students leave convinced that they have learned a great deal, and cannot say what. A tutor weeps with envy. The visiting god, afterward, whispers that the lecture was actually about remembering. You were the only one to notice.

choices.text: Ask them to teach you the other half

effects.log: The visiting god is delighted. They teach you for a week, a private tutorial, in the dark. It is the finest lesson you ever had and the least repeatable.

choices.text: Say nothing and enjoy being right

effects.log: You keep it to yourself. In an exam, a century on, you remember a thing you thought you had forgotten, and it saves you.

events.text: The Academy of {b3_acad} has a dormitory that is a single enormous bed, shared. There are six hundred students in it. Everyone snores in a different key. The result is, by custom, the Academy Hymn. The Dean proudly says it is the best in the cosmos. You are woken at three by a young god who, weeping, asks you to hold their hand.

effects.log: You hold it until the sobbing stops. By dawn the young one has told you about a family left behind, and a home they cannot go back to. You become the oldest friend either of you has.
The matron comes, warm and brisk, with soup. The young one recovers. You go back to sleep, aware you have done the sensible thing and wondering if it was the kind one.

events.text: The Academy of {b3_acad} stages an annual play in which the students play the pantheons and the pantheons attend. The audience is hard to please. This year you are cast as the god of rain, in a robe of silver tinsel. Your first line is 'It is only water.' You have three days to find the character.

effects.log: You play it small and true. The audience, hushed, listens to the rain. The god of rain himself, in the third row, is seen to wipe his eyes. You win the part for life.
You play it as a joke. The pantheons roar, the god of rain laughs hardest, and you are never allowed to forget it. The notices are splendid.

events.text: In the Academy of {b3_acad} students are marked on a sliding scale of worship. The mark is a number, kept secret, and updated each term. By the third year you have worked out the formula from the pattern of the tutors' sighs. It is a very simple formula. It is also, you suspect, wrong.

effects.log: You game the formula, and your marks soar. You are praised. A creeping hollowness comes with it. You graduate, high, hungry, and just a little ashamed.
The Dean is thrilled, appalled, and grateful. The formula is scrapped, and a better, stranger one installed. You are given a prize, and a new tutor who eyes you carefully.

events.text: At {b3_acad} the students' final trial is to lose a debate on purpose, convincingly, to an old opponent. It is a lesson in humility. Your opponent is a very ancient god of grudges who has defeated every student for a thousand years. They look at you with a deadly, tender smile.

effects.log: You lose with every grace. The ancient god, delighted, awards you the first mark of 'perfect defeat' in a thousand years. It is the best loss of your life.
You win. The ancient god looks at you for a long moment, then nods. 'Good,' they say. 'I was hoping to be beaten.' They retire the following spring.

events.text: {b3_acad} has a cafeteria that serves, by a mix-up with the Silent Hall's catering, a single dish for a month: porridge of remembered things. Each student's bowl tastes of a different memory, and nobody knows whose. Yours is a smell of lamp-oil and wet wool and someone laughing in the next room. You cannot place it, and cannot stop eating.

choices.text: Ask the cook whose memory it is

effects.log: 'Yours,' says the cook, with a shrug. 'From before.' You have the next bowl, and the next, and the memory is a little clearer each time.
You eat in silence, and when the bowl is empty the memory goes, as gently as steam. The cook, collecting the dish, murmurs: 'Good.'

events.text: A rumour runs round {b3_acad} that the school was built on the grave of a dead god, and that if you lie on the lecture hall floor at midnight you can hear them dreaming. The students have a rota. It is your night. The floor is cold. The hall is huge and dark. You lie down.

effects.log: You hear a long, slow, sweet dream of a field in summer, and a child running. At dawn you are damp-eyed, and the other students, who ask nothing, make you tea.
You hum a tune you did not know. The dream, for a moment, hums with you. Then it is silent, and the grave, if it is one, sighs. You never lie on the floor again, and you never forget.

events.text: The Dean of {b3_acad} is dying, slowly, of the ordinary old age gods are not supposed to have. They continue to teach from a litter, with a blanket, to a ring of attentive students. Today's lesson is how to say goodbye. The Dean looks at you and says: 'Show them. I will mark it.'

effects.log: You say it, simply, in front of the class. The Dean's eyes fill. The class is silent. It is the best lesson any of you has ever had, and the last they give.
You say goodbye to someone not in the room, long gone. The class understands. The Dean gives you the highest mark in the school's history, in a feeble hand.

events.text: {b3_acad} has a formal duel every spring, of wit, in which students are paired and given a topic. This year you are paired with the most arrogant student in the Academy, a bright god of thunder who never loses. The topic is 'Modesty'. The thunder-god looks at you and begins by announcing that they are the best in the world at it.

effects.log: You answer with a long, complete silence. The thunder-god waits, perplexed, then fidgets, then loses the thread. The judges award you the duel for the best modesty on show.

choices.text: Answer with their own speech, back

effects.log: You parrot their speech, word for word, in a mild voice. The hall collapses. The thunder-god laughs, to your surprise, and asks you to dinner.

events.text: The students of {b3_acad} are required to keep a dream diary, which is read by their tutors. Yours is, according to your tutor, 'worryingly orderly.' They ask you to dream something messier. You try. You dream, with some concentration, of a wardrobe full of eels. The tutor writes, with satisfaction, 'Better.'

effects.log: You dream wilder every week. Your dreams become famous in the Academy, and a minor industry of interpretation grows up. A god of dreams hires you as an adviser.
You go back to order. The tutor sighs, and writes 'Fine.' You find, to your annoyance, that you miss the eels.

events.text: A student of {b3_acad} has fallen in love with their tutor, and made a spectacle of it. The tutor is mortified, the class delighted, and the Dean has asked for a ruling on how to manage it. They have asked you, because you are the student the tutor trusts. The love-struck student is waiting outside, with a sprig of jasmine.

effects.log: You advise the tutor to be gentle and clear. The student is let down kindly, and goes on to write the Academy's loveliest poem, about someone else.

choices.text: Advise the student to wait a century

effects.log: You advise patience. They shrug, nod, and take it to heart, with a sprig of jasmine behind their ear. A century on, the tutor retires, and the student returns, graying and shy, and is welcomed.

events.text: The final examination at {b3_acad} is a prayer you must write, to a god of your own invention, and have it answered by the examiners. They give you a pen, a piece of paper, and no time limit. The room is silent. Somewhere beyond the walls, someone is practising the harp, badly.

effects.log: You write a prayer to the harpist, asking only for a better tune. The examiners, with straight faces, answer it, and the harp, from that moment, improves. You pass, and are known as the student who prayed to the practice.
You pray for the peace of the cosmos, and the examiners, impassive, answer with a calm that falls over the room like snow. You pass with distinction, and weep in the corridor.

events.text: {b3_acad} has an old, great clock which has not told the right time in a thousand years. The students are told to ignore it. This term it chimes thirteen, and the room falls still. A very old tutor stands, and murmurs, 'It has never done that.' The clock ticks once more, and a small door opens in its face.

effects.log: Inside the clock is a tiny, perfect room, lit by a single candle, in which sits a miniature tutor, writing. You close the door. The clock chimes the right time for the first time in ten centuries.
The Dean sends for a clockmaker. The clockmaker pronounces the clock sound. It chimes thirteen again in a hundred years, and the door is open, and nobody is inside, and the candle is warm.

events.text: The students of {b3_acad} have a tradition of exchanging gifts at the end of the year, which must each be made by hand and cost nothing. You have drawn a name: a prickly, brilliant god of nettles, whom nobody likes. You have a week. You sit up late, with a knife and a stick of wood.

effects.log: You carve a small, crooked bird. The god of nettles holds it for a long time, and says nothing, and puts it in a pocket. They are gentler to you for centuries.
You write a poem about nettles. It is respectful, admiring, and dry. The god of nettles reads it aloud in the refectory, and the poem becomes, at the Academy, a text for the stubborn.

events.text: An entrance examiner at {b3_acad} is drunk, on duty, and apologetic. The new students file past her in a long line and she waves each through with a flourish, calling them 'darling.' One new god, shaking, is turned away at the door by a clerk for forgetting a form. The examiner turns, blinks, and looks to you.

effects.log: You argue the case. The examiner, blurry but moved, overrules the clerk. The new student is admitted, and later the Academy's best archivist.

choices.text: Help the student fill the form

effects.log: You help them fill the form, and they are admitted. The clerk glares, the examiner winks, and nobody in the Academy mentions it again.

events.text: The Academy of {b3_acad} is known for a single great experiment that has been running for four thousand years: a pot of soil, in the central courtyard, under constant observation, in which nothing grows. The Dean is quietly certain that something will. This morning a green thing, thin as a thread, has broken the surface. The courtyard is deathly quiet.

effects.log: You water it. The sprout grows into something nobody has a name for, and the Academy adopts it as the school's emblem. The Dean weeps on the stairs.
You record it, and observe. It grows, unaided, and the observation, in the end, is the most valuable work the Academy has ever produced.

events.text: A gang of students at {b3_acad} has formed a secret society devoted to the study of the Academy's own staff, on the principle that nobody has ever looked closely at them. They have a file on every tutor. They invite you to join, with an air of enormous gravity. The first rule is that you must not tell the Dean. The second is that the Dean is already a member.

effects.log: You join. The files are extraordinary and sad and often funny. The Dean, at the first meeting, turns out to be the secretary. You are sworn in with a cup of cocoa.
You decline. The society is gracious. Years later, when you need an ally in a crisis, a note arrives from the Dean: 'You would have been good at it.'

events.text: {b3_acad} hosts a debate on the question: should gods die? It ends in a draw, which is permitted, and a single student sobbing at the back, which is not. You find them in the cloister afterwards, a pale young god from the Green Assembly, whose grandmother is dying. They look at you, red-eyed. 'I just want to know it is allowed,' they say.

effects.log: You tell them. They nod, and stop crying, and walk out into the evening with a lighter step. It is the most useful sentence you ever speak.

choices.text: Sit with them in the cloister

effects.log: You sit. The evening passes. At the end they say, 'Thank you,' and you say, 'I did nothing.' They say, 'I know.' It is a very good answer.

events.text: In the last month of your course at {b3_acad} every student is asked to write the Academy's motto for the next age, on a single card, and drop it in the box. The Dean reads them all. The best is chosen. Yours is, by a clear margin, the most popular, and also the one the Dean looks at longest, in silence.

effects.log: It was 'We Were Here.' The Dean tears up, and has it engraved on the gate. It is read by every new student for the rest of the age.
You say you copied it from a wall. The Dean smiles. 'Then it is older than we thought,' they say, and keep it anyway.

events.text: On graduation day at {b3_acad} each student is given a small bell and told to ring it when they have understood something. The bell stays silent for most of the graduates for a lifetime. Yours rings at once, loudly, in the middle of the ceremony. The Dean stops. The hall turns. You do not know what you have understood.

effects.log: 'It seldom rings for the right thing,' says the Dean. 'It rings for the thing you needed.' You take it home, and wait for the thing to turn up.
You bow. The hall laughs, kindly. You carry on, and a year later, in a small kitchen, you realise what it was.

events.text: The Dean of {b3_acad} invites you to teach a course, a small one, on a subject of your choosing. The Academy pays nothing and the students are tired. You have a week to decide the topic. You make a list of things you know. It is a short list, and every item on it is a small mistake you once made.

effects.log: You teach a course on mistakes. The students pour in. It is the most-attended in Academy history, and the exam is a single question: 'What did you get wrong?'

choices.text: Teach the one thing you got right

effects.log: You teach the one thing you got right. It takes twenty minutes. The students demand more. You tell them there is no more, and they are, unexpectedly, delighted.

events.text: {b3_acad} allows each student one request to the cosmos in their final year. The requests are granted, within reason, by the Academy's patrons. A fellow student asks for the sea to be a little bluer. It is granted. Your turn comes. The patrons lean forward. You have not decided.

effects.log: You ask for a particular morning, long ago, to be remembered by whoever lived it. The patrons are puzzled, and grant it. Somewhere a stranger wakes, smiling, for no reason.
You ask for the friend you lost. The patrons are quiet, and then kind. A dream is granted: one night, one table, one pot of tea. It is enough, and not enough, and it is yours.
You say you will ask when you know what you want. The patrons are astonished. A coin is pressed into your hand. It is warm. You keep it, unspent, for an age.

events.text: Midway through your course at {b3_acad} a travelling god arrives with a sack of books written by students of past ages, and sells them for a coin each. They are the notebooks the Academy threw out. Each has a name on the cover. You find one with your own, in a hand that is not your own, dated three thousand years from now.

effects.log: You buy it. The first page is a list of things you will learn. It is very short. The second is blank. You close it with a strange peace.
You keep it unread on a high shelf. It sits there, a silent promise, and you work harder than you ever have, to deserve it.

events.text: The lecture on Heavenly Court law at {b3_acad} is given by an advocate so dry that dust comes off her sleeves. Today she describes a case, three thousand years old, in which a god was put on trial for answering a prayer too promptly. The class is asleep. You are not. The case is, you suddenly realise, yours.

effects.log: You tell the class it was you. A hush. The advocate stares, then smiles for the first time in a century. 'Then you can tell them what the verdict meant,' she says.

choices.text: Keep quiet and listen to the end

effects.log: You listen. The verdict is read, a long, kind, strange one. You walk out into the corridor and sit down on a bench, and a stranger passes, and nods.

events.text: A fellow student at {b3_acad}, a small shy god of crumbs, has been bullied for a year and has finally snapped. They have called up a storm in the dormitory, a small violent one, all in one room. The bullies are pinned to the ceiling by wind. The Dean has not yet noticed. The little god looks at you, appalled and triumphant.

effects.log: You gently talk the storm down. It subsides. The bullies fall in a heap, chastened. The little god cries, and you walk them home through the courtyard, and nobody speaks of it.

choices.text: Let it run a minute more

effects.log: You let it run a minute. The bullies apologise at the top of their voices. The little god lowers the wind and is, after that, left alone, and is surprised at how much they like the quiet.

events.text: It is the Academy of {b3_acad}'s thousandth anniversary, and a procession of former students passes through the great gate, each in the robes of their age. The oldest are barely visible. The youngest hold their programmes. You are asked to walk at the end of the line, as the most recent graduate. Behind you, there is nobody yet.

effects.log: You walk the length of the procession with your head high. At the gate, an old robed shade turns and bows to you. You bow back. It is the most formal, the quietest moment of your education.
You look behind you, and the road is empty, and a little hopeful. You resolve to teach someone, someday, to walk behind you. You do.

events.text: The Games of the Novice Spirits begin at dawn on a cloud of hammered gold, in the sight of every pantheon. Your pupil is entered in the Race of Small Winds. They are a very small wind. The other entrants are all hurricanes in training. Your pupil gives you a nervous, upward look, and ruffles your sleeve.

choices.text: Tell them to race their own race

effects.log: Your pupil is small, and honest, and finishes last, and happy. The crowd likes this better than the winner, and your pupil is invited to three feasts.
You show them a trick of the draught behind the leader. They cut in at the last bend and finish fourth. A tiny scandal follows, and a larger legend.

events.text: At the Games of the Novice Spirits, the Contest of Domains asks young spirits to demonstrate their calling in a single act. A hundred rain-spirits make clouds. A hundred fire-spirits make sparks. Your pupil, a spirit of small hinges, steps up and opens a door. Nobody understands. The door, however, opens onto a great deal.

effects.log: You cheer so loudly the whole arena looks round. Your pupil's door opens onto a quiet room with a lamp, and the audience, one by one, falls silent, and loves it.
You watch the door, and it is simply lovely. The judges, baffled, award your pupil the Prize of the Unseen. The crowd applauds without knowing why.

events.text: The judges of the Games of the Novice Spirits are three elderly gods of the Will of Heaven, who have judged for ten thousand years and are bored. Your pupil, in the Contest of Praise, is performing a hymn. The judges are slumped. One is asleep. The pupil sings on. The hymn is, as it happens, very good.

choices.text: Wake the sleeper with a cough

effects.log: You cough politely. The judge wakes, listens, and is astonished. The pupil wins, and the judge, as is the custom, gives them their own gold ring.

choices.text: Let the pupil sing for the room, not the judges

effects.log: Your pupil sings to the audience, who weep. The judges, hearing, rouse themselves. The hymn is entered in the Games' book of masterworks.

events.text: The Games of the Novice Spirits include a duel with kites, in which each spirit flies a kite of their own domain's weather. Your pupil's kite is a cloud of wild bees. The judges are afraid. The bees are polite. A rival's kite, a kite of thunder, bears down. The bees look at your pupil, who gulps.

choices.text: Tell them to hold the line

effects.log: The bees hold. The thunder-kite breaks against them in a clap of surprise. The crowd roars, the bees hum a note of victory, and the thunder-spirit shakes your pupil's hand.

choices.text: Tell them to let the kite go

effects.log: Your pupil lets the bees go. They scatter over the crowd, and everyone, in a swirl of gold, is given a small sweet bee-kiss. The duel is declared a draw, and a delight.

events.text: In the final trial of the Games of the Novice Spirits, the contestants must give a gift to a stranger. Your pupil draws a stranger at random from the crowd: an old and tired mortal ghost, who has wandered up from below, lost. Your pupil looks at you in panic. The gift must be given in an hour, and must be real.

effects.log: You help them find a gift: a small bright memory of the ghost's own, restored. The ghost weeps, and thanks them, and is led away, comforted. Your pupil wins the Games' heart.
Your pupil thinks, and gives the ghost a seat, a cup of tea, and an hour of listening. It is the best gift in the history of the Games, and the judges bow their heads.

events.text: The pupil you sent to the Games of the Novice Spirits has gone missing in the middle of the Obstacle Course. Searchers have combed the course, the stands, the pavilions. They are found, in the end, asleep in the winners' chair, covered in confetti, having crept in for a nap after finishing last. The crowd, spotting them, begins to clap.

effects.log: You let them sleep. The crowd quiets, and tiptoes round the chair. When your pupil wakes, there is a small gold medal on their chest, awarded, the tag says, for Restfulness.
You wake them. They blink, startled, and then burst into a laugh that is picked up by the entire arena. The medal, a joke, is meant sincerely.

events.text: A pupil of yours has been disqualified from the Games of the Novice Spirits for using a cloak that belongs to a rival. The cloak was lent. The rival, a small stubborn god of frost, denies it. The pupil, honest, says nothing in defence. The judges are about to ban them for a century. The matter has reached your hands.

effects.log: A hearing is held. The rival is asked again, and, under a calm, kind gaze, confesses that the cloak was lent. The pupil is cleared, the rival chastened, and the two shake hands.
You pay the fine, a season of your worship. The pupil is cleared. The rival, hearing of it, sends a thank-you in a plain envelope, and a small frosted flower.

events.text: The Games of the Novice Spirits are shown on a screen of living water, which every pantheon crowds around in the evenings. It shows your pupil's final bout in a miracle of slow motion. A bell rings, and a hush falls, and the water ripples. Your pupil has just done something extraordinary, and you do not know what.

effects.log: 'A new form,' says the chief judge. 'We do not have a name.' You are asked to name it. You name it after a mortal child's word for rain, and it sticks.
Your pupil shrugs, embarrassed. 'I was thinking about my gran,' they say. The form is not named. It is simply called 'Gran', and taught.

events.text: The stands at the Games of the Novice Spirits are divided by pantheon. Each cheers its own. The Concord, the neutrals, sit in the middle with a flask. Your pupil is from none of these, and has no stand. A single mortal child, far below, is praying for them. The prayer is audible across the arena. It is a small, honest, shaky one.

effects.log: You send a small sign: a gust, a bell, a rainbow over the arena. The child far below shrieks with delight. Your pupil, hearing, finds courage, and the stands murmur.

choices.text: Pass the prayer to your pupil

effects.log: You pass it up. Your pupil, hearing it, stands taller. They win the bout, and never forget the child, and visit them, a century later, in a dream.

events.text: It is the closing of the Games of the Novice Spirits, and the tradition is that each school lights a lantern for the fallen. This year a school is missing: a small pantheon, lost to a quarrel with the Sky, whose young have been forbidden to attend. Their place in the line is empty. One of the older spirits notices, and looks along the row to you.

effects.log: You light a lantern in their place. The line is silent. After a pause, others follow, and by the end there are two hundred lights where there was one gap. The Sky's envoy leaves unreadable.
You go, at dusk, to the lost school and carry their young to the arena. They arrive in rags and the whole crowd stands. The quarrel with the Sky is not resolved, but it is forgotten, for the night.

events.text: Your pupil's first bout at the Games of the Novice Spirits is against a spirit of thorns who has never lost, and has a habit of hissing. Your pupil, a spirit of dew, is not afraid of thorns. They simply dissolve on them, and re-form, and dissolve again. The bout lasts an hour. The thorn-spirit, helpless with laughter, concedes.

effects.log: You applaud so loudly the thorn-spirit looks over, and bows. The two become the closest of friends, and tour the Games as a pair, in matching colours.
You pass them a flask. The thorn-spirit, cheered, shares it with your pupil. A new bond forms across the arena, and a thornless rose is entered in the Games' garden.

events.text: The Games of the Novice Spirits have a prize for best sportsmanship, and the winner is chosen by a jury of one: the oldest spirit at the Games, a small, translucent, ancient breeze. This year the breeze has swept straight past the favourites, and settled on your pupil's shoulder, and will not move.

effects.log: You thank it. The breeze swirls once round your pupil's head and drifts away. The prize is entered in the book, and your pupil, blushing, is the youngest ever to win it.
The breeze whispers, so faintly you could not swear to it: 'They picked up my hat.' You cannot find a hat, and are delighted.

events.text: After the Games of the Novice Spirits, the tradition is that the winners are carried round the pantheons in a procession on the shoulders of the losers. It is a joyous, shambling thing. Your pupil, who has lost, is carrying the winner, a huge god of the sea, who weighs a ton and sings. Your pupil is flat-out delighted.

effects.log: You walk alongside, carrying their shoes. Your pupil, scarlet and beaming, is carried round the entire cosmos by a very happy loser. The sea-god sings a verse about you.

choices.text: Take a turn under the sea-god

effects.log: You take a turn at the pole. It is dreadfully heavy and wonderful. You walk two pantheons' worth and return, bent and laughing, and the crowd cheers.

events.text: The Games of the Novice Spirits were nearly cancelled this year after a mortal storm tore the arena's roof off. The young spirits set about mending it themselves, with whatever they had: dew for glue, moonlight for thread. Your pupil is among them, on a ladder, holding a nail. They have been at it all night, and their hands are shaking.

effects.log: You hold the ladder through the dark hours. At dawn the roof is whole, a little crooked, silver at the seams. The first bout is held under it, and the crowd calls it the best roof in the Games' history.
You bring the young ones food and a flask. They eat in the rafters, giddy with exhaustion, and when the sun rises, the roof is done, and they sleep where they sit.

events.text: Your pupil comes home from the Games of the Novice Spirits with a cup, a cold, and a friend. The cup is small, tin, and engraved with a misspelling. The cold is formidable. The friend is a young god of frogs, who follows them everywhere, hopefully. Your pupil is shy, tired and wildly happy. They set the cup on your desk, and sneeze.

choices.text: Keep the cup on your desk

effects.log: You keep it there, among the more serious relics. It is, in the end, the one visitors ask about, and you tell them about the Games in a long, fond story.

choices.text: Make them tea and put them to bed

effects.log: You make tea, with honey, and tuck them in. The young god of frogs sleeps on the floor. In the morning the cold is gone, and the friendship, unmistakably, is here to stay.

events.text: A sworn member of the Concord of Domains, a thin and gentle god of rivers, has been found asleep at the edge of the sea, and nobody can wake them. The Concord's law is that they must be guarded, since a sleeping god is helpless. You are asked to stand watch. The river-god snores in a rippling, watery voice. Birds have begun to nest in their hair.

effects.log: You stand watch for a season. The river-god wakes at the first frost, bewildered, thanks you, and is the Concord's most devoted friend for ten thousand years.
You ask the birds to keep the watch. They are splendid at it. The river-god wakes surrounded by a loyal, chattering court of sparrows.

events.text: The Concord of Domains is asked to guard the sleep of a famous god of Thunder who has been made drowsy by a spell cast by a jealous rival. The rival has come to the Concord's door and denied everything. His eyes dart. He is holding a wand behind his back, and not hiding it well.

effects.log: You take it, politely. The rival is mortified, and gives a full confession, and the Thunder wakes in a rage of delight. The Concord's honour is high.

choices.text: Offer the rival a way out

effects.log: You say the wand must have been planted. The rival, stunned, agrees. The spell is lifted, and the rival is the Concord's most careful friend thereafter.

events.text: A young god comes to the Concord begging for help: her domain, small, quiet, a woodland of birches, is being cleared by a powerful neighbour who says she is not the real god of it.
