She is, in fact, still in the process of becoming one. The Concord's law covers sleepers, not the unfinished. Its rule is to protect the sleeping, but she has just woken.

effects.log: You argue to the Concord that the unfinished are sleepers of a kind. It is a daring reading, and carries by a vote. The birches stand, and a god is born under them.

choices.text: Send her to the Green Assembly

effects.log: You send her, with a note, to the Green Assembly, which takes her in. The birches are planted in the Root Hall's garden, and the neighbour, shamed, moves on.

events.text: The Concord of Domains has a tradition of sharing a feast with the sleepers: the members dine around a sleeping god, and tell them the news, and leave a plate. This feast's sleeper is a god of Dreams, and a small boy-spirit, wide-eyed, has crept under the table. They look at you, and put a finger to their lips.

choices.text: Share your plate with the boy

effects.log: You slide a bun under the table. A tiny hand takes it. The feast goes on. At the end, the boy has vanished, and the sleeper's smile is a little broader.

choices.text: Lift the cloth and say hello

effects.log: You lift the cloth. The boy, caught, giggles. He is a dream of the sleeper's, escaped, and he asks you to tell him a story. You do, quietly, until the plate is empty.

events.text: A stranger arrives at the Concord's hall claiming to be a sleeping god awake. The Concord's law forbids waking, and so the stranger's claim is a heresy. They are shabby and cheerful and certain. They sit down at the table and help themselves to the bread. A hush falls over the ring.

effects.log: You hear them out. The stranger is, in fact, a god woken by a mortal's well-meaning prayer, and wants only to be put back to sleep. You tuck them in, and the Concord sighs.
The stranger recites the oath perfectly, with an extra verse nobody knows. The Concord is awed. The extra verse is added, and the stranger is let go, with honour.

events.text: The Concord of Domains is asked to witness a promise between two gods who have fought for a thousand years: that neither will take the other's domain. They each carry a cup of water from their own country, and are to pour them into one bowl. The bowl is empty. They stand either side of it, trembling, with the cups held out.

effects.log: You pour a little of your own water, to show it can be done. They follow. The bowl fills. The promise is sealed in a brimming bowl, and each drinks, with a wry smile, from the other's cup.
You wait. After a long minute, one pours. The other follows. The bowl is a little overfull. The Concord records it as the quietest, most moving peace of the age.

events.text: A mortal prophet, a woman of the hills, has been collecting the dreams of a sleeping god in a bucket, and selling them. The Concord has an obligation. The sleeping god's dreams are his own. The prophet is cheerful, and honest, and says she is only trying to feed her children. She has a bucket, and a very small, hungry boy.

choices.text: Return the dreams, and feed the children

effects.log: You return the bucket to the sleeper's side and arrange a loaf and a basket for the children each week. The prophet, astonished, becomes a devoted friend of the Concord.
You take the bucket and give the prophet a firm warning. She goes, scowling. The boy watches you go, and you will think of him longer than you expect.

events.text: The Concord's greatest treasure is a bell that rings whenever a sleeping god is threatened. It has not rung in a thousand years. This evening it makes a small sound, like a throat being cleared. The Wardens look at one another. The bell tries again, and rings a single, uncertain, apologetic note.

effects.log: You follow it across three realms to a nursery in the Green Assembly, where a baby god in a cradle has rolled onto a sleeping god's foot. You roll the baby gently off. The bell sighs, and is quiet.
The Keeper, shaken, says it is the bell's first false alarm, and the Concord's first time to be glad of one. A small party is held in the bell's honour.

events.text: A god of the Hunt, a bold and swaggering one, has taken to using the Concord's sleeping gods as practice for his aim: harmless arrows, without barbs, that thud into the pillows. He says it is affectionate. The sleepers, naturally, cannot object. The Concord's code says nothing of pillows. It has been a very long week.

choices.text: Challenge him to a hunt of your own

effects.log: You challenge him, and win by a hair, tracking a deer he missed. He puts down his bow with a bow of his own. The pillows are mended and the practice stops.

choices.text: Tell him the pillows are cursed

effects.log: You tell him they are cursed with ticklishness. He pales, and stops. The Concord maintains the curse, as a deterrent, with a straight face, for a thousand years.

events.text: The Concord of Domains is called to an old shrine, where a god of Roads has slept so long that the road has grown over him, and tourists are picnicking on his stomach. The Warden in charge looks at the picnic and then at you. 'They are not doing him any harm,' they say. 'But it feels wrong.'

effects.log: You ask them to move. They do, with a good grace, and leave a flask of tea beside the sleeper. The road is cleared, and a small shrine is built, and picnics are held a polite distance away.
You leave them. The god of Roads, you decide, would have liked the company. He sleeps on, with a faint smile, and the picnic goes on above him, for an age, and nobody is the worse.

events.text: Three thousand years ago, a member of the Concord took the oath and then disappeared. Today a notice arrives, from a far-off country, that the member has died, in a bed, as a mortal, having walked away from godhood to be a baker. The notice requests that the Concord honour the oath, and remember. A small tin of flour is enclosed.

effects.log: You hold a small ceremony, with bread. The Concord eats it, silent. It is the best bread, and the saddest, and the member's chair is, from that day, never empty: a loaf sits in it.
You write to the family, in a mortal hand. They write back, three pages of recipes. The Concord adopts the bread of that country as its own.

events.text: A tidy-minded Concord Warden has proposed a new rule: that all sleeping gods be tagged with their names, domains and dates, to prevent confusion. The tags are small, brass, and ugly. The sleepers do not mind, the Warden says. The Concord is divided. Some think it dignified, others a violation. A tag has been prepared for you, in case.

effects.log: You support the tags. They are tied, gravely, to every sleeper. The effect is peculiarly touching: a whole ring of gods, labelled like jars of jam, and cared for with an extra tenderness.
You oppose them. The Warden is hurt, but yields, and compiles instead a beautiful book. The sleepers are named in ink, not brass, and the Warden is secretly delighted.

events.text: The Concord's oath is sworn on water. A critic from the Throne of Storms has pointed out, with some relish, that the water in question is always the same cup, passed around for a hundred thousand years, and is by now rather a lot of backwash. The Concord is stung. A fresh cup is proposed. The old one sits on the table, humble, with a faint crack.

effects.log: You vote to keep the cup. It is old, and dear, and sacred, and full of the lips of everyone who has sworn. The Storm's critic, mollified, apologises.

choices.text: Use a fresh cup, and keep the old as a relic

effects.log: You use a fresh cup, and keep the old cup in a case. Both are sworn on, in time, and both feel right, and both are somewhat less than the old one.

events.text: The Concord is asked to arbitrate a dispute about the ownership of a sunset. A god of the Sky claims it for his domain. A god of the Sea claims it for hers. A god of Fire says it is his. The sunset hangs, patient and gold, over a bay, and is sadly neglected. Each of the three has submitted a claim in verse.

effects.log: You award the sunset to the bay, and the people who live beside it. The three gods are outraged, and then, one by one, drift down to sit on the shore and watch.
You divide it by colours. The Sky takes the blue, the Sea the green, Fire the gold. The sunset is subtly incomplete ever after, and rather lovely for it.

events.text: It is the Concord's custom, on the longest night, to sit by the gods who have slept the longest and read them a letter from the world. This year's letter is written by a child. It is addressed to 'whoever is sleeping' and says, in a round hand, that the world is quite good now, and they should come out when they are ready, and there is cake.

choices.text: Read it aloud, to every sleeper

effects.log: You read it at every bed. The Concord sits through the night, hearing it again and again. By dawn, there are dry eyes in nobody's head, and no sleeper has stirred, and every one of them is smiling.

choices.text: Leave the letter at the oldest sleeper's pillow

effects.log: You leave it. It is there in the morning, and in the morning after that. A hundred years later it is found, creased and opened, in the sleeper's hand, as if read.

events.text: The Court of the Unlit Sun has asked you to take a message to a god of the Will of Heaven who owes the Court a favour. The message is a single word, written on a black card. You are not to read it. You hold it up to the light, and it is too dark to read in any case. The god, when you find them, goes the colour of ash.

effects.log: You stand by while the god reads. They bow their head, nod once, and say, 'Tell them yes.' You do. The word was 'Remember.' You do not learn what.

choices.text: Deliver it with a kind word

effects.log: You add, 'I am sorry.' The god looks at you, surprised, and says, 'You are the first of them who has said so.' They do what the Court asks, and send you a lamp.

events.text: A debtor of the Court of the Unlit Sun has fled to a mortal village, and hidden in a bakery. The Court wants them back. The baker, an old woman, has sheltered them, thinking them a lost grandchild. You are sent to retrieve them. The baker opens the door, covered in flour, with a pleased and bewildered face.

effects.log: You take the debtor, and explain to the baker kindly. She weeps, and gives you a loaf for the road. The debtor, paying their debt, comes back every Sunday for bread.

choices.text: Leave the debtor to the bakery

effects.log: You return to the Court and say the debtor was not found. The Court knows. A year later, an enormous loaf is delivered to the Court's table, and nobody remarks on it.

events.text: The Court of the Unlit Sun has a rite in which each member must bury something they love at the foot of an unlit lamp. The members dig in turn, in silence, in the dark. You have brought a small wooden bird. It is your oldest possession. The pit is shallow. The earth is cold.

effects.log: You bury it, and cover it, and stand a moment. The Court nods. Years later you find a green shoot at the lamp's foot, and think of the bird, and are consoled.

choices.text: Keep it, and bury a lie instead

effects.log: You bury a lie you have been telling yourself. It is the heaviest thing you have ever put down. The Court, who can tell, bows to you, and says nothing.

events.text: A member of the Court has been caught giving away a secret for free, out of kindness. The Court is outraged: secrets are currency. The offender, a thin pale god, stands before the Court and says that the secret was a mother's name and a place to find her. A child, in the corner, is weeping with happiness.

effects.log: You speak in their defence. The Court, grudgingly, drops the charge. The pale god, trembling, thanks you, and the child sends the Court a hand-drawn card with a sun on it.
You fine them a season of silence, which they accept with a bow. They return refreshed, and give away another secret within the year, and are not fined again.

events.text: The Court of the Unlit Sun is planning a theft of enormous scale: the stealing of an entire dawn from a rival pantheon. It is a gesture of defiance. The plan is elegant and cruel. You have been asked to supply the sack. It is a very large sack. Someone has stitched it with black thread, and it smells of sleep.

effects.log: You supply it. The dawn is taken, for a minute, and returned, with a note: 'Borrowed.' The rival pantheon is stunned, and then, grudgingly, impressed. A feud of cheerful sabotage begins.
You refuse to supply the sack. The Court shrugs, and finds another. The dawn is stolen anyway. You are not blamed. You are not trusted with sacks.

events.text: A sorrowful ghost of the Unlit Sun's own halls haunts the corridor outside your door: a former member, long dead, who owes a debt to nobody and wants only to say sorry. The Court's custom is to leave such ghosts alone. They stand there, night after night, with their head bowed, and a small lantern that does not light.

choices.text: Open the door and let them speak

effects.log: You open it. The ghost speaks, haltingly, of a wrong they did to a friend. You listen, and say you forgive them on the friend's behalf, which is not allowed. The ghost vanishes, and the lantern, for a moment, lights.

choices.text: Leave a candle at the door

effects.log: You leave a candle. In the morning, the candle has burned, and the ghost is gone, and the corridor is warm.

events.text: The Court of the Unlit Sun holds a market in the dark, where the members trade what they owe, what they are owed, and what they would rather forget. A vendor sells you, for a pittance, a jar labelled 'The Last Good Day.' It hums. Its lid is sealed with wax. The vendor leans in. 'It is not yours,' they whisper. 'But it is going cheap.'

effects.log: You buy it. In the jar is a morning in a kitchen, with sun, and bread, and someone humming. You never find out whose it was. You open the jar once a year, and are warm.
You ask the vendor whose it was. They tell you, after a haggle, and you carry the jar across a world to a dying god, who weeps, and drinks, and sleeps well.

events.text: The Hand of the Unlit Sun, who rarely speaks, has asked you to find out who has been leaving small gifts at the Court's gate: dried flowers, a loaf, a child's drawing of an eclipse. They come at dawn. The Hand wants to know whether it is a trap. You wait behind a pillar with a cup of tea.

effects.log: At dawn a small mortal girl arrives, leaves a flower, and goes. She prays to the Court, you realise, from far below, in the one hour she is allowed. You say nothing. You leave her a bun.
You catch the girl and she cries. The Hand, summoned, kneels, and says, in a cracked voice, that nobody has given the Court a gift in an age. They keep the drawing. They keep her.

events.text: A favour owed by the Court of the Unlit Sun is called in by a god of Fate, who asks for the loan of a single shadow, at noon, in a particular courtyard. The shadow must be of a particular person, who does not know. The Court accepts. You are chosen to take it. The person is a boy, asleep in a hammock, humming.

effects.log: You take it, as softly as a hair from a pillow. The boy stirs, sighs, and sleeps on. The shadow is returned at dusk. The boy's whole life, afterwards, is a little more at rest than it was.
You refuse. The Court is displeased. The god of Fate grumbles. The boy, you hear, grows up lucky, which is its own unsolved debt.

events.text: The Court of the Unlit Sun has a mascot: a small black cat, who is, in fact, a minor god in disguise, and the Court's only source of light. It sits in the Hall each evening and glows faintly at the whiskers. This evening the cat is sick. A hush falls over the Court. The Night Herald comes to you with a bowl of milk.

effects.log: You tend it for a week. The cat recovers, and sits in your lap, glowing, and then wanders off. It leaves a mouse on your pillow. It is the Court's highest honour.

choices.text: Take the cat to the Green Assembly

effects.log: You carry the cat to the Root Hall, where Saengmo takes it in, tuts, and cures it with a spoon of honey. The cat comes home happier, and fatter.

events.text: A rebel faction of the Court of the Unlit Sun wants the Sun lit, once, for a day, to see what it would look like. The loyalists are shocked. The rebels, led by a handsome and sensitive Lamp-Snuffer, have gathered a petition: five hundred signatures, in black ink. The Night Herald asks which side you are on, in a voice that betrays nothing.

effects.log: You sign. The rebels cheer. The loyalists scowl. The Sun is not lit, but the Court begins, quietly, to burn a single candle in the Hall, and the shadows lean in.
You stay loyal. The rebels sulk, then, one by one, drift away to other halls. The Court is darker, and more certain, and a little emptier.

events.text: The Court's Debt Collector, an enormous patient god in grey, has come to your door for a payment you did not know you owed: three sleepless nights, forfeit, in the service of the Court. You protest. The Collector opens a ledger, and shows you the entry, in your own hand: 'I will give three nights when asked.' You do not remember writing it.

effects.log: You pay it, in the Hall, keeping a vigil beside a dying lamp. You learn the shape of the dark, its friendliness, its sorrow. The Collector, when you finish, says: 'Interest waived.'
You argue the entry, and win, on a technicality about ink. The Collector bows, and says: 'Another time.' The ledger line is crossed through, in a different, lighter hand.

events.text: It is the Feast of Absent Friends at the Court of the Unlit Sun: each member sets a place for someone who is not there. The places are laid in a long ring in the dark. You have laid one, for someone you cannot name. You wait. The candles gutter. Then a cup, in the place you set, is slowly, softly, tilted.

effects.log: You sit with them. You do not speak. The cup is raised, and lowered. Somewhere a chair creaks. At the end, the candles go out, together. You are not alone.

choices.text: Say their name, whoever it is

effects.log: You say a name, in a whisper, and do not know where it came from. The cup is still. A warmth settles on the table, and the Court, around you, murmurs approval.

events.text: The Court of the Unlit Sun has been quietly paying the funerals of mortals who died alone, in far countries: a coffin, a bell, a handful of earth, a flower. Nobody knows. A grateful widow has traced the payments to the Court and arrived at the gate to thank them. She is old and plain and does not know what she has found.

effects.log: You receive her in the Hall, and show her a modest room. She thanks the Court, and weeps, and leaves a pot of jam for the Hall. It is eaten, silently, in a ring.

choices.text: Send her home with a blessing

effects.log: You send her home with a blessing. The Court does not stop the funerals. It does, quietly, start sending flowers on her husband's grave.

events.text: There is a legend in the Court that the Unlit Sun is not dark by nature but by choice, and that it could be lit, if one asked it gently. A pilgrim of the Will of Heaven comes to the Hall with a small oil-lamp, and asks to be allowed to try. Nobody knows what to say. The Night Herald looks at you.

effects.log: The pilgrim kneels by the cold sun and murmurs. For a long, long moment, nothing. Then a single warm spark lifts into the shadows, and the Hall, for the length of a held breath, is gold.
You send them away, kindly, with tea. The pilgrim understands, or pretends to. The Sun stays dark. The pilgrim returns every year, with the same lamp, and the same hope.

events.text: A prayer comes up from {sect}, the sect you left behind when you rose, written on rice paper in a shaky hand: 'The roof leaks. The elders are old. The rice is poor. We do not ask for a miracle, only to be remembered.' The paper smells of smoke and plum blossom. It is signed by the gatekeeper, who has the same name you remember.

choices.text: Send a blessing, small and warm

effects.log: You send a mild warmth over the old roof. The rain stops leaking, as if by luck. The gatekeeper puts a bowl of rice outside the gate each night for you, forever.
You appear in the gatekeeper's dream as an old friend with a cup of tea. They wake smiling, and mend the roof with their own hands, and tell the sect a god is looking after it.

events.text: The abbot of {sect} has died. The sect, bereft, prays to you, its only god, for a sign of who should succeed. They pray in a clumsy chorus, the way mortals do. Two candidates have been named: a devout, dull man and a clever, warm woman. The prayers pile up, day after day, in a heap on your desk.

choices.text: Send a sign for the woman

effects.log: You send a rainbow over the woman's practice-yard. The sect chooses her. She is a fine abbot, and prays to you with a plain, funny, brisk affection.
You send nothing. The sect argues for a year, and chooses the dull man, who turns out to be a gentle soul. They never learn you stayed silent on purpose.

events.text: A child of {sect}, aged six, has written to you, as a god, in crayon, to ask for a dog. It is a very polite letter, and a very practical one. It lists the qualities needed in a dog. They include: 'likes soup.' The letter has been left on the shrine in the sect's courtyard, where it has been read, by now, by most of the disciples.

effects.log: A scruffy brown dog arrives at the gate that evening and attaches itself to the child. The sect names it after the god. It likes soup.

choices.text: Send a dream of a dog

effects.log: You send the child a dream of a dog. They wake up with a lingering warmth and the sense of having been licked. A dog turns up a month later, an ordinary one, as if called.

events.text: The sect you came from, {sect}, has sent you a new sacrifice: not rice or wine but a poem, a very bad one, in verse, with an acrostic of your name. It is the product of a decade of effort by a sweet, awkward junior monk. The poem has been read aloud in the hall, to polite silence. The monk is asking, in a note, whether the god was pleased.

effects.log: You send a very small, polite miracle: a perfect quatrain, in the monk's dream. He wakes and writes it down, and writes better for the rest of his life.
You send a wisp of incense that rises, curls, and spells 'Thank you.' The monk reads it and cries. The poem is hung in the shrine, unrevised.

events.text: A prayer arrives from {sect}, in a voice you recognise, though you cannot recall where from. It is the voice of the old master who trained you. They are dying, in a quiet cell, and are asking not for a cure, only for a word. They say, in the prayer: 'I am not sure you remember me. I am not sure I mind.' The prayer is very steady.

effects.log: You descend, in a hush of light, and sit by the bed. The master looks up, startled, and says, 'There you are.' They die at dawn with their hand in yours. The sect hears a faint bell.
You send a dream in which you sit on the old doorstep together, and drink tea. The master wakes, smiling, and is gone by evening. You keep the cup.

events.text: The old sect {sect} has fallen on hard times, and its rivals are circling. They pray to you with great earnestness for the destruction of those rivals. The prayer is detailed and rather bloodthirsty, for a group of monks. You know the rivals. They are not wicked. They are merely hungry.

effects.log: You send a bountiful harvest to both sides. The rivals, fed, forget the quarrel, and the two sects begin to share a market. The prayers change. They are still, a little, aimed at you.
You send a dream to the leaders of both sides: the old sect is under a god's protection. The rivals back off. The sect thinks it was a victory. It was, in a way, the opposite.

events.text: The sect of {sect} sends you a prayer which is entirely a recipe. It is a recipe for the soup the sect used to make on your birthday, in the years when you were a lowly monk among them. 'We have lost the recipe,' says the note. 'We have only the memory of the smell. Do you remember?' You do, to your surprise, and rather precisely.

choices.text: Send the recipe, in a dream

effects.log: You send the recipe, in a dream, to the oldest cook. She wakes, writes it down, and cooks it that night. The sect weeps over its bowls. They name the soup after you, and have it twice a year.

choices.text: Send a taste, not a recipe

effects.log: You send the taste of it, in the mouth of a sleeping cook. She works it out in a week, by trial. The soup is a little different from the original, and a little better.

events.text: A group of pilgrims from {sect} have made a four-year journey to the nearest shrine of yours, on foot, and arrived with sore feet and sore hearts. They kneel. They pray for nothing except to tell you that they walked here. A thin boy among them has a limp and a shy, burning face. They have no idea you can hear them.

effects.log: You send the boy's limp a morning's ease, and a clear dream of the road home. The pilgrims go back with a lighter step, and the boy grows into the sect's best traveller.
You send each of the pilgrims a small, tender sign: a warm hand on the shoulder, a smell of rain. They go home certain they have been seen, and, for once, they have.

events.text: The sect you left, {sect}, prays to you each year on the anniversary of your leaving, and always has. This year the prayer is longer, and strange. They ask whether you are happy. It is a mortal's question, and a lovely one, and it arrives like a pebble dropped in a very deep well. You turn it over, and cannot answer.

effects.log: You send a dream: of a small, plain room, with a window, in which you sit, at ease. It is not a lie. They wake up smiling, and pass on the dream, and it grows in the telling.
You send the question back. The sect, startled, holds a meeting. They send a long, careful, funny reply, the sum of which is: yes, mostly, on Tuesdays.

events.text: A prayer comes up from {sect}, a young monk's, begging for the strength to leave. He wishes to be a farmer. He has wished it for years. The sect's rule forbids it. He has prayed for the courage to say it to the abbot. You see him, in the courtyard, with a hoe in his hand, shaking, gathering the nerve.

effects.log: You send courage. He tells the abbot, who is, to everyone's surprise, kind. He leaves in spring with a basket of seed and a blessing, and farms a hillside for sixty years, and is happy.

choices.text: Give him a dream of the abbot as a farmer

effects.log: You send a dream in which the abbot is a farmer too. He wakes laughing. He tells the abbot, who is mortified, and moved, and lets him go.

events.text: The sect of {sect} has been told that you are a god. This is true. They have built you a shrine. The shrine is a ramshackle hut next to the latrine, and the offerings are mostly dried persimmons. You look at it, and at the faithful, kneeling in a row. One of them is crying. It is the only shrine in all the cosmos at which you have been unreservedly loved.

effects.log: You bless the hut, and it does not fall down. The latrine is, thereafter, a little less offensive. The persimmons are sweeter. The sect is quietly sure it is a miracle.
You sit in the hut for an evening, listening to the faithful sing. The song is flat. You have never heard a better one. You leave a persimmon behind, to their awe.

events.text: A letter comes from the abbot of {sect}, apologising. The sect has been forced to sell the statue of you, the one that stood in the courtyard, to pay the taxes. It was a good statue, and not a likeness. It has been bought by a merchant who plans to put it in his garden as an ornament. The abbot is mortified.

effects.log: You let the statue go. The merchant's garden is a lovely one, and the merchant, who does not believe in gods, finds that he is happier there than he ever was. The sect, in time, carves another.

choices.text: Buy it back, in a dream

effects.log: You send the abbot a dream with the price. A strange purse is found at the gate. The statue is bought, and set in the courtyard, and the merchant is left, bewildered, with a small gold coin and a sense of being thanked.

events.text: The oldest nun of {sect}, who never prayed, prays for the first time, and to you. It is a very short prayer. 'I have been wrong,' she says. 'I am sorry. I should have said it years ago.' The prayer is not addressed to anyone in particular. You wonder if it was meant for you at all. It is sent anyway.

effects.log: You accept the prayer, and hold it a long time. You send back a warmth to the nun that is simply: all is well. She dies a month later, content, and the prayer is kept in the shrine.

choices.text: Pass it on to whoever it was meant for

effects.log: You trace the prayer to a sister, long dead, and carry it to her in a dream. The sister answers, kindly. You carry that back. It is the strangest postal route you have run.

events.text: The sect of {sect} has split in two over a question of how to hold the chopsticks during the ritual of thanks to you. Each faction accuses the other of blasphemy. They have written to you, in separate envelopes, to settle it. The letters are polite, adamant, and equally fervent. They are, somehow, both beautifully written.

choices.text: Rule that you eat with your fingers

effects.log: You send a dream to both: you have never used chopsticks in your life. The sects, appalled, then helpless with laughter, reunite, and eat with their fingers at the ritual from then on.
You say nothing. The sect remains divided for a century, and then merges, by marriage, and the question dies of old age. Your silence is called, in time, wisdom.

events.text: A woman from the village below {sect} prays to you, desperately, for the return of her son who left for the capital and has not written. She does not know you are the god of the sect. She has prayed to every shrine on the road. The prayer reaches you by accident, among the sect's. The woman has run out of other gods, and is down to you.

effects.log: You find him in the capital, thin and ashamed, working in a tannery. You send him a dream of his mother's kitchen. He wakes weeping and begins to walk home. She is waiting at the gate.

choices.text: Send the mother a sign of him

effects.log: You send her a dream: her son, alive, working, well. She wakes, and tells the village, and the village lights a lantern. A letter from him arrives within a month.

events.text: The monks of {sect} have started to hold a monthly 'conversation with the god', in which they sit in silence and then compare notes on what they felt. The notes are inconsistent. One felt warmth, one felt a cold draught, one felt an irritating itch behind the knee. The abbot has asked, in writing, which of them was right.

effects.log: You answer them all, by dream: everyone was right, and the itch was a flea. The monks laugh until they cry. The conversation is, from then on, the best-attended event of the sect's calendar.
You say nothing. The monks continue to compare notes, month after month, and the comparing becomes the point. They grow close in the telling.

events.text: It is the year of a great flood, and {sect} has been cut off from the road. The monks pray to you with a patient, practical fervour. They do not ask to be saved; they ask how best to use the grain left, and how to ration the candles. They are, you realise, praying for advice, as one asks a clever friend.

effects.log: You send a clear plan in a dream to the abbot, a plan of the larder. The monks follow it, and are fed for the full three months of the flood. They thank you with a plain, warm bow.
You turn the flood a mile east. The sect is saved, and a village is not. You never learn what became of the village, and the monks, grateful, never ask.

events.text: A prayer comes up from the novices of {sect}: they have found the old training sword that you once left there, and it has begun to hum when they pass the lumber room. They want to know if it is holy, or haunted, or merely loose. They have wrapped it in a sleeping-mat and stationed a boy to guard it with a broom.

choices.text: Answer that it is only a sword

effects.log: You send a dream: it is a sword, nothing more, and was once yours. The novices are crestfallen and enchanted. They hang it in the shrine, and it is, for the sect, the holiest object of the age.
You send a note, softly, through the blade. It hums, in your key. The novices, hearing, drop to their knees. The boy with the broom salutes it, with the broom.

events.text: The gatekeeper of {sect} has prayed to you every morning for fifty years, always the same prayer: 'Let the gate be kind today.' It is a strange prayer. You have, without noticing, been answering it, in a small way, every day. This morning the gatekeeper has not prayed. The gate stands open. You go and look.

effects.log: The gatekeeper is asleep in the sun on the step, a small smile on his face, the gate wide. He has died, peacefully, in the night. You sit beside him till the monks find him, and ring the bell.
You close the gate, the way he would have, with a gentle hand. The monks find it shut and wonder, and the gate, thereafter, never squeaks.

events.text: A message from {sect}, written as a prayer but plainly a joke: 'O mighty one, we have grown fat on your blessing, and the abbot's trousers no longer fit.' It is signed by every monk, in a different ink. There is a second page, with a drawing of the abbot. The abbot is aware of it. The abbot has, in fact, drawn the picture himself.

choices.text: Send a blessing for the trousers

effects.log: You send a small gift of linen, in a dream, to the abbot's wardrobe. It is a good fit. The sect's relationship with you is, thereafter, a happy and slightly irreverent one.

choices.text: Send a gift for the whole monastery

effects.log: You send a gift of cloth to every monk. They are all, for a month, in new robes, laughing, lighter than they had been in years.

events.text: The last prayer from {sect} before the winter is the shortest you have ever received. It is just one word, repeated twice: 'Home. Home.' It is not clear whether they are asking to go home, asking you to come home, or merely saying it. It echoes, a little, in the cold stone of your hall, and then there is silence.

effects.log: You answer with a single word of your own, across the clouds. It reaches them as a warmth in the fireplace. They sleep well that winter. You, in your hall, find that you have been humming a tune.
You descend, as a breath of warm air, to the old gate, and walk the courtyard. The snow does not melt where you step. The monks do not see you. A single one, passing, shivers, and smiles.

events.text: The Throne of {b3_order} was built for a body of a certain size, and you are not that size. The seat is too high, the arms too wide, the footrest absurd. The heralds are too polite to mention it. You sit in it for a week with your feet dangling. It is, on the whole, easier to rule, you find, from a position of slight discomfort.

effects.log: A cushion appears, of an ancient design, and fits. It is the Throne's first cushion in nine thousand years. The old throne creaks happily.

choices.text: Sit in it just as it is

effects.log: You sit as it is. Visitors stare at your feet and are humbled. It becomes the Throne's quiet joke, that its occupant has never once been comfortable, and has never once complained.

events.text: The first question of the Trial Before the Hall is: what are you? A herald with a ledger waits, quill raised. Under you the floor shows every answer you have ever given a worshipper, a little dimmed.

effects.log: You say what you are, in six words, and the quill scratches once. It sounds like a verdict, and you realise it is merely a note.
You answer for a quarter of an hour. The herald waits it out, then writes the six words you should have said.
The quill stops. It is the first time in four hundred years anyone has asked. The herald writes that down instead.

events.text: In the year of the Trial you are made to keep a lamp lit in the dark antechamber, and not told for whom. Gods file past all year without looking at it. Everyone knows the lamp is the trial. Nobody knows what it measures.

choices.text: Keep it bright and say nothing

effects.log: You trim the wick every night for a year. By the end you know the shape of every shadow in the antechamber, and they have started to know you.

choices.text: Light a second lamp beside it

effects.log: The second lamp is allowed to stand. A very old god pauses there, and for the first time that year someone looks at your work.

choices.text: Ask a passing god what it measures

effects.log: The god says, "How long you will sit with a thing that does not thank you." It is the kindest hint you will receive.

events.text: To pass the Trial Before the Hall you must answer one real prayer from below, in front of examiners. The one chosen is from a fishing village, and asks for nothing very large: that a boy come home from the sea. The examiners watch your hands.

choices.text: Calm the water for one night

effects.log: The tide lies down like a dog. A boy is carried in at dawn, furious and alive. The examiners note a slight overreach, and let it pass.

choices.text: Send word through the villagers instead

effects.log: A rumour reaches the shore before the storm does, and everyone is home by dark. The examiners call it elegant and a little mean.

choices.text: Tell the examiners the prayer is too small

effects.log: There is a long silence. You have just told the pantheons you outgrew a fishing village. Several of them find that very funny.

events.text: A gold scale stands in the hall of the Trial, one pan holding every offering ever made in your name. The other pan is empty. A herald says you may place one thing in it. The scale is rumoured to be bribable. The herald says that this too is a test.

effects.log: The pan sinks a hair, from the weight of your not cheating. A herald marks something in the ledger without looking up.
The scale hums and settles level. Gods much older than you lean in, because nobody has offered that in a while.
The scale is bribable. It also tells the herald at once. You are fined an afternoon of silence.

events.text: A rival candidate sits the Trial beside you: a shy storm-spirit of no family who has had to borrow even their robes. The examiners are plainly not fond of either of you. The spirit whispers that they have forgotten the second verse of the Opening Hymn.

effects.log: You murmur it under the herald's nose. The spirit sings, you drop the third verse by accident, and both of you are glared at fairly.
Their voice cracks at the second verse. You pass the Trial slightly more easily, and think about it often in the centuries after.
You sing it together. The examiners cannot decide whether this is cheating or hospitality, and the debate lasts so long that both of you are let through.

events.text: The Trial Before the Hall includes the Hour of Quiet, in which the hall asks you nothing at all. For a god used to being prayed to every second, it is an ordeal of a gentle kind. Somewhere far below, a hundred thousand prayers go unanswered by you.

choices.text: Sit through it, praying for your worshippers

effects.log: You listen for the whole hour, and the prayers come in like weather you are finally standing out in. It is a little like being forgiven.
You answer a farmer's prayer for rain mid-quiet. A herald coughs. Your pass is marked with a small, patient asterisk.

choices.text: Make up a hymn to fill the silence

effects.log: It is a terrible hymn. An examiner hums it on the stairs afterwards and then pretends not to have.

events.text: One of the halls does not question its candidates. It remembers them. A hooded herald reads aloud everything you were ever small enough to be ashamed of, and then asks if you would like any of it struck out.

effects.log: The herald nods slowly. "Then it is yours," they say, and it is, a good deal lighter.
It goes, and a draught of cold air takes its place. You will wonder for a thousand years what it was.

choices.text: Ask who else is on the list

effects.log: The herald allows a faint smile. "Everyone. Mostly they strike more." You are marked down as honest, which is the worst kind of memorable.

events.text: In one trial hall there are no walls and no shadows, and nowhere to stand where you are not being watched by gods of war. The examiners ask you to take a pose that means nothing, and hold it. You are told the rest of the trial is already underway.

choices.text: Hold it, still as a banner

effects.log: A day passes, then a season. The gods of war stop looking at your pose and begin looking at you, which is worse and better.
The hall goes tense. A very old god laughs once: they have watched ten thousand statues, and you are the first to move.

choices.text: Take a pose so absurd they must react

effects.log: A god of fire has to leave the room. You are asked to step forward afterwards, and the examiners are not entirely cross.

events.text: An assembly of the oldest gods gives no examination. They give you a seed and a patch of earth in a hall whose roof is the sky, and tell you to come back when you understand. The oldest sits cross-legged on the next patch, plainly waiting for a different answer from you.

effects.log: It sprouts in the fifth year, crooked. The old god asks why you did not straighten it. You say it had not asked. They nod.

choices.text: Plant it and sing to it

effects.log: The seed ignores the song for a century and then, apparently out of spite, becomes a fine tree.

choices.text: Ask what the seed wants to be

effects.log: The old god says that is the whole examination, and that you are the third in forty thousand years to ask it.

events.text: One trial is a hearing held in a gale. Three gods of weather shout their questions across the hall, and the winner is whoever is still standing and still audible at the end. Your robe has gone somewhere east.

effects.log: You are heard, barely. A god of thunder says you have a good chest and a bad argument, and writes both down.

choices.text: Say your answer quietly, and wait for the wind

effects.log: The gale drops for a moment, as if it were curious. Three gods lean in. It is the nearest thing to respect the hall has.

choices.text: Ask them to stop the wind

effects.log: They refuse. They also remember that you asked, and one of them will bring it up for a thousand years.

events.text: You are given a scroll sealed with seven seals and told it holds the answer to the Trial. It does not. It holds the question, in a hand you recognise as your own, from some life you have not yet lived. The examiner who handed it over pretends to look at the ceiling.

effects.log: It asks, "What did you do with the first prayer?" You think of one, and write the answer in the margin, and the scroll closes itself.
The examiner takes it, and is oddly relieved. "Most break them," they say. It is marked in your favour or against, you cannot tell.
It burns with a surprised sound. The hall decides you are either very brave or very dull, and decides to find out which.

events.text: A doorkeeper of the hall, ancient and unimpressed, tells you that the trial gate opens at the one hour no candidate expects, and that the hour changes with whoever stands at it. They have kept the same door for three thousand years, and have views about candidates.

choices.text: Sit by the door and wait

effects.log: You wait, and the doorkeeper pretends not to see you. After a season they offer you a stool.
They listen to all of it with a face of stone, and ask for the second verse at the end of the week.
The doorkeeper opens it at once, to your great surprise, and says, "That is not the hour." You have lost nothing but pride.

events.text: The doorkeeper of the hall remembers you. They have kept your stool by the gate, polished, and quietly moved it closer to the warm side of the antechamber. They ask, not looking at you, whether the hall has been kind.

effects.log: The doorkeeper nods. "Fair is the best the hall does," they say, and press a small pebble of old altar-stone into your hand.
The doorkeeper sighs. "I know. I have been here three thousand years." It is the first time they have said so.

events.text: The doorkeeper of the hall has changed. A young spirit stands there now, a little too eager, who does not know your name. The old doorkeeper has gone to the dark between the halls, they say, and left only a note: "Keep the stool."

choices.text: Take the stool and put it back by the gate

effects.log: The young spirit looks at you in awe and some confusion. By the end of the year every candidate sits on it.

choices.text: Tell the young spirit about the old one

effects.log: You tell them everything. They write it in the hall's ledger, where nobody has put such a thing in an age.

events.text: The new doorkeeper at the hall has taken a dislike to you, politely, with forms. Your name is spelled wrong in the ledger on purpose. You are told that a decent candidate knows how to make an old gate open from the wrong side of its own error.

choices.text: Correct the spelling in front of the whole queue

effects.log: The queue stirs. The doorkeeper corrects it with a flourish and a long sigh. Everyone in line has now seen that rules can be moved.

choices.text: Answer to the wrong name until they notice

effects.log: You answer to the wrong name for a month. The doorkeeper gives in with great dignity, and a faint respect.

events.text: Among the examiners is a god who failed the Trial themselves long ago, and has spent every age since failing others. Their questions are built so that no answer can be right. They look at you with something very close to hope.

choices.text: Give the answer that cannot be right, with confidence

effects.log: The examiner stops mid-sentence. For a moment their whole face changes. Then it closes again, and they write something kind and unreadable.

choices.text: Refuse to play, and ask how they would answer

effects.log: They are furious, then silent, then they answer. It takes a very long time and is, honestly, very good.

choices.text: Answer as asked, and fail well

effects.log: You give a wrong answer that is at least wrong in an interesting way. The examiner approves of nothing, but notices.

events.text: The examiner who once failed the trial finds you in a corridor of the hall, years later, and says nothing for a time. Then: "Do you remember what I asked?" You do. They press a tarnished token into your hand. "I never got through. I would like it to have gone somewhere."

choices.text: Carry the token into the hall for them

effects.log: You carry it in your sleeve. It is warm. Whatever the examiner needed, they seem to feel it arrive.

choices.text: Tell them to try the trial again

effects.log: They laugh, a short bitter sound. And, a century later, you hear that they did.

events.text: Candidates for the Trial are supposed to wait in perfect composure. The antechamber has one bench, and on it a young god is sobbing quietly into a banner, having been told they are the fourth to be refused this age. Everyone is pretending not to hear.

choices.text: Sit beside them and say nothing

effects.log: You sit. After a while a weary herald brings two cups of cold dew and says nothing either. It is the best of the hall's hospitality.

choices.text: Tell them the trial is rigged and means nothing

effects.log: It does not help. It also is not entirely false. A herald hears and puts a small mark on your sleeve.

choices.text: Offer them your best lucky charm

effects.log: They take it, tearfully. It is not very lucky. It is, however, accompanied by real kindness, and that carries them through.

events.text: The Trial demands a formal robe, and you have none. A tailor-spirit offers to weave one from your offerings at the usual rate. The usual rate, you note, is somewhat above the worth of the offerings.

effects.log: It fits as if made by someone who has watched you for a long while. Perhaps they have. The cloth is faintly warm with other people's prayers.

choices.text: Wear your travel-worn robes with dignity

effects.log: The examiners say nothing about the robes. Two younger gods say a great deal. You are, quietly, remembered.

choices.text: Barter a song for the cloth

effects.log: The tailor-spirit sings it back for centuries to anyone who will stand still. The robe is excellent.

events.text: A herald at the trial gate has the awful habit of telling candidates which pantheon they truly belong to. Theirs is a rare talent, and nobody knows whether it is gift or malice. They look at you for a long time, and open their mouth.

effects.log: They name a pantheon. It surprises you, and then it does not. You think about it over the whole length of the trial.

choices.text: Ask them to keep it to themselves

effects.log: The herald nods, curiously grateful. They keep it, they say, in a small drawer, for any day you might want it.

choices.text: Tell them they are wrong, and dare them to say it twice

effects.log: They say it twice. The second time is much quieter, and a good deal more certain.

events.text: There is a long stair of cold water at the Trial, where candidates must wade up to the hall in front of everyone. The water is every doubt that was ever prayed at you, in liquid form. Today it is rather high.

choices.text: Wade through slowly, reading each doubt

effects.log: Some of them are very funny. Some are very sad. You know a few of the voices. You arrive at the top soaked, wiser, and more patient.
You come out gasping with a head full of other people's fears. The herald hands you a towel of sunlight.

choices.text: Dry it with a small flame

effects.log: It steams, and the whole stair is wreathed in prayer-vapour for an hour. The examiners, bemused, are impressed with the effect.

events.text: A candidate needs a sponsor, and yours, an old god of a fading minor domain, has arrived late, smelling faintly of incense and stale orchard. They spend a quarter of the trial praising the wrong person. When they notice, they simply continue to praise the right one a little louder.

effects.log: They glow with surprising delight. For a moment the hall is a fairly warm place.
They are mortified and then grateful and then, helplessly, they weep at the whole thing. You are the first to give them a clean copy in a century.
The examiners exchange looks. You have turned an embarrassment into a feast, and nobody is quite sure how.

events.text: On the last day of the Trial, a herald says there is no more to ask, and you may leave by the left door or the right. Nobody has told you which is which. The hall has gone very quiet and, by the look of the nearest god, rather interested.

effects.log: It opens on a long corridor of gods, each turning to look. You are being seen, in order, by all of them.
It opens on a small bare room with a table, two cups and an old god. "Sit," they say. "Now we can talk."
You do not leave. A herald says that is the third answer, and it is the rarest. You are given tea.

events.text: At the end of the trial the hall sets before you a mirror in which you appear as the god you will be in ten thousand years. The mirror god looks tired, and kind, and not especially like you. They look back with great interest.

effects.log: The mirror god tells you, briefly, and you do not forget it. It is not a prophecy so much as a warning, written gently.
They smile faintly. "Be kinder to the one in front of you," they say, which is not what you asked for and is what you needed.
The mirror goes dim. You will be, a little, the person in it regardless.

events.text: Word has got round that a candidate with your name is sitting the Trial, and the gallery is full of gods with nothing better to do. They have brought cushions. Someone is selling honeyed figs. The examiner asks whether you would like the gallery cleared.

effects.log: You perform under forty gods and an astonishing quantity of figs. Whatever you do, it is remembered by more people than usual.
It takes an hour, and a great deal of grumbling. The trial is quieter, and you are thought a little cold.
The gallery roars. An examiner throws you one. You will be known for it, fairly or not, for a thousand years.

events.text: The Revelations of {b3_order} are truths too large to be said, so they are sung. A cantor of the hall sings you one for a year. It has no words you can keep. It has a shape, and when it ends you find you have been holding a door open for someone for a very long time.

effects.log: The cantor winces and allows it. The shape in you stays, a little crooked, and it is yours.
There are none, says the cantor, but you may have the pauses. You take them, and they weigh more than you expected.
You keep it unspoken for a thousand years, like a coal in a closed hand.

events.text: The archive of {b3_order} is looked after by a very old spirit who has been dusting the same Revelation for nine thousand years and will not say whether it has changed. They hand you a cloth. "If you are going to read it," they say, "you may as well be useful."

effects.log: You dust a truth about the nature of sorrow, line by line. It is oddly restful, and you read it all, one line at a time, without noticing.
The spirit sniffs. You get through half of it and are, in truth, rather better for the dust.
"No idea," they say. "I have only ever dusted." Then, after a moment, "It is a very good surface."

events.text: A Revelation of {b3_order} may not leave the hall, but it can be copied on a single leaf of shed starlight. A young herald offers to smuggle out a whole chapter in a sleeve. They want only to be remembered kindly, and perhaps one favour in a thousand years.

effects.log: The herald nods, pretending relief. You read the chapter in the hall, as you should, and it is more than enough.
It glows in your sleeve for a century. One favour is owed, and it has a long and patient face.
It takes you three years, and you get a great deal wrong. What you get right is much better than the original, which the herald refuses to confirm.

events.text: Two Revelations of {b3_order} contradict each other flatly. The hall's scholars have been quarrelling over this for six thousand years, with great courtesy. You are shown both, side by side, and asked quietly which one you would keep.

effects.log: The scholars murmur approval, and then disagreement. You have joined a faction without a name.
A scholar gasps. You will have an enemy and a friend in this room for a very long time.
There is a silence like a held breath. A very old god says that you are the first to ask the question in the way that it was meant.

events.text: The shortest Revelation of {b3_order} turns out to be a lullaby. It is sung to the newest god of each age by the oldest. The vaultkeeper asks, with a great show of casualness, whether you would mind singing it to them. They have waited a long time to hear it from someone else.

effects.log: They fall asleep in the vault, curled by the shelves, for the first time in seven centuries. The hall keeps a hush for the rest of the day.

choices.text: Ask them to sing it to you

effects.log: They do. It is dreadful and perfect. You remember the tune for ages, and never the words.
You copy the notes onto your sleeve in thread. It will come in handy, one day, to someone.

events.text: One shelf of the Revelations is closed with a seal marked "Not Yet", in the hand of a god long vanished. The vaultkeeper says it has been that way since before the hall. They say, almost to themselves, that the seal is looser than it was.

effects.log: The vaultkeeper looks relieved. The seal, you notice on the way out, is the only thing in the hall that is warm.
There is nothing to hear but a very faint sea. You stay until your knees ache, and the sea comes with you.
The vaultkeeper says "Someone who knew you would ask." They do not smile. It is quite the longest conversation they have had with anyone.

events.text: A scribe in the vault of {b3_order} has been copying the same Revelation by hand for eight hundred years, and makes a mistake in each copy on purpose, so that no copy may be mistaken for the true one. They show you the latest mistake with some pride.

effects.log: You find it in a quarter of an hour. The scribe is delighted and a little crestfallen, and offers you the best seat in the hall.
They flush with pleasure. It is, they say, a fine one. For a hundred years afterwards you will find mistakes of that exact shape in the hall, and they are all intended for you.
The scribe is aghast. You have restored the Revelation to perfect truth, and the scribe has to start again. You are not forgiven for decades.

events.text: A Revelation of {b3_order} is said to feed on those who read it too hungrily. A cautious vaultkeeper suggests you read only a page a month. You have, as gods go, no patience at all, and the page is the most beautiful thing you have ever seen.

effects.log: It takes you forty years. You are rather unbearable about patience for some time afterwards, and rather wise.

choices.text: Read it all in a night

effects.log: You are hollow for a week and radiant afterwards. The vaultkeeper says nothing, in a very loud way.
Two readers carry the weight between them. It is lighter, and the other reader becomes, curiously, a friend.

events.text: The cantors of {b3_order} are in dispute over how a certain Revelation should be sung: slow, as the founders sang, or quick, as the founders' founders did. They look at you, a visitor to the vault, as the nearest thing to a neutral ear.

effects.log: The slow cantors beam. The quick cantors accept it with grace, then quietly begin practising at night.
The quick cantors cheer. The Revelation, thus sped up, turns out to be funny, and the slow cantors are never quite the same.
The result is a dreadful noise that somehow explains the whole thing. The cantors are speechless for the first time in an age.

events.text: One page of a Revelation of {b3_order} is always damp, and nobody can say why. The vaultkeeper has tried drying it and burying it. You touch it, and for a moment it is very cold and smells of a particular sea.

effects.log: The vaultkeeper says, after a long pause, that it was once a god's grief. They ask you not to tell anyone.
The page dries. The vault is lonelier afterwards, and the vaultkeeper tells you so, very politely.
You put it back damp. The vaultkeeper breathes out. Something in the hall settles.

events.text: The vaultkeeper of {b3_order} says that a Revelation was left unfinished by its author, who stopped in the middle of a sentence and went away. They ask whether you would be willing to finish the sentence, in your own voice, for a year.

effects.log: You spend a year over one sentence. It grows into a paragraph, a page, and a small honest argument with yourself.
The vaultkeeper tells you what the author was like. It is the longest story they have told, and it will not leave you.
The vaultkeeper nods as if they had expected it. They put the page back on the shelf, very gently, and say nothing of it again.

events.text: Years on, the vaultkeeper of {b3_order} tells you that your finished sentence was read aloud at a gathering of the hall, once, without a name on it. It was quoted by a young god in a speech about a quarrel. Nobody has asked who wrote it.

effects.log: You say nothing. The sentence goes on being used, unsigned, like a path across a field.
You say it is yours. The hall is startled, then cheerful. The sentence, signed, is a little smaller than it was.

events.text: A long time after the unfinished sentence, the vaultkeeper of {b3_order} is gone. In their place on the shelf is a note: "I have gone to find who wrote the rest." Your finished page is sewn, with great care, into the binding of the book.

choices.text: Keep the page where it is

effects.log: It stays in the book. Readers a thousand years hence will think the author finished it themselves, and be quite right.
You write one line more, in small letters, and sign it with a mark only you know. It is, you suspect, the first of many.

events.text: The vaultkeeper of {b3_order} has gone, and in their place on the shelf is a note: "Someone signed my unfinished page." You are asked, kindly and in writing, to come and explain. The hall has put a small, dry chair in front of the shelf.

effects.log: You tell it. The new vaultkeeper listens, makes a note, and decides the signature may stay. It is the mildest thing about the day.
They say that gifts must be given by somebody. The matter, left there, will sit between you for a century.

events.text: There is a hall in the vault of {b3_order} where nobody has spoken for a thousand years, on principle. A very old herald hands you a slate. You are free to write anything, if you must, but writing is considered a form of noise.

effects.log: The herald notes it with approval and pours you tea in silence. You have never understood a room so well.
You write one word. The herald reads it for a very long time, and rubs it out, and smiles. It was the right one.
The herald makes a sound like a kettle, and spends several minutes recovering. Several scrolls shiver on their shelves.

events.text: A Revelation of {b3_order} is not a text but a memory: a former god of the pantheon lived through it, and left it sealed in a jar for the next to open. The jar is warm. A herald warns that you will be, for a year, someone else.

effects.log: For a year you remember a harvest you did not bring in and a love you did not have. You are not quite the same, ever again.
It is warm in your hands for a whole day. The herald approves of that more than they say.

choices.text: Give it to someone who needs it more

effects.log: You give the jar to a grieving young god, who weeps and thanks you. The hall decides to remember that you did.

events.text: In the Revelations of {b3_order} there is a bowl of still water that shows, to each reader, the one question they have not asked. It has shown the vaultkeeper the same question for four thousand years, and they have still not asked it.

effects.log: It shows you a question. You ask it aloud, once, and the water ripples like a bell.

choices.text: Ask the vaultkeeper what theirs is

effects.log: They go very still. "Perhaps one day," they say. Perhaps; you lay a hand on their sleeve, and they allow it.

choices.text: Cover the bowl with a cloth

effects.log: The water is stilled. The vaultkeeper almost smiles. Some questions, they say, want a night to themselves.

events.text: The vault of {b3_order} keeps a Revelation for each rank, and the one for {b3_rank} is, you find, a good deal shorter than the rest, and written in an oddly informal hand. It says: "It will be harder than it looks. It will also be funnier."

effects.log: You read it three times. Over the next thousand years it is, to your continuing annoyance, completely correct.
It is much longer. It is also, in one place, a recipe for a very good soup.

choices.text: Ask the vaultkeeper who wrote it

effects.log: They say "a predecessor". They add, "A tired one." It is the best answer you could have had.

events.text: Reading in the vault of {b3_order}, you find a margin note in a hand you almost recognise, disagreeing very rudely with the Revelation. It is the best argument you have read in an age. There is a second note below it, politely refuting the first.

effects.log: You write a third note. The vaultkeeper reads it, and cries out, softly, and says the argument has not had a third voice since before the war.

choices.text: Read all the notes in order

effects.log: It takes you a year. By the end you know three dead gods quite well, and are fond of all of them.
The vaultkeeper catches you at it. The look is unforgettable. You are not trusted with a pen for a century.

events.text: Reading in the vault of {b3_order} is done by a candle of consecrated wax that burns exactly one Revelation long. The chandler hands you a stub of unusual size. "That is yours," they say. "I measured you when you came in."

effects.log: It burns your whole reading and then, to the chandler's surprise, goes on a little longer. You finish a sentence by its light that you did not know was yours.
The chandler sniffs. "You have the length you have." You are given the same stub, with a bit of added grace.
The candle sits on your shelf for ages, unlit, giving off a faint hum. Some days you can almost read by it.

events.text: You find, hidden in the vault of {b3_order}, a Revelation that has been struck from the register, but never burned. It is about forgiveness, and an awkward one. The vaultkeeper says, without looking, that it is not in the vault.

choices.text: Read it quickly and put it back

effects.log: It is awkward. It is also true. You carry it out in your mind, and for years afterwards you are unaccountably gentle with the guilty.
You put it back. The vaultkeeper, who was not looking, gives a very small nod.
It is discussed for decades. It is returned to the register, with a long apology for its absence.

events.text: In the vault you find {b3_peer} of {b3_order} already reading the one Revelation you came for, and plainly in no hurry to finish. They look up with the look of someone who has been caught in a private kindness.

effects.log: You read the same page, a line apart. By evening you have argued three times and agreed on one thing, which is the best thing in the book.
They sigh, finish, and leave. You remain with the book, and the warm place on the bench where they sat.
You wait for a month. When {b3_peer} emerges, they are strangely different, and will not say how.

events.text: You expected the Revelations of {b3_order} to be vast. The one you are shown is small and simple: a few lines about doing the next right thing when the large thing cannot be done. The vaultkeeper says it is the most requested. Most readers hide the fact.

effects.log: It is not large. It is, however, never again out of your reach.

choices.text: Copy it out for a friend

effects.log: You copy it out carefully. A friend in far trouble finds it in their sleeve a year later, and writes you three words.
The vaultkeeper gives you one, and watches you try to carry it. After a decade, you ask for the small one back.

events.text: A Revelation of {b3_order} floods the vault whenever it is read aloud: a slow tide of memory, at ankle height, of the first age. The vaultkeeper has bought many pairs of waterproof slippers. They offer you a pair, and ask you to read quietly.

effects.log: The tide hardly stirs. You walk home with your slippers dry and your head full of an old, gentle ocean.
The tide goes knee-high. The vaultkeeper holds the shelves and weeps with joy and fury at once. It is the greatest day the hall has had in decades.
There are fish now, in the vault. They listen with surprising politeness. The vaultkeeper adopts one.

events.text: The vault of {b3_order} is opened to you one shelf further than to most. The vaultkeeper says it is not because you have earned it but because the previous reader of that shelf has asked, in a letter from far away, that it be you.

effects.log: They tell you a name you have heard in a different life. You read the shelf with a hand on your chest.
The letter takes a century to arrive. The reply, when it comes, is very short and very warm.

choices.text: Read the shelf in a day

effects.log: You read it all in a day, and are both lighter and more tired than you have been in a long time.

events.text: The Silent Hall keeps its Revelations by forgetting them on purpose, so that each reader must recall them. The vaultkeeper hands you a blank book. "It is all in there," they say. "You will see it when you remember."

effects.log: Years pass. Letters appear on the pages, slowly, in a hand you know. It is yours, from a long way ahead.

choices.text: Write what you think it says

effects.log: You fill it with your guesses. The vaultkeeper reads them with respect, and says three of them are right.
They take the book, hum a verse, and give it back. The verse is on the first page, in your hand, in ink that is still wet.

events.text: The Throne of Storms sings its Revelations as thunder, and a reader is meant to stand under it. The cantor lets you into the roofless vault for a storm that has lasted since before the throne. Your teeth ring. It is, you decide, rather beautiful.

choices.text: Stand under it with your arms up

effects.log: The thunder says something enormous. You understand perhaps a fiftieth of it, and that fiftieth is yours for ever.

choices.text: Shelter at the wall and listen

effects.log: You hear it all, a little muffled. The cantor, soaked, nods. Learning in comfort, they remark, is also a way to learn.
The storm pauses, offended or curious. Then it answers you, in your own key.

events.text: The Will of Heaven reads its Revelations in full light, so that nothing is hidden. A very bright cantor stands you before a mirror-wall and reads it all at once. You are asked afterwards what you saw, and you are fairly sure you saw yourself.

effects.log: The cantor nods. "That is the Revelation," they say, "and it is the only one we have."
They smile. "That is also a Revelation. Rarer." You are taught the second reading in the evening.

choices.text: Ask them to turn down the light

effects.log: They do, a very little. The pantheon has made a note of it, as a concession to the mortal in all of us.

events.text: The Green Assembly's Revelations are not read, they are grown: a vine of old truths up a wall of the vault, picked by the season. The vaultkeeper cuts you a sprig and asks you to eat it, and not to be frightened by what it tastes of.

effects.log: It tastes of the first rain you ever answered. You weep a little, and the vaultkeeper pats your shoulder with a leaf.
You plant it, and the vault gains a vine that climbs, over the age, to your own door.
You give it to a passing minor god, who is changed by it. They never say how. The vaultkeeper looks very pleased.

events.text: Inside {b3_foe} you have been given a face, a minor domain nobody wants (the Third Draught, of Stairwells) and a rank low enough to be ignored. Within a week you have learned that being ignored is a mighty privilege. Everybody tells the stairwell god everything.

effects.log: You note it all, in a hand like a bad drawing of a tree. The stairwell has more secrets than the throne room.
You keep your cover and your conscience, and bring home only a few things. They are the right ones.
The stairwell god is, by the end, much loved. You tell your own hall less than you meant to, and sleep better.

events.text: The kitchens of {b3_foe} send up a plate of offerings every evening, and it is remarkably good. You are sent to fetch it, over and over. The cook, a minor spirit of ovens, asks nothing about you, and gives you a second helping each night.

effects.log: The cook tells you a great deal, and none of it was for the hall. You carry home the recipe and keep the rest.

choices.text: Ask the cook too many questions

effects.log: The cook gives you a sidelong look and a smaller portion. You have learned something, and been noticed.

choices.text: Take notes on the food only

effects.log: Your report is eleven pages long and entirely about pastry. It is the most useful thing the hall ever received from you.

events.text: You find, in the robes of a senior god of {b3_foe}, a letter that was never sent. It is to a god of {b3_order} that they once loved, and it is exceedingly kind. It would be a very effective weapon in the wrong hands. It could be a gift in the right ones.

effects.log: You slip it back into the robes. The senior god finds it, goes pale, and looks, thereafter, rather more kindly at you.

choices.text: Deliver it to the one it was meant for

effects.log: It takes nine years to arrive. The answer takes ninety. You are told, much later, that it was the start of a very long peace.
You keep it in a locked box, and never use it. It is a long-lived guilt, and a hall of its own.

events.text: The gods of {b3_foe} have a hymn of greeting that you must sing every morning, in tune, with real feeling, to keep your cover. You find it moving. You find it, in fact, rather better than the hymn of {b3_order}. This is very awkward.

effects.log: You carry it home in your throat. A song is hard to count as treason, but you wonder.
The choirmaster winces daily. You keep your integrity and lose most of your standing.

choices.text: Teach it to your own hall

effects.log: The hymn passes through {b3_order} like a cold, and by the next age it is theirs. Nobody remembers where it came from.

events.text: In {b3_foe} you meet a god of your own age and rank who is, plainly, also a spy, sent by a third hall. You recognise one another in a week. You do not say anything for a year, and then, over a bad wine of stars, you both do.

effects.log: It is the most honest year of your life. You each learn something real, and owe each other a great deal.

choices.text: Agree to say nothing of each other

effects.log: You keep one another's counsel to the end. In an age, one of you will have occasion to be glad of it.
It earns you merit and a crushing silence from your own conscience. The other spy is taken in the spring.

events.text: The only way to see the great ledger of {b3_foe} is to be on the night watch, in the cold archive, alone, with a lamp. The watchmaster has set a trap in the form of a very comfortable chair. You see the chair, and the ledger, and the lamp.

ok.log: You read all night without sitting, and are home before the watch changes. It was a good ledger.

fail.log: The chair creaks even though you did not touch it. You flee with half a page and a sprained ankle.

choices.text: Sit in the chair and read from there

effects.log: The chair is the trap, but its trap is only comfort. You sleep through the hour and wake to a polite cough.

choices.text: Leave the ledger and read the room

effects.log: You learn which gods the lamp has been lit for, and by whom. It is not in the ledger, and is worth more.

events.text: After a year, the gods of {b3_foe} give you a place at their long table, as one of their own. You are asked, very gently, to pledge. They mean it, and that is the horror of it. A pledge made under a false face is a very strange thing to carry.

choices.text: Pledge and mean part of it

effects.log: You pledge to the table, not to the hall, and it holds. You will feel the weight of that half-truth for an age.

choices.text: Refuse the pledge, saying you are not ready

effects.log: They accept this with a patience that makes you ashamed. You were, in a sense, truthful.
Your voice is perfect. The table cheers. You carry back the whole of their trust, and you will have to decide what to do with it.

events.text: Disguised as a lamp-trimmer in {b3_foe}, you are given the quiet task of tending the prayer-lamps in a hall that sees many visitors. The lamps tell you everything: who prays, how often, for what. Prayers are the real ledger. You alone can read the soot.

choices.text: Read the soot for the hall

effects.log: In a year you know the pantheon's fears better than its own members. It is a great gift, and an ugly one.
You answer, anonymously, a few of the smaller prayers on your own account. {b3_foe} is the better for it, and does not know.

choices.text: Trim the lamps and nothing else

effects.log: You are a very good lamp-trimmer. The hall of {b3_foe} brightens, and the visitors are grateful.

events.text: A god of {b3_foe}, wounded by some quarrel of their own, falls at your feet in the corridor. Nobody is about. You know their face from the reports; they are a dangerous enemy of {b3_order}. They look up and do not know that you are a spy.

effects.log: They never forget it. In an age, when the war is bad, they will remember a stranger who was kind.
Someone else comes, shortly. You tell yourself it was prudence. It was a little prudence.

choices.text: Question them while they are weak

effects.log: They tell you everything, as the wounded do. You carry it home with a taste like old coins in your mouth.

events.text: In the rival hall of {b3_foe} you are given a bed in a long dormitory of newly minted gods, and every night one of them talks in their sleep. They are a young god of the harvest, homesick for a village, speaking its name. You are the only one who hears.

choices.text: Write the name down for the hall

effects.log: It is a good piece of intelligence. You feel, writing it, a faint nausea you cannot account for.

choices.text: Sit with them till they wake

effects.log: You sit up with a stranger and an enemy, and neither of you mention it. They are never quite as lonely again.

choices.text: Ask in the morning where it is

effects.log: They tell you about a village of beekeepers, and you spend the year learning about bees. It is excellent cover.

events.text: A senior god of {b3_foe} takes you aside and says, quietly, that they know what you are. They have known for a month. They want to talk, they say, and not to a hall: to someone who has seen both of them from the inside. They suggest a walk on the roof.

effects.log: On the roof, in the cold, they tell you what they want. It is not what you thought, and not simple.
You report it to your hall. It is, you are told, a very good catch, and a trap you may have just sprung.
They shrug, kindly, and let you deny it. You will be tailed by an invisible courtesy for the rest of the year.

events.text: The senior god of {b3_foe} sends word that they would like to see you again, on the roof. They have, they say, something to give you: a list of every god in your own hall who is also, quietly, in the pay of {b3_foe}. They ask nothing for it.

effects.log: You take it. It has three names on it you have trusted for ages, and one you have not thought of at all.
They fold it away. "I did not think so," they say, and seem pleased, and more worried for you.

events.text: Now the list is in your sleeve, and your own hall has begun to look at you strangely. You can use it to purge them; you can warn them in private; you can burn it. The senior god of {b3_foe}, you notice, is waiting to see which.

choices.text: Warn the named ones in private

effects.log: Two of them are grateful. One is furious, one dangerous. The hall tightens, quietly, from within.
It is a triumph and a disaster. Gods are cast out; others begin to hate you; the senior god of the foe sends a short note of regret.
You burn it in a lamp. Nobody ever knows what you held. You carry the list, in memory, like a stone in a boot.

events.text: The ovens of {b3_foe} are kept by an old oven-spirit named Ember-of-the-Back-Stairs, who sees everything and says nothing. You are fed daily, and it is, quite plainly, the best food in any hall. They ask for one thing: that you never use what you learn at their table.

effects.log: You promise. It is an easy thing to promise and a hard thing to keep. The oven-spirit nods.
They shrug and feed you anyway. "Then eat," they say, "and be honest about it."
You promise with a smooth face. The oven-spirit watches you eat, and does not look at your face.

events.text: You have kept your promise to Ember of the Back Stairs through a whole year in {b3_foe}, and have, as a result, learned very little the hall can use. Ember hands you a pot of something wrapped in cloth, with a note that says "For the road home." It is the recipe.

effects.log: The hall of {b3_order} eats it for ages and never asks where it came from. You do not say. It is, in its way, a very good piece of spying.
