You leave the pot on the sill. Ember keeps it for you, and feeds the next spy from it, silently.

events.text: Ember of the Back Stairs knew all along, it turns out. Word reaches you, in the winter, that {b3_foe} has fed, scolded and thoroughly outwitted three generations of spies from your hall, and that your one was the best-fed. Ember sends no message; the oven simply goes cold at your name.

effects.log: It takes a decade to arrive. Ember, who cannot read, has it read to them by a young god, and the oven warms by one degree.
The silence sits in the corridor between your halls, and is noted by the cooks.

events.text: In {b3_foe} you are invited to attend the Naming of a new god, a ceremony closed to outsiders and very private. You are, tonight, not an outsider. The new god is trembling, and looks around the hall, and by chance meets your eye, and smiles.

effects.log: It costs nothing, and it is the only true thing you do all year. The new god never forgets that someone there was kind.

choices.text: Memorise every word of the rite

effects.log: You carry the whole rite home. It is a beautiful and ancient thing, and now, unforgivably, a secret you have stolen.
You tell yourself it was not yours to see. In the corridor you are surprised to find yourself weeping.

events.text: Leaving {b3_foe} at the end of your year in disguise, the gatekeeper stops you with a look. They say nothing. They lift the barrier, and touch their brow, in the way of one who has seen through a disguise, and decided to be merciful.

effects.log: You go. It is a mercy you will not forget, or repay, or tell.
They wave it off. "I did not see anything," they say, and look at the sky. It is a very good lie.
You leave a pebble of your own domain on the barrier. They keep it on their desk, to the end of the age.

events.text: Back in {b3_order} after your year as a whisper in a rival hall, you find that nobody asks what you learned. They ask whether you were afraid, and whether the food was any good. It is an oddly human homecoming.

effects.log: They listen with absorbed joy. For one evening the whole hall is a rapt audience for a story about dumplings.
They are quiet. A very old god says, "Then you were paying attention." It is the highest praise they have.
They listen, impatient, to a report on the doings of {b3_foe}. It is not the part you remember.

events.text: In the Silent Hall, spies are expected, and the hall keeps a quiet register of them. The god at its door, whose job it is to forget, tells you they have forgotten your face the moment you came. It is a courtesy. It is also, they say, a warning: you will be forgotten, as a god, if you stay.

effects.log: You leave and are, you realise, a little less remembered by your own hall than before. It is a fair price.
It is a strange year, in which nobody remembers you. You find it freeing and also unbearable.

choices.text: Ask them to remember one small thing

effects.log: They think for a long time. "A cup of tea," they say. It is the loveliest thing anyone has ever kept of you.

events.text: Spies are rare in the Throne of Storms; the weather gives them away. Every time you lie, a small cloud forms over your head. By the third week you are a leading attraction of the corridor. The gods are charmed, and decline to ask.

effects.log: The cloud goes away. You pass the year, as it were, in clear weather, and learn more than you did under cover.
The cloud becomes a storm, and a very good one. The gods applaud. You are given a medal for weather.
It follows you home, small and amiable, and rains lightly on the fields of your domain for ages.

events.text: In the Will of Heaven there are no shadows to hide in, and every spy is, as a matter of principle, seen at once. They give you a seat in the open hall, with a banner saying SPY, and treat you with unfailing politeness. The hall is determined to teach you something by it.

effects.log: You wear it all year. The gods of sky and war find this the most disarming thing they have seen, and tell you more than a hundred spies.
They pretend not to see the cloak. They do, however, see you, and treat you with the warm politeness of those who have won.

choices.text: Ask them what they want you to learn

effects.log: They tell you. It is not what you expected; it is, in fact, true.

events.text: A spy in the Green Assembly is greeted by a very old god of the harvest who tells you, kindly, that they do not mind a guest, and have always fed spies, and that you are welcome to the garden if you will help weed. It is, you suspect, the most effective interrogation you have ever met.

effects.log: You weed for a year. The old god tells you the history of the world, in passing, between beds of onions.
They shrug and put you at a table with a book. You get less out of it, and are kept more careful company.
A small row of your own domain's flowers comes up in their garden, and stays, and is one of the finest things in either hall.

events.text: The report you must write on your year inside {b3_foe} is read aloud in your own hall, and you realise, as you hear it, that you have left out the best parts. They are the parts about people. The hall wants a plan of attack. You have given them a portrait.

effects.log: The plan is thorough, cold and useful. You do not read it again.
The hall reads it in a profound silence. Then, unexpectedly, they begin to discuss peace.
You hand over two reports. The hall chooses one in the first hour, and the other in the last.

events.text: In {b3_foe} you wear a name tag, as every new god does, with your false name on it in a florid hand. By the fourth month you answer to it in your sleep. When the year is over, a herald asks what name you would like on your certificate of departure.

effects.log: The false name goes on the certificate. Years later you find it on a plaque in the hall, listing the unknown friends of {b3_foe}.
The herald looks up, startled. "I knew it," they say, almost to themselves. They write it with great care.
The herald nods, as if at a sensible answer, and stamps it. The certificate is, to this day, blank, and has been much admired.

events.text: On the last night in {b3_foe}, you stand at a window and watch the sea of stars the hall looks onto, and for once nobody is watching you. You realise that you will miss it. You realise, at the same moment, that you were never in danger, and that this is the more frightening thing.

effects.log: You stay. The hall thinks you very diligent. You know that you are simply avoiding home.
You go. The corridor is long. At the end of it the gatekeeper has left a lamp lit.
You write a letter, in your own name, that says nothing and means thanks. It is answered within the month.

events.text: Your copying of the mole-reports has stained your fingers with the ink of {b3_foe}, a peculiar blue that does not wash. For a year, wherever you go, you leave small blue prints. Everyone in {b3_order} has noticed. Nobody has said.

effects.log: It takes months and some of the skin. The stain fades, and your standing goes with it.
They are very fine gloves. They are also, by the end of the year, the subject of a poem.
You tell the hall exactly what happened. They are, to your surprise, delighted, and many bring you ink.

events.text: A choir of {b3_foe} practises every dusk under your window. They are dreadful. You find yourself, with real alarm, beginning to worry about their high notes. You have become the unofficial adviser to the choir, and are reporting nothing.

effects.log: By midwinter they are quite good. It is the finest service you ever rendered to an enemy, and you are proud of it.
They stay dreadful. You listen anyway, and are fond, and a little ashamed.
The choir is an excellent distraction, and you are in and out of five halls in the dusk. It is an undignified use of art.

events.text: A very old god of {b3_foe}, unmasked as a spy for your own hall long before you, comes to you in the corridor and says, in an undertone, "I was one of yours." They are the oldest mole in the cosmos. They have been there six thousand years and have, in truth, forgotten whom they report to.

effects.log: You smuggle them back to {b3_order}. They are, to everyone's surprise, treated as a hero and a little as a stranger.
They nod. "It is a good place," they say, "once you stop counting." They have, you think, chosen right.
They tell you in six sentences, the sum of six thousand years. It is, you think, the best report you will ever read.

events.text: The hall of {b3_foe} is kept by a tide, as all halls are, that comes in at the hour of prayer and out at the hour of rest. A spy learns that tide. You learn it. It teaches you, in a year, more about the foe than any ledger could, and much about yourself.

choices.text: Time your work to the tide

effects.log: You work with it, and with ease. In a year you are another feature of the hall, like the tide.
You exhaust yourself and gain a reputation for energy. You also, in a rough hour, are caught in a flood.
You pray with the hall at the hour of prayer. It is a lie, and you mean most of it.

events.text: You read the dossier {b3_foe} keeps on {b3_order}, and on you. It is full of mistakes, flattering ones. They think you taller. They think your temper is controlled. They credit you with an affair, and a very large plan.

effects.log: You leave a corrected copy on the desk. The next spy to read it will be baffled, and the foe a little more truthful.
You let them think you taller. It gains you, over the age, a small and constant advantage.
You add a sentence. It is a lie so lovely it is quoted in the foe's hall for generations.

events.text: You are the Throne-Bearer of {b3_order}, and {b3_oldhead} yielded it in front of everyone. The first thing you learn is that the Throne is uncomfortable. The second is that nobody has been told how to fix it. The third is that the hall is waiting for you to say something.

effects.log: You say five words. The hall applauds, mostly from relief. The chair is still uncomfortable.
You sit, and let the silence do the speech. It lasts an age, and is the best-attended event the hall has had.
Gods laugh in relief. A cushion is found, with a thousand years of consecrated embroidery on it, and the hall relaxes for the first time in a very long while.

events.text: {b3_oldhead} stays on in the hall after yielding, in a smaller chair, to the side, in the manner of one who is unsure what the rest of eternity is for. They watch you with a patient, not unkind face. The hall watches them watching.

effects.log: They give a great deal of it, mostly contradictory. You accept it all with grace. They are, for the first time in an age, delighted.

choices.text: Ask them to leave the hall

effects.log: They go. The hall holds its breath, and you feel, for years, the cold where they sat.

choices.text: Ask them to teach the young

effects.log: They agree, and the young adore them. You have turned a rival into a founder of something, and slept better.

events.text: The Throne comes with the Ledger of {b3_order}: every promise the pantheon has made to its worshippers, in eleven thousand volumes, many of them overdue. The Keeper of the Ledger hands you the first page with some ceremony and a clear look of dread.

choices.text: Read the first page and weep

effects.log: It is a promise to a village that rain would come. It came, but late. You pay what you can, in kind.

choices.text: Appoint a clerk to the task

effects.log: The clerk, a minor god of dust, is overjoyed. It is the first time they have had a promotion in six thousand years.
The ash rises over the hall in a slow blessing. It is, the Keeper says, the most honest thing the Throne has done in an age.

events.text: Envoys of every other pantheon arrive within a week, each with a gift, a speech and a hidden request. The gifts are lovely. The speeches are long. The hidden requests, laid side by side, contradict one another comprehensively.

effects.log: It is a sea of presents, and a sea of obligations. You will be a long time paying for them.
The envoys depart, mortified and relieved. You are marked as a god who cannot be bought, which is both a reputation and a target.
It takes a year. By the end you understand the entire world of the gods better than anyone who ever sat the Throne.

events.text: The first hymn sung to you as Throne-Bearer is badly written, hastily rehearsed and far too long. The choir looks terrified. The cantor, who composed it, has plainly not slept. They look at you as one looks at a judge.

effects.log: The cantor weeps with gratitude. You have bought a lifetime of loyalty for a small fib.
They shorten it, grumbling. It is a much better hymn, and you, to everyone's surprise, are right.

choices.text: Ask them to sing it again, to the end

effects.log: The choir sings it again, to the end. It improves in the second hearing, because you listened.

events.text: You wake in the first night of your seat to find a small god sitting at the foot of your bed. They are the Weight of the Throne, a minor spirit who has attended every Throne-Bearer, and tells each of them the same thing. They tell you, and it is very short.

effects.log: "You will be tired," says the Weight, "and it will be worth it, mostly." It is quite true.

choices.text: Ask them what they told your predecessor

effects.log: They tell you. It was, word for word, the same. It is a strange comfort.
They accept, astonished. In the morning the Weight is nowhere to be seen, and the Throne is slightly lighter.

events.text: A god of {b3_order} who contested the seat with you, and lost, comes to you in the dawn, and bows, correctly, and says nothing. They are very proud, and the bow is costing them. You can feel it cost.

choices.text: Raise them up and ask their counsel

effects.log: They stiffen and then, slowly, soften. They become, over the age, your best adviser and a quiet friend.

choices.text: Accept the bow and say nothing

effects.log: It is correct, and cold. You are a Throne-Bearer, and the cost of it is, as always, someone else's dignity.
They are startled. The hall sees it and is delighted. A good deal of old hurt, that day, goes quietly out of the room.

events.text: Your first decree as Throne-Bearer is expected within the month. The hall has drafted six for you to choose from, and they are all, as far as you can tell, about the arrangement of chairs. You suspect the gods of {b3_order} are afraid of you.

effects.log: The chairs are rearranged. The hall breathes out. You have achieved nothing, and made them very happy.
It is short, and about worship. The hall, in some shock, sets about carrying it out.

choices.text: Ask them what they actually fear

effects.log: They tell you, haltingly. You spend a year on it, and it is the best use of the Throne you will make.

events.text: In the first week a very small god, newly made and unclaimed, wanders into your hall and asks, politely, whether the Throne-Bearer would like a pet. They have a very large beetle. It is, they explain, their only friend.

effects.log: It lives on your throne arm for ages, and eats the more tedious petitions. The small god is promoted to the household.
The small god nods, brave, and goes away. You send a gift of leaves after them. The beetle has never been forgotten.

choices.text: Ask what the beetle thinks of the hall

effects.log: The small god translates. It has views. They are, in the main, correct.

events.text: The prayers of {b3_order} reach you now as a Throne-Bearer, every one, all at once. For a month you cannot sleep. You learn how many people are asking for the same small thing. It is not very much. It is, you find, exactly everything.

effects.log: You answer the smallest first, and then the next. It takes years. It is the only way you can bear it.
The loud are served and the quiet starve. You know it, and you do it, and you will not forget.
You hand the lesser prayers to your heralds, and sleep eleven days. When you wake, the world has survived.

events.text: On the Throne you find a note under the cushion, from some long-ago Throne-Bearer of {b3_order}. It says: "It is not as important as it looks. It is more important than you think. Both are true. Be kind to the heralds."

effects.log: You pin it under the cushion again, and add your own beneath it, for the next.
The heralds are astonished. The hall, in a month, is the best-run in the cosmos.
Nobody knows. The Keeper of the Ledger shrugs. It is, they say, a very old note, and a very old kindness.

events.text: Your first walk as Throne-Bearer through the halls of {b3_order} is attended by a hundred gods who stand to attention, and one very young god who does not, being asleep. Everybody sees. Nobody moves. You have the whole of the hall's breath in your hands.

effects.log: You step round them, quietly. The hall learns something about you that no decree could have taught it.
They wake in terror, then relief, then gratitude. They are your devoted servant for an age.
The hall stiffens. The young god is mortified. You have made a point, and been, at last, a Throne.

events.text: A great cathedral of the pantheon, the oldest it has, has been closed for repair for four thousand years and the repairers have never reported. You are the first Throne-Bearer in an age to ask why. The head repairer, at the gate, looks guilty and very tired.

effects.log: It is a ruin, and a lovely one. The hall holds the first service in four thousand years in the rubble. It is superb.
It takes forty years. It is very good. The head repairer weeps, and so does the cathedral, rather.
You spend a year laying stone. It is the happiest of your seat, and nobody quite knows what to do with a Throne-Bearer in a hat.

events.text: At the feast for your taking of the Throne, the gods of {b3_order} propose toasts to you for a very long time. Each is a little more extravagant. By the ninth toast they are comparing you to the sun. By the thirtieth, they have forgotten it was meant to be about you.

effects.log: The hall hushes, then roars. It is a gracious thing, and a bit of a trick, and it works.
You leave. The toasts go on without you, and are, by all accounts, the best part of the evening.

choices.text: Propose a toast to the hall's servants

effects.log: It is a long toast, and a warm one. The heralds weep. The hall, for a season, is unusually humble.
